THE COMING ELECTION. Tune: " NAPOLLAS, TALKS OP WAS?' Unfold the true did flag, boys, Of justice, truth, and right. We oft have rallied to its call, And won in glorious fight. We've still our Grand Old Leader, Brave warriors in his train; He led us on and won, boys, And so he will again. "Home Rule" still holds the field, boys, So says the Grand Old Man. . _ -

We've waited long, but all in vain, To see their "better plan." None else can clear the stain, boys, From England's tarnished fame; The right has won before, boys, And so it will again. The day will soon be here, boys, How soon none here can say; But we must ready be for fight Whenever dawns that day. The victory must be ours, boys, We'll fight with might and main True courage won before, boys, And so it will again.
Runcorn.

At a ball one evening a plain country gentleman had engaged a pretty coquette for the next dance; but a gal- lant captain, coming itung, persuaded-the young lady to abandon her previous engagement in favour of himself. The other, hearing all that had passed, moved toward a .card-table, and sat down to a game of whist. The cap- tain. in a few minutes afterwards, stepped up to the young lady to excuse himself, as he was engaged to another he had forgotten. The coquette, much chagrined, approached the whist-'table, in hopes to secure her first partner, and said,, "'I believe, sir, it is time to take our places." The old-fashioned suitor, in the act of dividing thepack for the next dealer, courteously replied, "no, madam; I mean to keep my place. When ladies shuffle, I cut."

- ANT IN APAX.—The artistic Japanese -shows nothing in a room, absolute4y nothing, except a lovely flower and a screen, and perhaps a beautiful verse or some -clever sentence indited in freehand writing, placed beau- tifully in the room iii'just relation to its surroundings. . You would never know from the rooms of a Japanese that he was a great picture owner or collector. The wealthy collector keeps all his treasures stowed away in what is called a'"go-down"—his storehouse—and his pictures are brought up one at a time if any visitor is present or -expected. Generally speaking, a single pic- ture will be brought in and hung un. so that you see and enjoy that beautiful picture by itself. It is very much like bringing a bottle of wine from the cellar—no one would want the whole bin at a time.—The Magazine of A rt. . . . .

There resided a short time ago, in a thriving colliery village not a hundred miles from Gateshead, a person of the name of Lamb, blessed with a numerous family. One day they were all sitting round the table, preparing to dine off a sheep's head, which was the favourite dish of the master of the household. There came a knock at the door, and on one of the children opening it, the minister stepped in, with profuse apologies for calling at so unreasonable an hour but he was stopped short by

the father exclannina: "How way in, tnirsor ; thor's ne 'easion for onny o' them fal-de•rals. How way in, an' aa'll show thou the most wunnorful seet thoo's ivvor seed." " Why, Mr. Lamb, whatever can there be 2" asked the minister. " Wey, if thoo comes in, thou'll see twe aad lambs and a lot of young uns feeding on a sheep's heed r —Newcastle Chronicle. THE DERE AND Tan JEsma.—The jester used to be an . .
important personage in the household of kings and noblemen. Though it was part of their duty to.be . .

merry, and cause their master's time to pass pleasantly, the court jesters were generally shrewd fellows; and under the cover of their folly they offered advice and opinions, and even gave rebukes which would not have been taken from anyone else. This was the case with Charles the Bold's jester. Charles, Duke of Burgundy, was an ambitious and violent man, and often boasted that he would rival Hannibal as the greatest general of all ages. It so happened, however, that in 1476—the year before his death—the Swiss inflicted a severe defeat on him at Grandson. His fool was the Duke's partner in the flight from the battle-field. "Ah ! your Grace," was the jester's sage remark, "They have, for once, Hanniballed us ! "—Little Itolics' Magazine. CRAFT OF THE Fox.—A writer in Scientific Netc3 fur- nishes an interesting example of the craft of the fox. A tame fox that was kept in a stable yard had managed to strike up an acquaintance with several of the dogs, and would play with them, but the cats could not beinduced to approach him. Cats are very sensitive in their nos- trils, and cannot endure the vulpine odour. They would not even walk upon any spot where the fox had been standing,. and kept as far from him asyossible. The

crafty animal was not long in perceiving is repugnance on the part of the cats, and of making use of it to cheat them out of their breakfast. As soon as the servant poured out the cats' allcwance of milk Revnard would run to the spot and walk round the saucer, knowing that none of the rightful owners would approach the defiled locality. For several days this went on, until the strata- gem was discovered, when the milk was placed beyond his reach.
- MATTHEW ARNOLD'S " PHILISTINE."—A nineteenth-

, century "Philistine is the embodiment of what Carlyle called respectability with its thousand gigs," or as he elsewhere puts it, " gigmanity." But though Carlyle in- veighed against the class, he coined no word to define its members. Matthew Arnold introduced the term "Philis- tine" in 1865 as a translation of the German Philister, which is applied by students in Germany to all who are not, and never have been, members of a university. He protested against Carlyle's misuse of the word " respect- able "—a misuse of which Barham is also guilty in the lines:—

No doubt he's a very respectable man, But—l can't say much for his taste, which almost define a "Philistine "—and said "if the English are ever to have a word for the thing we are speaking of, I think we had much better take the term 'Philistine' itself. 'Philistine' must have originally meant, in the minds of those who invented the nick- name, a strong, dogged, unenlightened opponent of the chosen people. The representatives of the modern spirit regarded themselves, with the robust self-confidence natural to reformers, as a chosen people, as children of the light. They regarded their adversaries as humdrum people, slaves 0 routine, enemies to light—stupid and oppressive, but at the same time very strong." And so "Philistine" came 0 mean one whose ideas are material and commonplace as opposed to one who aims at a loftier ideal of intellectual life.—Cassell's Saturday Journal. WHAT Sds Trtoroity.—" How funny some people are," she said. "Funny?" "Yes, some people are going to be married." "Oh!" "Yes, some want to be married in a balloon, some on the middle arch of a bridge, some in a boat, some in a railroad train, some on horseback, some on the edge of a precipice, some down in a coal "Yes, I have noticed it." "What is their object, I wonder?" "Marriage, of course." "But I mean their object in getting married out of the usual way?" "Well, I'll tell you what I think. They get married in this way so that they can tell their children they were married under peculiar circumstances, as, for instance, Your mother and I, children, were married in a coalmine,' or 'Your grandmother and I, children, were married in a balloon.'" • "Perhaps that is the reason," said the maiden. "Of course it is the reason." There was a pause. Then the maiden with a glowing cheek, said, "I've been thinking, John." "Yes," he said, interrogatively. "I've been thinking how funny it would be—" (a pause and a deeper blush). "Well, B&la, you've been thinking what?" "I've been thinking how funny it would be if—" "Yes." "If when the subject of marriages comes up th.rty or forty years heme, you could point to me and say, Why, children, your grandmother proposed to me in leap year and we ,;:ere'married a few weeks later.'" John is very busy these days furnishing a nice little cottage, and Bella is *operintending the making of her wedding dress.— Vv ,k Journal. e .1. all kinds of domestic: sewing, Bagley and Wright sottoa is the best.—.Acivt.
THE GAS QUESTION.

Sir,—The question that is agitating, and very pro- perly agitating, the public mind at the present moment is the proposal of the Gas Committee to pay to Mr. Paterson' their retiring manager, what practically amounts to an annuity of ElAk. It seems to me that the matter is one which should not take long deciding. for I should think that, outside the Council Chamber, there is but one opinion about it—that such a thing should by no means be allowed. The argument that Mr. Haddock is either unfit for the post to which at a very fair salary it is proposed to appoint him, or that it is in reality inten- ded to pension Mr. Paterson, is to my thinking one that cannot be got over. If Mr. Haddock is capable, as I ' have no doubt he is, why on earth should someone receive £lOO a year for looking atter him and his affairs. ' The proposal is an insult to Mr- Haddock himself, as well as to the general body of ratepayers who pay the pipbr. I think, however, that there is not much fear of the Town Council sanctioning such a proceeding. There is another matter that I should like to mention. I have heard it said with some show of authority that some thousands year are wasted in consequence of leakages in the pipes. If that is so, how is it that some inquiry into such a de- plorable state af things has not been made. Surely the Gas Committee must know whether that statement is correct or not. If they don't know, it is time a radical change was made in some direction. It might be as well if-some of the money it would take to pension Mr. Pater- son was spent in sifting this mattes to the bottom, and remedying the evil.—Yours, fr.c. INDIGNANT. 'June 14, 1888.

div.head: TORY INTELLIGENCE!
div.p: TORY INTELLIGENCE!

bOine t dinner—to-day in the company of a Tory friend of mine, who is on the list of voters for Warrington, I casually mentioned the withdrawal of the compensation clauses by the Government, and asked his opinion as a Conservative on the question. To my utter surprise, for he is one who almost nightly visits the Con- serv,ative Club, he said he had never heard anything about the matter. He did not know there was such a measure before the House of Commons as a Bill for the extension of local government. In reply to my ques- tions, he admitted that he never read what he styled "the humbugging political news." He was never inter- ested in political matters except at election times, when he always voted Tory as his father had done before him. He knew nothing of Irish history. He did not know that Mr. Parnell was an Irish Protestant. He was under the impression the Irish were a lott, of lazy vagabonds, who, whenever they came into his shop, wanted one shilling's worth of goods for sixpence. His remedy for I,rish grievances would be "a long rope and short shrift's' Such, sir, is an instance of the dense ignorance by which those desirious of a just settlement of Irish claims are assailed. Well may there be a Tory majority in the town of Warrington! But let us hope for better things. There is abundant evidence that the country is getting heartily sick and weary of this Government by coercion. The Irish star is at present in the ascendant. Neither Papal Rescript nor Balfourism will move the Irish peo- ple one inch from the direct goal they have marked out for themselves, viz., self government. Sir, how often has the unanimous voice of this nation been raised against oppression and wrong, and in favour of human liberty? And yet we overlooked the Poland at our own doors. Let us be consistent, and remember that "For justice all place a temple, and all season sum- mer." Ours is a winning cause. We can afford to wait in patience 'for the consummation so devoutly to be wished; and when that time arrives we shall be a united kingdom indeed, united in the bond of acommon brother- hood, united in defence of our common country, united for the advancement of civilisation and liberty through- out the world.—;l am, sir,
FELIX HOLT.
THE COMPENSATION QUESTION.

Sir,—lt seems somewhat strange that you cannot even discuss the question of the licensing clauses of the Local Government Bill without pursuing your usual tactics of misrepresenting the Liberal Unionists. lam afraid the extinction of the Liberal Unionists, which you are in the habit of continually prophesying from time to time, is of more importance to you than even the passing of the licensing clauses. You accuse certain Liberal Unionists, with Lord Hartington in the chair, of taking into favour- able consideration the action of the present Government in giving compensation to brewers, rather than, as Mr. Gladstone puts it, run the risk of bringing in a Govern- ment that would give Home Rule to Ireland. Their de- gradation is, therefore, complete. Evidently what Mr. Gladstone swears, his supporters will do likewise, let the ends or the means be what they may. But the Union is safe; let your tactics be what they may. There are many Liberal Unionists who are strongly opposed to corn- .pensating the brewers, and who intend to do theirutmost to prevent it, through earnest conviction; and I fan vouch this much that there are many Conservatives also, who are opposed to its principle. But they are Unionists nevertheless, and will take good care that when this compensation question is settled that Mr. Gladstone will never again have the chance of introducing his late scheme of dismemberment. He did right to tell us it was dead. How could it be otherwise when none of his supporters were able to defend it. At the end of your leading article a fortnight ago you concluded with these words:—" Mr. Gladstone's plan holds the field." This quite stunned me, for I was not aware that Mr. Gladstone had a plan, seeing his other plan was dead. Well, now, if you are in possession of Mr. Glad.stone's new plan the best course for you to do is, seeing that you are so very anxious for the extinction 0f the Liberal Unionists, to produce the plan so that we can give it its serious consideration. Because we case- not again give him our support in the dark, upon such a vital subject as the unity of the United Kingdom, being left in his hands to settle without knowing what it is. The subject is too serious to be thrust upon us with a rush, It wants consideration, and now is the time. Mr. Gladstone and his supporters are very anxious to throw out the Government on the licensing daises, or any other question, just as he did when he spoke in favour of Mr. Collings's amendment to grant allotments, which threw out the then existing Government, and after com- ing into office again, threw overboard the interests of the agricultural labourers. Yes, if Mr. Gladstone suc- ceeds in overthrowing the Government on this question of Local Government, will he pledge himself to deal with the subject at once, or will he take the opportunity of thrusting his pet scheme of dismemberment before Par- liament before anything else. In conclusion let me ask you to explain how it was that when Mr. Gladstone was in power, that the reason he gave to Sir Wilfred Lawson when he introduced Local Option, for not supporting it was because it did not in- clude some reference to the principle of equitable com- pensation; and then we shall see who is the party of degradatlon2—l remain, yours respeotfully RADICAL UNIONIST.

THE COMPENSATION QUESTION. Sir,—ln your issue of the 2nd instant there is a letter signed" G. H.," and the author tells us he is a Scotch- man. He obiects to my Cockney quotation; and I regret I was not aware that a "Saint frae the Land o' Cakes" was about to reply to me, or I would have inserted one from his great national poet, entitled " Holy Willie's Prayer," which would have been prophetic, and have been so thoroughly descriptive of his style, as to have "checked his mad career," that is, if " exquisite sarcasm could penetrate his unsanctifieel armour." "G. H." says they are not accustomed in his country to read letters characterized by such beautiful frankness as mine are. Not now, perhaps, but in Burns's day it was usual to speak plain, especially when cant and in- justice reared their wicked heads. "G. H.," however, manages to brand me as a thief, which is good, coming from such a source, but it happens that I have not stolen anything, and have no wish or intention so to do whilst he is eager to do so, and on this showing, 1 fancy a jury would pronounce him, not me, the thief. In the fatuous blindness of these " unco guid " folk, and their yelping before they are hurt—fearing that they might have to subscribe to 'compensation for wrongs" barefacedly committed—lies the whole gist of their howling. They can't—because they won't—see that the publicans would have to find the compensation fund for themselves by paying an extra 20 per cent, on their licenses. They would make the nation good by Act of Parliament, and would ram down our throats their peti-

And the Scotchman and Welshman who have not seen this are hopelesslyiost to all chance of being convinced by actnal facts, and not chapel-going theories. div.head: TOWN COUNCIL AND THE RATEPATERS' ASSOCIATION.
div.p: THE TOWN COUNCIL AND THE RATEPATERS' ASSOCIATION.

Sir,—You will perhaps allow me to express a few opinions fromthe point of view of a burgess of the "good old town" with,regard to what took place sigt the .last meeting of the Town Council. I was glad to see that there was a pretty general opinion in favour of the motion of Councillor Henry Roberts, directed against the Gas Committee for privately entering contracts contrary to an express resolution of the Council, and think Coun- cillor Platt hit the nail very smartly on the head when he said that the resolution should apply to sales as well is to purchases. There is no doubt that a lot of things ip con- nection with Corporation matters might be done openly and above board that are now done privately, not to :say secretly—always "for the public interest" of course. "Mere light' ought to be the motto of municipal purists and reformers. Of course nobody suggests that Corporation officials and members of Corporation Com- mittees areany worse than other men, or that they have been "blessed " with a doublodose of original sin; but it has often been remarked that there is a wonderful amountef human nature in men, whether they be mein- hers of Town Council or servants of a Town Council. And besides, experience teaches us on every hand that , abuses and corruption of the most flagrant kind do creep lath Corporation affairs, generally throughthe supineness a.nd weakness of public representatives who do nOt like to say anything disagreahle. The best preventive of all this that has ever yet been discovered is the letting in of light into dark places; in other words the doing of all public business openly and above-board. The resolution which the Gas Committee treat so con- I temptuously has the effect of letting in light in one direr. tion, and I was consequently vastly surprised to see that the only councillor who said anything against the resolu- tion Nyasa" ratepayers' man," and! believe a member of the committee of the "Ratepayers' Association." It seems to me, sir, that the ways of Councillor Wright— the councillor alluded to—like those of the "heathen Chinee" are very peculiar. If I remember aright, it was not lone after his election under the auspices of the Rate- payers' Association, that Councillor Wright arose in his place in the Council and said he must be " loyal " to his Committee. Query, to /which Committee ? "Oh, to the Ratepavers'Committee, of course," I can imagine an unsophisticated ratepayer hastily reply. But, not so. It is true the Ratepayers' Association was formed in direct antagonism to the Sanitary Committee and its policy, and that Councillor Wright was elected under the auspices of the Ratepayers' Association. But, neverthe- less, so peculiar are the ways of town councillors some- times, when Councillor Wright said he was loyal to his Committee he did not mean the Ratepayers' Committee but the Sanitary Committee. The Ratepayers' Com- mittee in fact was the sucked orange. It had served its purpose and was then discarded. Imagine a person eleetedto Parliament under the auspices of a Home Rule Association, and directly afterwards getting ,up in the House of Commons and saying he must be "loyal" to the Anti-Home Rule Government in power. What a howl dindignant rage there would be throughout the country. But our local Ratepayers' Association is a humble body; in fact some people, in a rough, unfeeling, colloquial way, say it is a "fraud_" Ido not go so far as that. I merely say that in the opinion 9f some people ' it has served its purpose; it has got them into the Coun- cil and that's enough. It is the ladder they have climbed by, and now they would kick it down. To the members of the Association I would say if it is not to sink into contempt and to become a bye-word, they must assert themselves, and demand of their representatives in the council a support of the policy they were sent to re- present.
A BURGES3. P.S.—Perhaps it Is not necessary to explain that the "A" in my signature does not signify "Alderman." Warrington, June 12th, 1888.

UNITARIAN CBAPEL.—The annual sermons were preached in the above place of worship on Sunday after- noon and evening, by the Rev. C. C. Coe, of Bolton. There were good congregations at each service. The hymns were heartily sung by the choir and congregation, and Mr. John Holland, of Astley, presided at the organ, in the absence of Miss Monks, of Risley, through sick- ness The collections amounted to £l3 17s. .

CRIUST CHIITCH.—The annual sermons on behalf of the Sunday school and choir were preached in the above church, on Sunday morning and evening, by the Rev. T. W. Richardson, re6tor of Golborne. The prayers and lessons were read by the rector, the Rev. T. P. Kirkman. The services werei,full choral ;special hymns were sung, and the anthems were " Lift up your heads" and "Make a joyful noise." The collections amounted to £l2 ss. Mr. F. W. Ball was at the organ. BOWLING BANDICRP.—On Saturday afternoon, a bowl- ing handicap sweepstakes was commenced on the bowl- ing green at the General Elliot Hotel. The game was confined to residents, and the entries numbered 24, at an entrance fee of fkl each, to which was added Ll, given by the proprietor, Mr. R. Owen, junr. The prizes were divided as follows :-Ist, 16s; 2nd, les ; 3rd, es. The draw for partners having taken place, play was com- menced, but, owing to the rain, only seven pairs of players bowled, when the game was adjourned. The first round was played on Monday, the green being in splendidcondition, and the game will be continued each evening until the finish.

div.p: SA
BY SIGIL. (From the "Blackburn Times.")

tracluded.) When we got to the Wild West, which we did a little before six, we found the gates closed, and ascertained that we should have to wait until six before being ad- mitted to the camp, for which purpose we had come an hour early. Presently the gates were opened, when we at once secured tickets for the camp by paying sixpence extra.

We found, upon beipg admitted to the camp, that it was a large oblong *ooden building. It was very lofty and airy, and was well lighted. Along each of the sides a 'flooring of timber, a few inches high, was laid, upon which were rows of Indian tents, and tents for the cow- boys and vaqueros. In the middle of the floor was another raised flooring for two more rows of Indian tents. At the further end of the building, and in the centre, was a larrr and different shaped tent from the Indian tents, which, I was told by Buck Taylor, the king of the cowboy's' was Buffalo Bill's tent. The building was warmed by steam, and was very comfortable. When we got inside there was not a single person to be seen, except two or three visitors, who had got in just before us. There were odd bits of bunting here and there, principally the stars and stripes, hanging list- lessly from improvised staffs. Not a ripple or move- ment of either tent cloth or flag could be observed anywhere and not a sound could be heard except such as we and the other visitors made with our feet. This was a disappointment to me, because I had gone to Man- chester with a greater desire to see the Indians and cow- boys in their camp than I had to see their performance. I wanted to have a word with some of them, and I wanted to have a close view of Sitting Bull, the hero of Little Big Horn; he who massacred General Custer and the whole of his command. I thought for some time that there was no one in the tents, but, presently,a little elderly man came out of the tent nearest the door and went to a water tap for some water. He was a white, with longish grey whiskers, and was dressed in civilian clothes. Intercepting him as he was coming back, I said, "Excess me, but are the Indians not about just now?"
7-He- said, Oh, yes i they're inside the tents; but they are resting, 84 haying something to eat after the afternoon performance. Some of them'll be out in a bit." ,
I said, "Ire you one pf the company ?" He said," Yes; this 4 my tent," poutting to the first one in the centre.

"Might I ask who you are P' "Yes; I 11.113 John I)Telson." "A scout, I suppoke?" " Yes ; scout, guide, and trapper. I conducted Brigham Young and the Mormons across the desert to Salt Lake." I said, "Oh, indeed Then you have seen something of the Indians?"
" What me? Yes; I've seen so much of them that I married one, and haves family. But you must excuse me, I'm wanted inside." _

Upon further innpiry I found that this man had actually married a maiden of the Ogallala tribe, Chief Lone Wolf's daughter, and that he had six children, the results of the marriage. Walking up between the tents, I came across a young girl in a short frock, standing in front of one of the side tents, and behind the rope barrier, which ran round the place, to keep people from getting too near to the tents. i Accosting her, I soon engaged her n chat, and by a little dexterous questioning I elicited from her that her name was Lillian Smith, and that she was the champion rifle shot of California. She had a most charming manner of speaking, but, evidently, thought no small change of herself. She, however, proved herself to be as good as her reputation during the performance' later on. I had no sooner left Miss Lillian Smith, and was, along with Ted and Joe, walking across the raised centre flooring, in front of Buffalo Bill's tent, than I met a very tall man in a tvhite sombrero, buckskin breeches, leather leggings,snd a red slop or jersey. Accosting him, I said, "Excuse me, but will any of the Indians be coming out of theig tents before the performance commences ?'' _

"Oh, yes," said he, smiling, and with a little of the nasal twang peculiar to some Americans—" You'll see some of them knocking about directly. There goes one !" said he, pointing to the other end of the camp. I looked in the direction he indicated, but only just in time to see an Indian pop inside a tent. Offering him a cigarette, which be accepted, I said, "I suppose you are one of the company ?" He said. "Yes, I'm one who is generally known as Buck Taylor." "Then you're a cowboy ?" "Yes," said he, lighting his cigarette. "Well, you're a very fine boy, at any rate. They might safely call you a cowman, I think; that is, if your size has anything to do with it," I said. Laughing, he said, "That's all right; but we're all boys here except the redskins. But you must excuse me, I have some shooting-irons to attend to," and he went inside a tent near Buffalo Bill's wigwan. Buffalo Bill was absent. His wigwam was forsaken. I was very unfortunate with regard tePthe Indians for a considerable time, for I could not get to see any of them at close quarters. Sometimes one would pass from one tent to anotherl but it was sure to be at the other end of the camp to the one where I was. But they looked a tremendous size even at that distance, for they all had blankets which reached from their heads to their feet, and they held them in such a position that they made them appear, in stature, fully a foot taller than they really were. I had made up my mind that if I could get half a chance I would have some talk with one. At last I walked down to one corner where a young man was selling photographs of the noted characters in the show, and to my delight I saw an Indian leaning against a railing just behind, and off one side of the young man. I stood and took stock of the Indian for a few minutes to my heart's content, and I think he was about the ugliest cuss lever put my eyes on. Ho stood on one foot with the other foot resting against the calf of his leg. Like the other Indians I had seen, he had his blanket, which he kept close under his chin, and about his face. He had a look on his countenance which made me think that at some period in his life he had, in mistake eaten something which was intensely disagreeable, and had found out while he was eating it what it was, und that at that time he had assumed a disgusted look which he had never been able to get rid of. I asked the young man who he was, and he told me that he was a Sioux chief called Na-pa-na-wa-pa-he (Flies Above). I may be a little wrong in his Indian name, but I know I have the translation right. The young man showed me bis photograph, and I saw his name at the bottom. After contemplating the Indian chief for some time, I decided to speak to him. Looking him in the face, I said, "Good evening,Napanawapahe.' Looking at me with a pair of eves that seemed to be too heavy to lift, be said, "Ugh !" I said, "Are you like middling in health 2" He said, "Ugh !" I said. " Ugh !" He said, "Ugh !" I repeated, "Ugh !" camp, so then,l w He went inside the tent and came out with a toma- hawk in his hand, and said, "Ugh l" the bethoughtothbethoughter end o the mfe suddenly,that I withanoutetdretoplrintgo to Flies Above. I daresay he was disappointed, but I thought that if I stayed he might get into trouble, be- cause I felt a bit vexed. After my interview with Flies Above, I walked about the camp, that is about the other end of the camp, where I met with a man who was taking bottles of medicine round to those who were out of sorts. Being deter- mined to have some talk with some of the redskins, I asked him to point me out a chief. There were by this time several Indians standing and walking about. He pointed one out, who, he said, was called Wa-pa-ha-ha- no-pa-wa-cha-ho-nock (Man with the Dirty Shirt). I went to him, and, adopting tactics different front those I had practised upon Flies Above, I said, " So-pa-sa-so-ne- pa-no-na!" He said, " Winnehaha panohaho," and he put out his hand to shake. I shook it and said, " Sapolio nahepa sapoo." He said, " Sapelio zoedone." I replied, "Erin go bragho, multum in parvo," and I felt that my stock of Indian° was becoming somewhat exhausted and mixed uppo. He said, " Wis. pin tak o; su pe no." I said, " Wita u tako a cigaretto," for I felt that I wouldn't be the first to break down in foreign language, and I held out my cigarette case. He said, "I don't mind," and he took one. Finding that he spoke English, I said, "What is your opinion of the present condition of the red man as com- pared with his past ? Do you think yourself and your braves will ever have the same amount of hunting- ground as you used to have; and haw do you like being under the American Government ?" He said, "Noble paleface; lam a withered tree. I am like the oak that has stood the blast of time, the cold winds of winter, and the summer suns, and has been riven by the lightning's flash. My occupation is gone, and I wander upon the gameless prairie where my forefathers hunted the noble buffalo and the spotted deer. No more do my warriors hear my voice calling them to lift the topknots of the palefaced foe. The winds whistle through the trees of the forest; I hear the cawing of the rooks and the sweet tones of the mocking bird, but their voices have no meaning for Man-with-the-dirty-shirt. "Once I was the idol of my race. My limbs were like the limbs of the deer for fleetness, and strong as the panther's. Their strength is gone, and I am a toothless old man, bald as an egg. My pride has de- parted, for my scalplock has forsaken my head. When I call to my warriors they hear me not, for my voice is like a two cent, trumpet of the palefaces. Soon I shall die of a broken heart, and shall join the warriors of my race who have hopped the twig in the happy hunting. grounds before me..

"Noble paleface! The American fathers are 'good to me. They have taken away my game, but they give me other meat which is as good. They give me no work, but leave me at liberty to hunt the firewater, with which I give my stomach a pleasant bulge. In the summer I spend my days paring my corns, and in the winter 1 nurse my rheumatic through the long watchea of the night. Man-with-the-dirty-shirt will go to the

great hence. His wigwam will know him no mo, , and his squaw will call his name in vain. But so long as the white fathers send him bay rum to keep off the winter's chill he will try to live on. I have spoken." I took Man-with-the-dirty-shirt to have a glass of bay rum. He drunk both mine and his before I could stop him. He ordered two more glasses, but I was gone when the waiter looked round, so he put them back

-Meeting Joe and Ted coming out of the camp, I turned back with them, and we went to see the performance, which was within ten minutes of commencing. It was a splendid performance, and the most realistic of any I ever saw. The riding of the Indians and cow- boys was superb. It entirely put in the shade any- thing I have ever seen in a circus. Were it not that so many people saw the performance I would describe it. It was the biggest treat I ever had in my life.

div.head: CHAPTER XXIL A SHADOW.
div.p: CHAPTER XXIL A SHADOW.
Nearly a fortnight has -passed since Simon Knight's funeral, and Phyllis is as completely settled into the business at the brick house as if she had been all her life its sole mistress.

_ She has even managed to wake up hermother's dor- mast energies, sent to sleep as they have been for some years by Simon's constant repression. Now, under her daughter's reign, she has consented to take the entire management of the kitchen and house- wifely department. She would have been scarcely human—certainly not feminine—if she had not made a tow grumbles about her late husband's will, and pronounced it as only fair to Phyllis—she being the mistress and having to keep her—that she should fill the post of head servant m the establishment. Phyllis took no notice of these remarks, which after all were only uttered sotto voce, since Mrs. Knight was in reality quite devoted to her child. Phyllis was only too delighted on any terms to see her mother taking an active part in the cares of life, she herself being one of those people who believe that health both of mind and hotly deperOs very greatly on having plenty to do. In truth, too, she earned out her own maxim on this subject to the very fullest. Never had even Simon Knight himself done the amount of work that Phyllis undertook; but then, of course, he thoroughly understood the business which as yet-she was only learning. Every morning she was up by 6 o'clock ready to see the workmen and have a little conversation with each before he started for the day. "Make the men• happy and their 'homes com- fortable, and they will serve you better," was one of Phyllis's maxims, and in giving herself this care she far exceeded her father, who scarcely ever troubled himself about the name of his work- people; as long as his work was properly done, that was all he was interested in. _ _

Phyllis, however, determined to go and visit their wives, help them in every way she could, get up clubs for their benefit and evenings for their amusement ; in fact, she intended to have a regular reform practically carried out, and in order to do this she saw from the first that much thought and time, as well as a good deal of patience, would be requisite. But in devoting, herself to this hobby as her neighbours were already beginning to call it, Phyllis in nowise forgot the essential or business department. Of course she was compelled to trust a good deal to Greaves, whom she know to be a faithful soul, though not perhaps the very wisest man in creation. For this reason, perhaps, had he been selected by shrewd Simon Knight; for this reason did his daughter, but little behind her father in acumen, think it expedient,while she picked Greaves' brain of all the technical knowledge he could give her, yet never to allow him to conduct a single business tran- saction without her authority. All the accounts, both of labour and material, as well as of customers, passed through her hands, and al- though she in deference always consulted Greaves, yet she could give an estimate for work to be done with almost as much nicety of calculation as he could, surprising the old man too not a little by her capabilities. Who would have thought now," he would say to his intimates, "that Miss Phyllis—her that not a month ago was the worrit of the yard, and the plague of her father's life with her mad ways —would, all of a sudden, have tempered down into his very image as it were." Yet so it was; Simon Knight had judged correctly that Phyllis was made of the right staff, and that under the pressure of necessity the effervescence of youth would pass away and real sterling working habits develop themselves. There were two individuals who noticed this change in Phyllis with very little pleasure, both, though, from different causes, finding themselves outside the pale of her life. Tom Chilton, she had more or less dismissed for two years ; and though, without intending it, she had given him hope at the end of that time, yet she felt that she had not the slightest intention of allowing him to interfere with her mode of conducting her life and business till then. Naturally he hoped hhe would make a thorough fiasco of the whole affair, and was by no means pleased to find that she started with sound theories and on lines wide!) it only required perseverance and determination to develop into a great and brilliant concern. The admiration that Tom Chilton felt for Phyllis, under these circumstances, was only equalled by his exceeding annoyance, that this beautiful clever girl had elected to walk alone, or at all events unshZkled by any capital or assistance he could tender hem He would watch, however, he determined— watch very closely; the time and the hour would come, he made no doubt, when she would be very thankful for his strong arm and willing right hand. As for Geoffrey Stanhope, very different were his sentiments when lie heard the contents of Mr. Knight's will and witnessed the result. Those two years of probation—the thought of which was as a ray of hope to Toni Chilton—brought to Geoffrey something akin to despair. In two years what changes might not have come about, especially as Phyllis had taken her place so thoroughly in the trade to which she seemed in a manner born, and outside the pale of which he felt himself more thoroughly to be than did even Torn Chilton. He had not seen her so fre- quently since Simon Knight's death; of course he had come more than once to the brick house, but she was generally too much engaged settling her ac- counts, et,cetera, to speak more than a few words to him; and as for the Eaton-square painting-room, where she used to pass so many hours, she had not once entered it since the fatal morning. It seemed to Geoffrey as if something more than the two years fixed by Simon Knyht had been set up as a barrier between him and Phyllis; as if she herself, for some reason which he could in no wise divine, was anxious to keep him at a distance.' Honourable in tone and act though Geoffrey Stanhope was, he could- not understand how in the very spirit, as well as the letter, Phyllis was determined to carry out her father's will. God only knew how deeply she loved Geoffrey, since to no human being, not even to her mother, had She acknowledged - the fall intensity of her feelings; and yet she was almost cold to him, be: cause she knew now that she could not marry him for two years—two years in which it was abso- lutely incumbent on her to devote the very largest portion of her time and thoughts to the advancement and working of that business which her father had bequeathed to her. It did not occur to her that this behaviour of hers would make Geoffrey miserable, though there is little doubt that whenever she paused in the plan she had laid out for herself to consider the state of her own feelings, it was scarcely a sense of happiness that came over her; and it was with a despair far deeper than that felt by either Geoffrey or Tom Chilton that she looked with terror on those two years, and wondered if they would ever end, and, having ended, into what new epoch all her hopes and fears would have worked themselves. She,however, marched Steadily on ; never for a moment did it occur to her to change the course of her life, because the strain was sometimes so intolerable that it well-nigh drove her mad. But Geoffrey was shackled by no such chains as Phyllis, and kicking furiously against the pricks he 'determined at last to have the situation fully ex- plained by Phyllis, and some definite arrangement arrived at. He was the more resolved on this since for the first time in their lives he had had such a tiff with Irene that it amounted to a .quarrel, on the subject, of course, of Prince Sergrus, against whom Geoffrey raged more violently than ever, and of whom Irene told him she would not hear one word, since if she did not marry Prince Sergius she would never give her hand to any. other. They had discussed the subject till both of them had become so angry that they vowed it were better not to speak to eacliether at all, and Geoffrey,utterly disgusted with everything in life, betook himself to the desolate painting-room, where he walked up and down like an angry lion fretting in its cage; but not for long—he could not bear the solitude and the oppression of his thoughts for long. He would put on his hat amigo and see Phyllis, no thought; not that he expected much consolation or satis- faction from his visit. It was about twelve o'clock when Geoffrey reached Wandsworth; in fact, it was as much to avoid the family luncheon hour as from any other cause that he went off so immediately. As far as Phyllis was concerned he could perhaps, scarcely have chos en a worse moment, that is unless he wished to see her in the full swing of her new avocations.

It was a Saturda,y. She was in the little office, one door of which led into the yard and another commu- nicated with tha house. Geoffrey entered from the house She grew deadly white when she saw him, but since there was a knot of workmen standing by the, outer door she only said, trying to steady her voice into a pleasant tone— "how do you do, Mr. Geoffrey I am very busy

paying my men, as you may perceive; please down there on an office stool, that is unless you at` in agreat hurry." "I am not in any hurry, thank you," mutteretio Geoffrey. But more than one of the men noted th angry flush that was on his brow and came to the conclusion that this young arist:ocrat did not cute about being put on one side for the likes of them. . Phyllis, however, took no notice of his wrath, bu" went on systematically. "Henry Jones—sixteen shillings—one Bhilliflg t° take off for a month's club money; that's right, Ye° have worked well this week, Jones. "David Cross' twelve shillings. So I hear 37°1 are going to get married; not many savings to VI/ on one side on twelve shillings a week—suppose ir make it fourteen, and you stay till quite six o'cloe_., instead of giving over work at half-past five as r" have done more than once of late." David Cross's face beamed and his mouth e/e; panded from ear to ear, while the group of ta round him raised a cheer for their mistress,which 513: I however, at once repressed by a wave of the hut'd 'Bolt—Bennet--Fitz-James," she went on I them rapidly without much further comment, till came to the last a hump-backed boy of about Seli' teen. He had for some years been the brick errand boy; kept out of charity, though r believed him to be well nigh useless. Five 1 lay before Phyllis on the table, but she did attempt to give it to the lad she only said— " That is the sum my father agreed to give ' weekly, Bobby—take itif you think you have The boy hung his head, but did not move or "Well 1" said Phyllis, a little impatiently. "I'm not a bad boy," he began to whimper; " 0 was not for mother I'd say keep the money, bet ' poorly off, and I've no father.' "You did not give your last week's money to mother," said Phyllis. "What did you do with 0, "Bought these 'ere shoon as I've on my feet. eighteen pence and with the other three-and-six lived all this blessed week, never been anigh mol for a sup—ain't going anigh her no more. " Is that what you call helping her ?" "Well, if it ain't—what is it? If she ain't go) to keep that's summat. I used to give her the! but she wasn't content, and said as I cost j.• than I brought. If she's been complainin' to) miss, 'taint just; I've done the best I can." n "Naturally your mother wondered what lieu come of you; she came here yesterday to see if ; were at work, Where have you been sleeping, "In the yard under the timber ; please don't Mr. Greaves." "And you have managed to live on five a week ? " "Aye, and buy my shoon." "Well, you deserve the five shillings more theilo thought, only I may believe you—all this is trde "As the Bible, miss—folks say as I is sly, bn ain't, only when lam bean and hard hit. r roe to turn over a new leaf when I coined to serve - you ain't cross as the master was." "Hush, Bobby, take your money; give t shillings of it to your mother, keep two shillings, your clothes and against a rainy day,and come P, the kitchen for your meals; only mind, you laws' home to sleep or no victuals here." The boy began to cry and murmur something a blessed. angel, but Phyllis pushed the five slia into his hand and told him to be off, she had no for more talk ; only let her see that he was 7 ing and his wages would be raised. Having succeeded in sending him about ness, she turned to Geoffrey, who, instead of ing, gazed at her in utter amazement. In fae the love he had come to plead was changed such intense surprise that for the moment love to be absolutely dead. This practical business-like woman was WA Phyllis—the Phyllis of the painting-room—it Impossible. A light, however, came into V' eye as she looked on Geoffrey,e. fight that had shone there of late; it glimmered gradually- k the darkness that had come over him, and' ing at last his whole being with a sort of ad( he felt himself worshipping her in heart and , before one word had been uttered. . At length, ere she had time to stop him, the torrent of his long-pent love flowed forth p spontaneous stream ; never before had the little' been so filled with the outpourings of a I heart, and out of keeping with the time and though that raotilton stream of heart-burning yet Phyllis made no effort to stop it. She had Buttered so much of late from chillness that froze the atmosphere of her da that the eruption of this heart volcano, ins) terrifying her, served rather to warm and glad( She let Geoffrey say all that his stror prompted and not till she had drunk in to the she attempt to repress him by reminding him two years probation they had to endure. 11' minder, however, only drew Geoffrey on the He assuied her that neither time nor distance elf ever divide them; that she was his very ovld ever, and suiting the action to the word, wa reminded her of his possession, he Attenipte of encircle her by his own arm as he had dolle 9;jiio times before. For a moment her bead sank 0:40 shoulders in a sort of rapturous forgetfulness, i,");i0 dark shadow seemed to eome• between her and and she started up. 04° . It was no delusion, but a real tangible 51154 foreboding difficulty in the future; Geoffrey, too saw it, was well-nigh as startled as been, for it was the shadow of Henry Stanhope himself stood in the doorway. div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

The life of Ralph Waldo Emerson, by Dr. R. Gar- nett, is issued by Mr. Walter Scott, in the Great Writers series. Emerson's life was not an eventful one, and, apart from its even calm, he shrunk from self-revelation. But he is so great as a man and as a writer that cariosity is stimulated, and a life such as this admirably written one, reveals much which admiring readers like to know. It is Written in a sympathetic vein, for who could understand the great American, and write of him other than sym- pathetically? The world believes in great men, and Emerson in the region of morals was the greatest man of his age.

- In the Canterbury Poet, we have this month, the Odes of Horace, as translated, with notes, by Sir Stephen E. De Vera. These translations have been enlarged for what is now issued as the third edition; and it may thus be said that the purchaser of this shilling volume gets the fullest and therefore the best edition. The notes are of course explanatory, and are invaluable to the student. The translator seems on the whole to have done his work well. _How graceful for instance are these lines :

Sleep hovers with extended wings Above the roof where labour dwells, Dr where the river murmuring, Ripples beneath the beechen shade; 0! where in Tempes dells No sound save Zephyr's breath throbs through the. syl- van shade.

Democratic Vistas, and other papers, by "Walt Whit- man," is published by the same firm in the Camelot Series. There is a good deal in this volume; as there is in all that Whitman writes, that is auto-biographic, and hence the strength of statement and often the charm of style. lie is, of course, a great believer in the future of Anierica, but he looks not to politics, but to literature— "a new, superb, democratic literature as the machine and lever, and (with art) the chief influence in modern civilization." Englishmen with their narrow, insular ideas,, will do well to read thoughtfully such a work as "Democratic Vistas."

.The West mater Review is to the front as usual in discussing the topics of the hour from a broad stand- point. "The Claims of the Parish" are urged with great force as the proper basis of the Local Government Bill ; and there are, besides, articles on "The Papal Rescript," "Some aspects of the London School Board," "The Irish in America," "France and Boulangism"—all of im- mediate interest. Mr. T. W. Russell, M.P., has an article in the Independent Section on Ireland. He stands to his guns as a Liberal Unionist; but it is becoming more and more evident that he is not fond of the new flag under which he fights. He declaims against "the monstrous and wicked compensation clauses ; " and plainly tells the Government that it is the very reverse of wise statesmanship "to heap up future trouble by refusing to deal with arrears of unfair rents." We join with him in the concluding wish "that those calamities which have rent in twain a great historic party may soon be over-past."

Scribner's Magazine for June will be of especial interest to those who desire to know something of the "Building of a Railway" as that work is carried out in America: for the first paper, lengthy and profusely illus- trated, is devoted to that subject. Mr. Augustine Birrell contributes a vigorous article on Cardinal New- man, which is graced by two,striking portraits; and there is another illustrated contribution on "Hospital Life" by A. B. Ward. Mr. R. L. Stevenson discourses pleasantly on "Some Gentlemen in Fiction ;" and there is the usual supply of high-class story and verse. "Royal Academy Pictures, 1888, is one of the most charming of the many charming things Messrs. Cassell and Co. have issued. It is a supplement, in reality, to the "Magazine of Art," and contains no fewer than fifty-three illustratiens of the principal pictures and sculptures in the academy for this year. Many of them are full folio plates, and all of them are wonderfully fine pieces of work. It is to be hoped that this will prove to be the beginning of an annual series. The issue shoukl be in the hands of all who have a love of the beautiful, or a taste for art.

"The Magazine of Art" opens with a fine photogra- vure reproduction of "A Summer Day." painted by Ferdinand Heilbuth. Mr. G. F Watts has somethinc, pertinent to say on "The aims of Art," while Mr. M. Menpes writes upon and illustrates "A personal view of Japanese Art.' There is a powerful engraving of Solomon's " Niobe," one of the principal pictures of this year's academy exhibition; and an important illustrated paper on the crowns of various countries. "Charles Dickens, and his less familiar portraits," is particularly interesting from the reproductions which are given of these presentments of the great author. "The Woman's World" for June is varied, if not striking. Lady Dorothy Nevill has a chatty paper with the title of "Some Recollections of Cobden.' There is an interesting contribution on the late Marie Baskirtseff, the Russian painter_; and an illustrated article by Mr. W, L. Courtney on " The Women Benefactors of Oxford." There are other contributions by the Countess of Munster, Miss Emily Faithful, Miss Mathilde Blind, dr.c.

Cassell's Family Magazine for Tune leaves nothing to be desired. "Al at Lloyd's " is historically sketched by Mr. R. Holland, and illustrated by Mr. S. P. Hall; the Family Doctor chats pleasantly with th9se who are "Hard of hearing " ; " Going a-borrowing "is espe- cially written for those who are troubled with impecu- niosity; Gordon Stables tells of "A family of boys, and how they were started in life " ; and there is no lack of stories, music, and verse.—" The Quiver" is also varied and bright—theillustrations improving in quality year by year. The current issue includes "Playrooms for children," illustrated by Dorothy Tennant; A trip to Norway," by the Rev. Archdeacon Gore; "Some Historical Hymn Tunes" by J. C. Hadden ; "Working- men's Worries, by Rev. F. Hastings; "Nonconfor- mist Work in Islington," by a special Commissioner, drc., Szc.—" Little Folks" loses none of its charm either of text or illustration. There are two serial stories, and half a score of finished tales, and odds and ends in prose and verse—all suitably hit off by clever artists. We have also to hand from Messrs. Cassell and Co. part 5 of Milton's Paradise Lost, illustrated by Gustave Dore; part 29 of the Illustrated Shakespeare (covering a large portion of the play of King Henry V.) ; part 53 of the Encyclopcedic Dictionary, which has the merit of [giving a history of each work; part 11 of "The Sea; its stirring story of adventure, peril, and heroism " ; 'part 28 of Familiar Wild Flowers ; and part Bof the new and admirable Dictionary of History.

CHAPMAN & CO.. St. Bpnedict's. Norwi ch.—Advt. They were in the parlour, occupying one chair, with but a single thought. They had discussed the tariff, the sleighing, the opera, the weather, and other important topics, till conversation was about fagged out. After a long pause, "Ducky !" " Whatty ?" "Do you think I'm making any progress in courting ?" "Well, I should say you wae holding your own !" Tableau. . This small boy, while out walking the other day, be- came much interested id the movements of a lot of feathered beauties, headed by a handsome rooster, Which were crossing the roadway just ahead. They got over in safety, but one of the fowls had a narrow escape from being run over by a passing team, and her frantic attempts ,to flee from impending danger excited him considerably. Just as she reached the side-walk :the rooster crowed lustily, and Master Bert turned to the Historian,with indignation in histone. " Uncle ! uncle !" he cried, "isn't that rooster naughty to laugh at a poor hen so ?"

HARD OF HBARING.—We often hear one friend say to another, "You are very deaf to-day," and perhaps the reply is, "Well, lam a bit deaf to•day, I vary with the weather." This is a species of deafness common in the nervous, and really arises from debility, consequent perhaps upon some temporary derangement of the digestive organs. People subject thereto should live carefully slid abstemiously. They should try to live so as to be independent of the use of drugs. I have heard it said that the deaf hear better when any noise is going on, probably because then other people are bilking loudest. I really believe that is the true rea.son. But my grandfather used to relate an instance of the deaf colonel of a regiment who was so convinced of the truth of this opinion, that whenever be had to converse on parade with any of his men or officers, he used to have the drummer to beat up close along side.—A Family Doctor, in Cassell'. Family Magazine.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MoNney.
The Lord Chancellor took his seat ehortly after 4 p.m PEERS AND _PARLIAMENTARY ELECTIONS.

An interesting discussion took place on the right o' peers to interest themselves in Parliamentary elections Lora &LISETTEi spoke of the sessional order as an in teresting piece of archftology, and his speech was not without humour, for, pointing out that the proceeding. uf both Houses were full of strange antiquarian relics he mentioned amid laughter that at the beginning oi every Parliament they solemnly constituted a Commit- tee of their Lordships' House to hear appeals from Guienne, but the French Government hod taken ne notice of the resolution for four hundred wears. As,hcre ever, it might now be assumed that the House of Lord. assented to the conclusion that the resolution was good in law, it was advisable that their lordships shoulo accede to the suggestion of the noble earl, and appoint committee.

The motion was agreed to. Early legislation was promised with regard to reforma- tory and industrial schools; and after some discussioi, on the urgent need of defences at Esquimalt, the thrivin., seaport on Vancouver Island, their lordships adjourned at 7 5 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY.

Mr. Speaker took the chair shortly after 3 p.m. Mr. Etrrrpt asked a question with regard to the prisonment of newsveudors for selling copies of certain Nationalist newspapers, including the Cork Herald, Cork Examiner, and United Ireand, but the IRISH SECRETARY asked for more information in reference to the questions put. Sir J. Goarr, in response to Mr. Schwann, stated the, the Government of India had no intention of pursuing policy of aggression towards Thibet. In answer to Captain Cotton, the SECRETARY for WA,: said that steel ingots were being made by Messrs. Whit- worth .for a priveta firm, hut they were not intended directly or indirec'l,- for the French Government. THE INVASION SCARE.

Lord GEORGE HAMILTON, answering Sir Richard Temple, said that his estimate that 480,000 tons of ship- ping would be required for the conveyance of 100,000 men from France to England was based on two con- siderations—first that the disembarkation would ly simultaneous, and secondly that the army so disem- barked was capable of rapid movement. The esti- mate of 480,000 tons gross was on the assumption that the force would be equivalent to three army corps con- stituted as regards cavalry and artillery accordinp to the scale laid down in the "Soldier's Pocket-book," and the 480.000 tons gross tonnage estimated to be re- quired was equivalent to 300,112 tons net, which was re the rate of one and a half tons per rrian, and four ton, per horse. The details contained in the "Soldier's Pocket-book" as regarded sea transport were furnished by the department 13 years ago. Since that time th, department had had greatly enlarged experience, but th, estimates then made for long and medium voyag,es hel,l good, as modern steamers did not afford sufficient deel, space to allow the standing of horses. His figures wer based on practical data, and he would consider whethel he could lay some statement explanatory of them on th, table of the House. Mr. Hanhury and Sir FL Havelock-Allen put to Lori. George Hamilton supplementary questions, but the Firs Lord made no reply of importance. THE COMPENSATION CLAUSES...

Mr. Smithwas qrieetioned by Sir Wiivflin L kIPSON, fl to a reported speech of the Solicitor-General to th, effect that the Standing Orders of the House would bc suspended in order to pass the Local Government Bill Mr. SmnstEns asked whether there was any foundatier for the statements that the Government had determine,: to drop the licensing clauses. (Opposition cheers.) Mr. Sstrrit : I think the hon. member who asked th., last question is probably puffins., an interpretation upor, the paragraphs which appeared in the papers whiel accords with his own wishes—(laughter) ; but I hay, the satisfaction of telling him that these paragraphs de not convey the impression likely to be obtained from his statement, and that the Government have not come to any determination of the kind to which he refer. Ministerial cheers and ironical Opposition laughter.) In answer to the question of the hon. baronet, I have to say that I think he must. expect the Local Governmen, Bill will be taken diligently, and that the Government will use every effort that is in accordance with the rule !- of the House to press the bill forward.
