div.head: LOCAL GOVERNMENT RILL.
div.p: THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT RILL.
The House aE,,ain went into Committee on the Lner' Government Bill. On Clause 2

Mr. STANSFFLD MOVCA as an amendment that all tip councillors shall be el*tive councillors, and that there shall be no aldermen, conte,nding that this would brin,. the bill more into accordance with the principles o' trust in the people laid down in moving the second read ing of the bill. ' . _

Mr. RATHBONE supported the amendment.—Sir R Lwrnanincv accepted the principle of " trust the people' to the fullest extent. If the President of the hoes' Government Board did not act up to that principle in his bill, "it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck and he were thrown into the sea." (Laughter.) Mr. W. F. LAVMENCR was strongly in favour of th, dual system of representation. Mr. llgisvaon opposed the amendment. Mr. nircrri R said the,Government did not propose any- thing which would affect the system of election in the boroughs which were to be made counties. If Ulm were to accept the amendment an anomaly would b., created. For the larger areas of the county the mor important councillors will be elected without any Selecterl members at all, the smaller areas would alone have selected members on the Council. It was not because any want of trust in the people that they propose,l what they did, but because it was desirable there. should he some other means than that of the elective principle in the bill. There was a great deal of force in the argu- ment as to the danger of the selected element being use, for the perpetuating of the majority of one particular party. (Opposition cheers.) The Government did no, intend to adhere rigidly to the provisions of the Muni- cipal Corporations Act with reference to that point, and lie shook' be glad to consider the amendment for provi- ding that the remaining selected councillors should nol vote for the new selected councillors whose names wer submitted for election. That would do away with tnan of the ohjections that had been raised. (Cheers.) Mr. 11. Fowt.sa said the theory of the selected prin- ciple was not carried out in practice. The proposal that the Council shquld fill up its own vacancies was most reactionary one.

, Mr. GrAnsvoms urged that direct election was much better than secondary election. He suggested that as it was necessary to get the element of experience on County Councils the minority should be elected for A longer period and the majority for a shorter term by the constituency. Mr. M. W. Mierrtsrsom was glad to think that her Majesty's Government were going to stand 0 their guns. The Marquis of HARTINOTON said that it was ad- mitted by all that it was desirable to have men of experience, and to ensure continuity on the new councils. He thought that Mr. Gladstone overlooked the necessity for securing the experience of those who had taken hitherto a very prominent part in county government. The Committee divided on Mr. Stansfeld'samendment-- For the amendment 214 Against The announcement of the figures was received with cheers by members of the Opposition. Mr. RITCHIE said it had been objected that the words "selected councillors" were invidious, and he therefore moved to leave them out —Sir Wm. HARCOURT asked why they should not call a spade a spade? The words selected councillors exactly expressed what these gentle- men were.—The amendment was withdrawn.

_ Captain 13BITIRLL (flolderness) moved to leave out the words "selected councillors" and insert " reeveman."— Mr. Rrreitts was afraid the word "reoveman" would not be at all familiar to the ears of the common people.— It was agreed that the selected councillors should be called aldermen. Mr. CIIANNING moved an amendment that the alder- men should sit for three years only. Mr. LONG said the amendment would destroy one of the chief objects of their creation, namely, to ensure eontinuity.—The Committee divided—For the amend- ment, 111; against, 148-37. The amendmeqt was therefore rejected. Mr. Amsox moved an amendment providing that the counts, aldermen should be selected from the county councillors.

Mr. BITCHIER said there might be gentlemen outside the Councils who would render very useful service.—Mr. F. S. POWELL said if there was one official who ought to bl elected by the popular vote it focal the mayor of a borough.—TMr. STANSFELD contended that the whole argument of Mr. Ritchie in support of the principle of sidemen was founded on mistrust of the people.—After some discussion, the amendment was defeated by 217 to 170. _ _

On the motion of Mr. FIAT'S, the name' "elective councillors" was changed into" county councillors." Mr. RATEBONE moved an amendment that the county aldermen shall not vote in the election of county alder- men.—The Government accepted the amendment, and it was agreed to. Sir W. IikaTTELOT moved to make the terms of office for councillors six years instead of three years.—Mr. RITCHIE recommended the Corporation to adhere to three years as the term in the Municipal Corporations Act. —Mr. ILLINOWORTIT advocated the term of three -years. —sir W. HARCOURT hoped the Government would adhere to the term of three years. After further discus- sion the Committee divided—
For the amendment
_ Against

Pmegres;wa9 then reported. After some discussion, the llouse went into Committee of Ways and Means, when the resolutbn on the Wine Tax was agreed to. The Ilouse adjourned at 12 25. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUBSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4 15.
Brus AnvaNcEn.—The City of London (re Inquests) Bill was read a third time and passed.—The Rochester Bishopric Bill, as amended, passed through Committee.
Thg Orainev Disciruma BILL.—The Archbishop of Carmatattar moved the third reading of this bilL—The

Archbishop of YORK presented 23 petitions against t hill, and explained the reasons why his opposition to tb bill had come so late. Some of the provisions of th, bill he described as marvellous and extraordinary, and affecting the interests of the clergy to a very consider- able extent. The bill provided a very bad and novel Court of First Instance, and provided absolutely w. Court of Appeal. The Court of First Instance was to b-• constituted by a Chancellor, two laymen, and three clergymen, and in order to give this assembv the air of a Court, absolute power was glven to the Chancellor in all matters of law, but the Court VMS neither judgn nr.r jury. The Chancellor would no doubt be a good judge if not hampered by the rest of the Court. and the re- maining five would no doubt form a good jury if no, 'tampered by the Chancellor. A Court sf, institute,: would not meet with general acceptation. The old Con- 4istorial Court was to be destroyed entirely. What Fligh Churchmen were asking for was not met by the bill. Hi- ebj,‘et in opposing the bill now was not to reject it ce, its third reading, but to secure delay so that its provisions !night be adequately considered by those most deeply in- terested.—The Bishop of LONDON said the bill was drafted ,vith the approval of the whole bench of Bishops.— Lord Ifsascrtvrr, agreed that the law at present was un. satisfactory, he' +he house was not much helped by speech on the !, 1.1 reading, which was simply an invi- tation to another place to reject the measure.—Lor COLF.RIDOR thought that the state of things as the. existed were better than the bill before th, House would make them—The Bishop of CAP- LISLE supported the bill on the ground that it would enable the proposed court to deal rapidly and cheaply with immoral and criminous clerks.-- The BISHOP OF LIVERPOOL objected to that part of th, bill giving a veto to the bishop of the diocese in whict, the offence alleged was committed. The bill ought to he thoroughly sifted before it became the law of the 'encl.—Los-4J SELHORNE supported the RIMTHORPR opposed and the LORD CHANCELLOR sup- ”ortod the bill, which was then read a third time awl passed. QLI A RTE R SESSIONS BILL.—The Lour. CHANCIMILO, .toved the second reading of a bill giving the justices e wider discretion when they would hold quarter session or gaol de4iveriea. The bill was read a second time. The House adjourned at 6-40 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS—TUESDAY.

„ The first of the” morning" sittings for the consider:, 'inn of the Local Government Bill, in Committee, wa yesterday, the Speaker taking the chair shortl t her two o'clock. There was not a large attendano many members being engaged on the various Self r "ovnmittees, whose proceedings are now in operatic) -emtemporaneously with the business of the House. There were few questions of interest on the paper. Si • JAMES FERCirSSON, answering Mr. Bryce, said it was trn. lhat Nubar Pasha had retired from the service of ti Khedive of Egypt, and that Riaz Pasha had undertake• the formation of a Ministry. He believed the Ministr was now complete. The Government of this countr:. had taken no part in bringing about the change. Notice was given by Mr. 5t...k00 to ask the Under-Seers tary of State for India whether it, is true, as stated in Ti Times, that the Government of India contemplate th raising- of a spcial loan to meet the cost of the frontie ,let ences.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 16, 1888.

div.head: WITHDRAWAL 01? THE LICENSING CLAUSES. MR. RITCHIE'S EXPLANATION.
div.p: WITHDRAWAL 01? THE LICENSING CLAUSES. MR. RITCHIE'S EXPLANATION.

Mr. RITCHIT, risinl amid ironical Opposition cheer. said he had to inform the House that it had been th dutY of the Government to consider the state of publi, iusiness, in connection especially with the principl: measure of the session, and he had now to ask the HOW, to permit him to communicate the views at which HI ,- Government had arrived on the subject It smith, ha remembered that in introducing the bill h, informed the House that the Government had fel. it to be their duty to make propoulls in th, hill dealing with the licensing qu.,stion, but ,lso said that they did not consider these proposals ;) o any sense vital to the bill. The proposals they mad were of such a nature that they hoped they would hay( teen received as a substantial concession, for by then• t hey would have been able to reduce the number o! üblic-houses in places wherever it was desired. gut was very clear that their proposals would meet witl strenuous opposition. There were on the pape• 7:0 fewer than 200 amendments to the licensinr clauses, occupying thirteen pages of the notier riper. The HOIISP had not yet complejed th onsideration of the second clause-of the bill, which con sted of 15 clauses. They were now within very Iltt', ;nom than two months of the close of an ordinary :ossion. The chances, therefore, of being able to dee' with this question, as well as many other importan^ ,nestions in the bill, were, in the face of the opposition. --pry small—(cheers).--and the result of the determina- ' nto adhere to the clauses might very well be that they ould find themselves, after a prolonged struTrgle, with ) little time as to make it prectically impossihl, • pass the remainder of the bill, a result Which, he he- !ieved, would be regarded, both by the House and by he country, as little short of a disaster. (Hear, hear.) The Government had, therefore, resolved not to ask th, House to proceed with the licensing clauses. (Cheer •flid counter cheers much prolonged.) Mr. J. C. STBV:eNSON expressed 0 hope that the Govern- ment would not drop the °tense which dealt with sun- Jay closing, and which die not aff^ct the gwnern' !icensing questions, such as compensation, Sr.c. Mr. TIFF-ma We include all the licensing clauses it our determination.

Mr. STANSFELD said be thought he Was entitled to ~neratulAte the Government on the conclusion at which they had arrived. BRADLADOTT gave notice to rail attention to the grievances of the native popuiatinn in India. NEW BILL—Mr. H. GARDNER brought in a bill to emend the Public Libraries' Act, 1885.

div.head: LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.
div.p: THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.
The House then went into Committee on the LOCal ovornment Bill.

Mr. Suaw-Laraval.proposed that there should be RE election for the County Council, in every third district each year, that is that one-third Should retire each year. instead of the whole body retiring at the end of each third year. His proposal. Mr. Sbaw-Lefevre pointed out, followed out the practice of the Municipal Corpora- tions Act, the principle of which the Government Adopted, as the basis of the present measure. ThiF method of election, the whole body retiring at the end n' three years, had been tried in the ease of School Boards. and had not proved very successful. (Hear, hear.) Mr. R. G. %Berea, from the Conservative side of the i:ouse, and. several members from the Opposition side o' the House urged the Goverpusent to accept the amend- ment. —Mr. RITCHIE urged the Committee to adopt the Government proposal. He adnaitteil that it was a de- parture from the practice of the fauna-mai dOrollitttiOnF Act, but it must be remernbered that there were material differences betyrtezn County Councils and Town Councils. The area winch the Town Council ruled was divided into three prineipal areas, and there was an elec- tion every year on each area, so that every elector in every part of the borough was able to record his vote annually. The material difference in the present pro- posal of the Government was that they suggested that single member areas should be set up, and because of this, and on the score of expense to the candidates and the county, the Government would urge the Committee to accept the proposa The discussion was continued by Mr. Rathbone and Mr. Curzon, who supported the Government; Sir R. Paget Mr. 0. H. Fowler, and Mr. F. S. Fowler, who supported the amendment, —Mr, W, H. Swim said the Govern- ment felt that the disturbances of the life of the county arising from elections 4hould not be more frequent. than was necessary to 'keep the Council in touch with the electorate, The suggestion he had to make was that the right hon. gentleman should withdraw his amendment at this stage, and allow the Government to consider whether it might not be possible to adopt, in some measure, the suggestion of Mr. H. H. Fowler, that there should be an election for a proportion of the Council every two years. (Hear, hear.) Whether the term of office should be four or six years would be a matter for consideration. For his part he inclined to- wards a term of six years. (Cheers.)—Proressor STUART ' Will you reconsider the aldermanic question?— Mr. H. H. Fownza That is an essential part of my pro- posal. (Cheers.) It was to do away with aldermen altogether, elect councillors for six years, one-third retiring at the expiration of two imam There was no reason, however, why there should not be ample time for the Government to consider the question. (Hear. hear.)—Mr. SMITE said the Government would consider the whole question on this and the report stage in hope nf arriving at a decision.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said the experience of the United State, and of this country showed that when people were so constantly being called to give votes they fell into the hands of caucuses and machine politicians—(loud laughter and cheers)—a state of things which had not hitherto existed in this country -,—(laughter)—arad one which. he for one should earnestly deprecate. (Cheers and laughter.) The suggestion of the right hon. gentleman opposite would, he thought, give the continuity of policy in the cooracil which they all de- sired to see. (Cheers.)- After some further discussion the amendment was by leave withdrawn. Sir JOHN Lasso.= moved an amendment having in view the adoption of proportional representation on the County Council, and was supported by Commander Bethel, Mr. W.. Morrison Whitmore, and Mr. Bradlaugh. —Sir W. Hammer hoped the Government would ad- here to their own proposals; and Mr. RITCHIE said they would do so.—Mr. Crrszrester.sui thought it would be a great misfortune to. abandon the present system,which had worked well in favour of these curious and intricate devices of proportional representation, each supporter of which had a different plan by which it was to he carried mit. (Laughter.)—On a division the voting woe--.

For the amendment. 94 Against .... . . -..—....- ..... ...... 372-278 Mr. Itircrun presented an amendment to Clause 2, with reference to a casual vacancy amongst elective councillors, providing that in cases where a vacancy occurred within a period of twelve months from the end of the term of °face of the inditodual who had vacated his seat it should be filled up by the councillors. He thought how members would hardly consider it a desir- able thing to hold anelection for a vacancy when another o.lnction for the same seat would have to be WA

perisape at the end ot two or three mouths.— Sir WALTER Fovren thought the Committee ought not to tamper at all with the principle of ceuncillors being elerted by the people.—Mr. Fovrtita asked why there should be any departure from the custom which pre- vailed, not only in municipal but in Parliamentary elec- tions.—Mr. RITCHIE signified his willingness to reduce die period to six months. (Cries of " No.") It would he wise to have some limitation.—Mr. TREVELYAN thought it would be better, if the vacancy occurred within six months, to leave it unfilled for that period. Ind this suggestion was eventually adopted. Ittr. ACLAND proposed the following amendment t- l'hiuse 2:—" Every councillor shall be entitled to clain, a sum in payment of the expenses actually and reason thly incurred by him to and froin the place of meeting Jf the Council' Unless this were done representatives of the working classes and small tradesmen would be unable to occupy seats on the Councils, as was the case with municipal bodies. All he wished was to make a real equality between these large areas, wtich could not he traversed without expense, and existing municipal Feiewicx, in supporting the amendment, thought that it should go further, and to avoid invidious listinctions make it imperative that County Councillors :=liould be paid.—Ple Surrri s,ald this was a very im- oortant point for consideration, and as it was nearly seven o'clock he moved that progress be reported, which was agreed to. The report of the wine duties resolution was received, and the sitting was then suspended until nines clock.
ADMIRALTY REFORM. DEFEAT OF THE GOVERNMENT.

On the House resuming at nine o'clock, Mr. JENIqINGS called attention to the abuses connected with frequent and costly reorganisations in various public offices, his motion being to the effect "that the reorganisations in ;he Accountant-General's and Secretary's departments if the Admiralty have been injurious to the public in- terests, by resulting in increased charges for those de- partments and by bonuses; and that in any further re- organisations officials who are still able and willing te render service for the public money shall be provided with employment in other departments, instead of being forced to become useless burdens upon the country." The hon. member, in a speech of considerable length. cited cases showin., how public officials in the prime a t,fe were presented with liberal bonuses and extravagant pensions in so-called reorganisation schemes, and he declared that in one department now higher poets had been created, and the work of a superinftndency in the lccountant's department cost £20,000 yearly or more, when it used to be done for £2,000 per annum. He was once told in irmerica that a man must be doing well, as he had been made hankrupt six times In as many years. In the English public service the test of well-doing was the number of times a man's office bad been abolished. In the vaunted re-organisations the saving in the salary list formed the subject of much boasting. As a fact the Pension list was increased to an extint which exceeded the saving of salaries, to say nothing of the outlay in bonuses. He maintained that the *hole system was wrong, that able public servants could be obtained at much lower salaries without pensions, and•that the r anitry was sick and tired of 'the system of providing ,ffileers from what were called geed families. He might he accused of being a Radical for attacking these abuses, but he would prefer to attack them as a Radical than to defend each defects as a Tory. (Cheers.)—Major RASCA. seconded. Mr. CECILDISTV3 said the Ministers at the heads of the departments by no means 'cared for reorganisation schemes, which v;ere always productive of Much disap- pointment to them. The right hon. gentleman quoted statistics showing that reorganisations of the services had resulted in vary substantial savings of the public money.
- - Lord George Hamilton opposed the resolution, and suggested an inquiry when further re-organisation was necessary.

Mr. Surirr pointed out that if the resolution which tlie hon. member for Stockport had moved was given effect to by the Government the immediate result would be that a number of redun• dint officers must be retained in the public service, and that any charges which were being !intro- duced for the good of the public service must be stopped. The,resolntion, if carried, would seriously tie the hands of the Government in the changes which they were contemplating, and he hoped the hon. • member wsuld not press it to a division. Mr. JENNIPOR, in reply, did not consider that a suffi- cient answer had been given to the facts and figures he bad brought before the House to justify him in with- drawing his resolution. (Opposition cheers.) At twelve o'clock Professor STUART moved the closure., which was agreed to without a division. The Sous, then diVided, with the following result:— For the resolution Against

The result was received with 14)1.0 o,„vo,sition cheer, and bantering cries of "resign." Mr. Carrots HARDY moved the second reading of the Accumulations itill.—lt 'ants opposed by the krrort• Nwr-GattsseAt, but eventually pasted. Mr. flutrrsa moved the sec9nd reading of the Trawl- ing (Scotland) Bill.--It was opposed by the Losa ADVOCATE. At 12 50, Mr. MARK STIMART moved Oh alj )urnment of the debate.—The House divided, with the foliowing result v—For the adjournment, 77; against, 53. The House adjourned at 1 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDLY. -
_ The Speaker took the chair at a quarter after twelve o'clock.

Law OF LIBEL BlLL.—There were no questions on the paper, and the House went into Committee on the Libel Law Amendment Bill. The clause providing that where a defendant had proved the absence of actual malice or gross negligence and had published an apology the plain- tiff should not be entitled to recover unless he had suf- fered special damages was carried; so was the clause giving the defendant liberty to give evidence that dam- ages had been obtained from other papers in mitigation of damages in his own case. The clause giving the de- fendant power in certain cases to obtain security for costs was rejected, butthe one setting forth that no per- son shall be found guilty who is not proved to be party to the publication of a libel was carried.—The bill passed through Committee. OATHS BILL, &C. The Reformatory Schools Act Amendment Bill was reported with amendment, and the House went into Committee on the Oaths Bill.—Mr. Nu- xis moved an amendment to clause 1, excepting from the operation of the clause persons who stated that they had no religious belief.—Mr. BRADLAUGH said it was clearly impossible to accept the amendment, which was in the teeth of the opinion of the House.—On the motion of Mr. ANDERSON, progress was then reported. Wined SISTER BILL. Mr. MCLAREN moved, on the the motion to go into Committee on the Marriage with a Deceased wife's Sister Bill, that it be an instruction to the Committee to extend the scope of the bill so as to in- clude between a woman and her deceased husband's bro- ther.—Mr. TALBOT, who considered such alteration would be unwise, was speaking in opposition to the motion at half-past five o'clock, when, in accordance with the rule, the debate stood adjourned. Clause 2 of the Partner- ships Bill was passed, and progress was reported. The House adjourned at twenty minutes to six o'clock.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.-THURSDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.-THURSDAY.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after four o'clock. COMPANIES Acrs. Attention was drawn to the Com- panies Acts, the Loup CHANCELLOR presenting a bill on the subject. A bill, he said, had been promised in the Speech from the Throne, but there was no chance of a measure of consolidation thik session. The Government had been compelled, therefore, to deal with prominent points requiring immediate amendment; but they could not do anything to restrict the various industrial associa- tions, on which so much of the commerce and trade of the country depended. He made a comprehensive reference to the promoters of bogus companies however, and maintained that the machinery the State had invented must not be used for fraudulent purposes. The chief machinery of the bill would be the reintroduc- tion of a system of provisional registration.—Lord HER- SCHELL, while sympathising with the noble lord in his endeavour to remove evils declared that no provisions could be framed that could not be walked through by those who had fraudulent intentions. The bill was read a first time. . .
Their Lordships adjourned at twenty minutes to six o'clock.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THIIRSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at ten minutes past three o'clock. _ _

CONVICTIONS UNDER TITE CRIMES Acv.—Mr. GLADSTONE asked the Chief Secretary for Ireland whether he could assure the House that in every case where an individual had-been convicted under the Criminal Law and Proce- dure (Ireland) Act, 1887, of conspiracy to compel or in- duce some person not to deal with or work for some other person in the ordinary course of trade, business, or occupation, evidence had been taken to prove not on4y the refusal of the individual to work or deal as above, but to prove that he was implicated in a conspiracy for some one of the said purposes.— Mr. A. J. BALFOUR replied that in every ca-se tried, with the exception of one, evidence of conspiracy was ten- dered.—Mr. GLADSTONE said he was afraid there was some misunderstanding between him and the Chief Secre- tary. He was strongly underthe belief that in more than one case evidence of conspiracy was not forthcoming, but simply evidence of a refusal to deal. (Hear, hear.) The right hon. gentleman was proceeding to give notice of a further question when the Speaker intervening said he was sorry to interrupt the right hon. gentleman, but there was a rule of the House that written notice should be given of all fresh questions. (Hear, hear). THE RELEASE OF TRAVIS.—The HOME SECRETARY, in reply to Mr. W. Redmond and Mr. Tatton Egerton, said it was true that the convict Travis had been uncondi- tionally released, in consequence of fresh information which had been laid before the Government. It was not usual to give compensation in such cases. HARCOURT asked Mr. Goschen what he proposed to do with the consols still unconver- ted.—The CHANcgm.on of the Exennanna could not admit that the holders of new consols were in a worse position than those having unconverted stock. His statement that`out of a total of £590,000,000 theamount now outstanding wal £47,000,000 was received with cheers. Wmnt Durr.—The second reading of the Wine Duty Bill was moved by Mr. JAexsori, who explained that still winos would be exempted, but on sparkling wines there would be a tax of Es ed per gallon on those over 308 per dozen, and of is per gallon on those under 30s per dozen. —Mr. GiAissrofm, rising soon after Mr. Childers had spoken against the proposals, congratulated Mr. Goschen on having so modified his plan that we heed have no fur- ther apprehension about France, but he did not look favourably on this falling back to ad valorem duties. The plan might lead to undervaluing, disturbance, and loss to revenue, and he did not know whether the pro- posal would last very long—in fact, he should not be surprised if experience led to its removal altogether.— The debate was continued by Mr. Illingworth, Mr. Brad- laugh, Sir G. RELEASE OF A CONVICT.-EXTRA- ORDINARY CASE. Albert Tritvis; formerly the landlord of the Swan Inn. Sutton, Cheshire, who in 1886 was convicted of the murder of Mrs. Wintyre, at a house in Rock Ferry, and whose death sentence was commuted to one of penal servitude for life, was on Saturday unconditionally released from Chatham Prison, and he reached home the same night. Travis was engaged to be married to a Miss Platt, a sister of Mrs. M°lntyre, and on the night of the 12th February. 1886, Mrs. Wintyre, Miss Nati-, and Travis were drinking together, and all appeared to have got drunk. Early next morning screams and the tirgh of a scuffle were heard, fol-lowed b, a sound of breaking glass, ami on ,tht police gaining an entrance Travis Was found lying- in the yard with his face and hands bleeding, be having apparently jumped or fallen through a window of a bedroom. In this bedroom Mrs. Brlntyre was found lying dead with serious injuries to her head. Miss Platt was sittine one chair in the room with marks of blood upon her dress, and there was blood about the room and upon a pair of broken tongs lying near the deceased. Travis and Miss Phitt were both arrested and charged with the murder. The woman subsequently turned "Queen's evidence," and Travis was convicted. At the time he strongly pro- teeted his innocence. The following official statement in rep reldo the case was made on Monday by Major Barker, Chief Constable of Fiiikerthead:—" The police can state on authority, with reference to the unconditional releaseof Robert Travis, that this satisfactory result has been broughtabout by the exertions which have been made on his behalf by Sir Edward Harriley,M.P. for Birkenhead. It si as known to the police authorities after the case had been till& investigated before the justices that Travis did not commit the murder, and it was against their judgment that the prosecution took the course they did at the trial at Chester a,ssizes in putting Miss Platt in the box as a witness against Travis. The police autho- rities' view was entirely shared in by Mr. R. B. Moore. the solicior engaged on behalf of Travis, and it was solely owing to that gentleman's exertions that the Home 14cretary in May, IhB6, commuted the capital sentence to One Of penal servitude for life. Subsequently the police authorities submitted the case to the considera- tion of General lir Edward Hamley, who used his best exertieris to secure Travis's release. He was for some time unsuccessful, but so deeply was he impressed with Travis's innocence that he persevered, and with the assistance of Lord Bramwell, who became greatly interested in the subject from a perusal of the documents, he finally prevailed upon the Home Secretary to have the case revised by Lord Esher, the Master of the Boils, the result being that Travis has been released."

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

It is stated at Longford that Mr. Parnell has selected Dr. Fitzgerald, of London, as Nationalist candidate for South Longford, to fill the tramncy pending by the ,etirement of Mr. Laurence Connolly, M.P., through ill health.

At Belfast Police (amrt, on Saturday, W. K. Matthews and W. Press were charged with being concerned in a vnriety of ways wi6i the recent life assurance frauds in Belfast. No evidence was given. The accused were re- manded on heavy bail. Captain Plunkett, divisional magimtrate, arrived at Mit- chelstown on Saturday to investigate the circumstances attending the resistance to the payment of the Leahy compensation tax, and held a consultation with the resident magistrate on the subject. Only a few cess- payers have paid the tax.

A report has reached Galway that a hut on Arran Island, in which explosives are "stored. was broken into on Sunday night, and a qvisntity of dynamite and powder stolen. At the *tome time, notices were posted, cautioning people not to pay rent, or their houses would be blown up. The Rev. Father Donohoe, being incensed at the outrage, has stopped the relief works that were proceeding in Arran. No clue to the perpetrators has been obtained.

THE WESTMEATH 'MURDER. Later particulars of the tra& affair at Littleton Police Barrack, co. West Meath, state that Constable Simpson first fired with a revolver at Sergeant Mc.Gowqn, who fell wounded. Simpson then stabbed him with a bayonet, afterwards shooting himself. The motive of the crime is said to besevenge, the sergeant having reported Simpson several times. An inquest was held on Saturday on the bodies of Sergeant Mc.Gowan and Constable Simpson. The jitry returned a verdict of wilful murder against Simpson, who after murdering the sergeant committed suicide. The people in the dis- trict will not allow the body of Simpson to be interred in any of the neighbouring graveyards. Two bayonets were driven to the hilt into Mc.Gowan's body.

div.head: DR O'DWYER AND THE PAPAL DECREE.
div.p: DR O'DWYER AND THE PAPAL DECREE.

Dr. O'Dwyer, Roman Catholic Bishop of Limerick, addressing a synod of clergy in St. John's Cathedral, on Tuesday, referred to the recent Papal decree condemning the Plan of Campaign and boycotting. He said the force of the decree was binding, as was distinctly stated in a letter from Archbishop Walsh read at the conference of Irish bishops, at Clonliffe, on the 30th ult., and sent by direction of the Pope himself, to remove the doubts raised by Cardinal Monaco's reason for the decree. There- fore the decree became a definite law of the Church, and it would be sinful to disobey it. There was no difference of opinion between him and the other Bishops as to the meaning and binding force of the decree. The sooner the plain truth was known about boycotting and the Plan of Campaign the better. He believed there never was a greater scandal to religion in Ireland than that caused by the present .agitation. Boycotting and the Plan of Campaign would have to ceaai in his diocese, as well as covert or open attacks en the Pope. If necessary a few rebellious Catholics would be put outside the fold, to avert the greater evils to religion. The Freeman's Journal says :—The documents from Rome, and the resolutions of the Bishops of Ireland, have been submitted to dignitaries, admittedly qualified in the highest mariner to judge. Yet in no quarter can be found warrant for the violent language used by Dr. O'Dwyer. Are all the other bishops wrong, and is Bishop O'Dwyer alone right ? The un- common, almost unprecedented, character of Dr. O'Dwyer's procedure, makes his address publicproperty, to be discussed with perfect freedom. The pronounce- ment of the body of the Catholic Parliamentary repre- sentatives is before the public too. Nothing in it has been controverted, and, on reflecting, tbe Bishop of Limerick will see that these men, members of the Church of which he,is one with them, are not men to be made targets erhis blunders, or the marks for his ill- placed and VI-tamed secrets. Iris himself he has belittled. It is to the benth of biz:hems he has given pain, and to Vv. people who desire to regard that armlet assembly, together w'th their elected representatives, as dui; guardians, their protectors, their defenders.
Major Shelden Smith was committed for trial at Alton, Hants, on Wednesday, charged with the fraudulent ap- plication of £ll,OOO left in trust for the benefit of his son, a Ininor.
THE MURDER OF A WARDER.-
EXTRAORDINARY C,APTURE AT BRADFORD.

Jackson, the murderer of toe warder Webb, at Strangeways Gaol, Manchester, was captured on Mon- day, at Bradford. About 2 a.m., P.C. Flood apprehended a man for attempting to commit a burglary at Bradford Moor. A terrible struggle took place, in the course of which Jackson's head was injured. He was at length secured, and lodged at the Town Hall, and then gave the name of Harrison, Garnett-street. Brad- ford. No suspicion that it was Jackson was then enter- tained; but on the detectives visiting the cell subse- quently they noticed the man covering his hands. At once this raised suspicion; they examined him, and found a mark on the hand corresponding with the description of Jackson. They then stripped him, and found marks on the groin and neck, similarly corresponding. Prisoner, on seeing his case was hopeless, admitted, "Yes, I am the man. lam glad you have 'copped' me; for I have had a hard time of it." Jackson was known to be in the neighbourhood on Saturday, but Constable Flood had no suspicion when apprehending a housebreaker what an important capture he was making. On being searched at the charge office, the prisoner was found to have only a knife in his possession.

div.head: PRISONER IN COURT.
div.p: THE PRISONER IN COURT.

At Bradford Borough Court, on Monday, Jackson was brought up on the charge of breaking and entering. His appearance was haggard and worn,and he looked greatly dejected. Although the proceedings were very brief, h 6 was accommodated with a chair. As soon as he became seated, he leaned his head upon his hands, and quite hid his face from view. When asked, after the charge had been stated, if he had anything to say to the magistrates, he merely shook his head by way of reply. The prosecutor stated in evidence that upon hearing the noise he ran to the chamber window to look out, and, upon seeing the prisoner making off, said to the young man who lodges with him, "Get up and let's go and collar him." They accordingly went, and found the prisoner in an outhouse. When the prisoner came out he said, "Now, Marsh, don't say anything about it," but witness replied," You'll have to go with me." The Chief Constable stated that it was not until that morning that the man was identified as Jackson. He at first denied it, and said that Ile had only just Come from America, where he had been for some time, but then his clothing was not of American manufacture or cut, and on being questioned afterwards he admitted that he was the man wanted, and sta,.6l.d to the officers that he had had a hard time of it since the tragedy was committed. Ho also expressed a wish that he was "dead and done for." The prisoner was remanded in order that the Manchester authorities might be commu- cleated with.

div.head: JACKSON'S AUDACITY AS A BURGLAR
div.p: JACKSON'S AUDACITY AS A BURGLAR

- The news of the capture spread rapidly about the town, and occasioned great excitement, as there had been a suspicion that. Jackson was in the neighbourhood, and public interest had been at fever point. A few days ago a robbery was committed in Hustler-place, not far from where the prisoner was captured, which the police are confident was his work, and in which his actions were characterised by his usual consummate cool- ness. After ransacking the lower rooms of the house, he helped himself to a hearty breakfast,and smoked for some time on the doorstep. Before he left the place on Satur- day the police heard of him being in Manchester-road. Bradford, but he managed to get out of their way. Since his capture Jackson has acted as if he considered the game was up. He seemed to collapse completely when recognised, and the desperate courage which he had shown all through his career of crime appeared to desert him. He hung his head, muttering that he wished he were dead. Since making his es.mpe from gaol Jackson has shaved off his moustache, and his general appearance very slightly resembles the portrait and descriptions of him which have been published. His body marks, however, and his confession left no doubt as to his identity. According to his own state- ments, after he broke out of gaol, and provided himself with a suit of clothes.at the house he broke into in Old- ham, he made : his prison clothes into a bundle knd tlitew qem lwN,. .He then t2.2k the train to Halifax, and the day aftir reaching there he had his moustache and side whiskers shaved off, and his hair cut. He went to Bradford last Satur- day, having knocked about the district in the interval between leaving Halifax and arriving there, and visited amongst other places his native place. Birstall, where he was recognised by several people. When asked why he killed the warder, he on Monday, said he could not tell, he must have been mad. MARSHALL BOOTH'S STJSPICIONS. . . _ _ . _

, When interviewed by a reporter Marshall Booth, the ' real captor of Firth, said he made the acquaintance of the man on Monday week. Being, a mason and desiring another man, named Boocock, to work at the same job, he went to the White Bear Inn, Bradford Moor, for the pur- pose of seeing Boocock. On arrival at the inn he saw Boocock in the company of the stranger, who was pay- ing for beer, and by this means he succeeded in induc- Boocock to refuse Booth's offer of employment. About half-past five on Tuesday, Booth again went to the White Bear, and once more found the stranger there scattering his money somewhat profusely in paying for drinks for the company. He paid particular attention to Booth and Boocock and their friends, and at closing time asked the former if he might stay at his house. Booth objected at first, saying he did not know the man, and turning to the land- lady of house asked if she was personally acquain-fed W:itii-hitn. She replied in the negative, but said he appeared respectable enough, and accordingly "Jackson" was taken to Lee-square, where he stayed overnight. Before going, however, Booth insisted on the prisoner leaving his money with Mrs. Watson, the land- lady of the inn, and accordingly 28s. was left in Leicare. On the wednesdly the men all assembled at the same house, and spent their time drinking at various houses, the "stranger" still btifiz lavish with his money. At night he did not go With Booth, but with Thos. Briggs, of Rupert-stre't, Bradford Moor, and slept there over- night; but Thursday, Friday, and Saturday nights were spent at Lee-square. None of the mep went .to work, and on Jackson being asked where he was last 'em- ployed he said at "Johnny lye's, Shipley." He Scent on the spree, on Monday, he said, and on going to the place on Tuesday they. ref used to allow him to resume his work. His address, he said, was "29, Gr'arnett- street," but all along his companions entertained sus- picion,with regard to him,. and openly accused him of being the Manchester murderer. On one occasion Booth said "I'll bet 10 to 1 th'art Jackson," but the accused only laughed and turned the conversation to some more palatable topic. Only one of the party appeared to believe the man innocent, and that was Joseph Pearson, who resides with Booth at Lee-square, but despite their convictions, no one gave information to the pelice. On Sunday, Jackson's companions intended to bring their "spree" to a close, and accordingly Booth suggested to Jackson that be should go home. This he consented to do, and left the rest of the party at the Waggon and Horses at half- past nine p.m. After his departure the men and the landlord had tome conversation, and all arreed that their companion was none other than the murderer of Webb, the gaoler. Eventually Booth and Pearson went home and retired for the night, but shortly before one o'clock they were awakened by a noise in the house. Hearing the sounds continu- ing, Booth shouted "Who's there," and receiving no reply, put on his boots and went downstairs. At his ap- proach the intruder fled, but was followed by Booth and Pearson to a closet adjoining the premises of the Waggon and Horses Inn, where he had taken refuge. He closed the door, and thus prevented his friends from effecting a capture. Booth, however, obtained a plank and forced the door, with the assistance of Pearson and the land- lord of the Waggon and Horses. Jackson, on seeing escape was hopeless, said, "It's all right, Marsh; it's me; let's go ;" but in reply to this he was told he would have to ego with his captors first. On being seized he made a desperate struggle to rmain.his liberty, but was overpowered by the others, and eventually given into the custody of Police-constable Flood.

div.head: JACKSON AS A VOCALIST.
div.p: JACKSON AS A VOCALIST.

The prisoner is a " vocalist" of no mean powers, and on Saturdays, since his arrival at Bradford. highly grati• fled the company at the White Bear Inn with his songs. To the taproom company he sang "The Thorn," and afterwards he was introduced into the bar parlour and rendered the song "The pilgrim of love." He must have been possessed of a tremendous nerve, for immediately behind where he stood in the bar parlour was a bill describing him end the murder for which he was wanted. One humorous incident occurred in connection with his stay in Lee-square. On the first night he spent there Booth introduced him without the knowledge of his mate, and during the course of the night, in consequence of there being three in bed, the prisoner fell off on to the floor. "What's up?" asked Pearson. "Oh, it's noblatit Jackson here," said Booth in a jolting manner, and the three went off to sleep again.

div.head: CLOSING SCENE IN THE BRADFORD POLICE
div.p: CLOSING SCENE IN THE BRADFORD POLICE
COURT.

Firth spent' a quiet night in the cell at Bradford, and c.ave his guardians,' Detectives Talbot. and Butterworth. ,o trouble. He was very unwell, and had to be treated hy the police surgeon. He was extremely depressed, sat all night in one attitude, and did not talk at all. Jackson was visited on Tuesday morning by relatives and a friend, but he Made no communication to them. His demeanour had undergone a complete change in cap- tivity, and he seemed completely broken down and ill in mind andbody. Yesterday morning he was brought up at the Bradford Police Court, before the Mayor (Alderman Morley) and a full bench of magistrates. Great interest was manifested in the proceedings by the pub- lic, the Town Hall being besieged by people anxious to crowd into the court; whilst a score or so of reporters from different parts of the kingdom were in attendance. There was a very evident murmur of excitement when the prisoner entered the dock. He seemed very weak and nervous, and buried his face in his hands, which he rested on the dock-rail as soon as he took his place, and remained in this position until he was led down the dock steps again. Chief Constable Withers detailed the facts of prisoner's apprehension,already set forth,and said that during Mon- day the prisoner had been fully identified as Jackson, alias Firth, by his two brothers; by Sergeant Girdham. If the Manchester Detective Department; and Warden Farley and Digging' of Strangeways. He had also been examined by the police surgeon (Dr. Lodge), who

had fottnd the scars on his groin, and the other marts, to correspond exactly with the description given. Under the circumstances, he asked that the charge of burgltry, on which prisoner was apprehended, should be with- drawn, and that he should be handed over to Superin- tendent Hicks, of the Manchester police, who was wait- ing to receive him, to convey him to Manchester to bake his trial on a more serious charge. Alderman Morley asked for evidence of identity, and Sergeant tiirdham then entered the witness-box, an 3 swore to the identity of the prisoner with a man named Kitson whom he had formerly had in custody, and also to his identity with the man imprieoued at Strangeways, under the name of Jackson, and " wanted" on the chargo of murder there.
The Chief Constable: Is there any doubt about itl-- Witness : None at all. _ _ _

The Chairman then directed the prisoner to lA handed over to the Manchester police; and he was led down the dock steps by Detective Talbot (to whom the credit of establishing his identity is due) and another officer, being then apparently in a fainting condition.

div.head: PRISONER PHOTOGRAPHED.
div.p: THE PRISONER PHOTOGRAPHED.

After Firth hici-Wee-ti.;;;nc;v-ecit-a-the-c;l1.-th; Bradford police took the precaution of having a photograph of him in his then condition. He submitted to the op- eration of photography without resistance or complaint, and an admirable negative was taken. ARRIVAL IN MANCHESTER—AN EXCITED CROWD. Immediately before the train started from Bradford, it with blinds closely drawn, was tacked to the front of the train, and was surrounded by immense crowds of people, who had scaled the walls and barri- cades in order to get a peep at the prisoner. This morbid curiosity manifested itself at all the stopping. places along the line, and crowds of people lined the railway just outside the station. The fact that Jackson was travelling by the train had been signalled to the principal stations en route, and somehow the news leaked out to the public, many of whom gathered round the saloon. No one, however, succeeded in getting sight of Jackson, the blinds effectually concealing him from view. At each station policemen mounted gnarl- At Todmorden, Superintendent Hicks opened the window for a second to receive a communication which had arrived from his colleagues in Manchester. At Roch- dale the fact of his journey had evidently not transpired. At Manchester, there was an enormous crowd of people at Victoria Station. The train stopped for a couple of minutes outside the station, opposite Red Bank, whence Jack-on made his escape a month ago. When the plat- firm was reached an ugly rush was made from both sides of the line to the saloon. With the utmost diffi- culty the police cleared a passage, and the crowd raced after the prisoner and officers down the subway, and heartily hooted the murderer. Jackson was, however, hustled into a cab, and driven straight to the Town Hall.

Firth was charged at the Manchester County Police Court, on Wednesday, with the murder of Ralph Dyer Webb at Strangeways Gaol on the 22nd of last month. The court was crowded, and a large number of people assembled outside, unable to gain admission. The pri- soner on being brought into the dock rested his face on his hands and remained in that attitude till the end. The proceedings were very brief, lasting about an hour and a half. Major Preston, Miss Little (matron of the gaol) and several warders gave evidence regarding the circumstances which immediately preceded the murder. The Stipendiary then committed Firth for trial at the Manchester Assizes next month.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT TO A. CHILD AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT TO A. CHILD AT WARRINGTON.

On Monday afternoon a child named John Cain, aged 5, the son of a labourer, living in Rose Yard, met with an accident that was attended with fatal consequences. John korster, a carter in the employ of Mr. Wm. Owen, mineral water manufacturer& was delivering some cases of ginger beer from a lurry drawn by two horses at a house in Mersey-street, when the child mounted on the wheel. On the lurry starting he was thrown to the ground, and the wheel passed over his neck and shoulders. Dr. Jack was called In, but before his arrival the child expired. On Wed- nesday evening, Mr. Samv.el Brighouse, coroner for South-West Lancashire, held an inquest in the Parade Room at the Warrington Police Station, touching tha death of the child. On the assembling of the jury, how- ever, the coroner announced that the carter, who was one of the principal witnesses, had in consequence of a misunderstanding not arrived, and the inquiry would therefore be adjourned until the following morning in order that the jury might not be inconvenienced. On Thursday evidence was given to the effect that whilst William Harrison, a carter in the employ of Mr. Williatri Owen. mineral water manufacturer, Earlestown, was delivering some cases of ginger beer at a house in Mer- sev-st., the boy climbed upon the wheel of his lurry, which was drawn by two horses. Not seeing the child, a youth named William Forster, who was with Harri- son, started the horses and the child fell under the wheel, which passed over his neck and shoulders. De- ceased was at once taken to the Police Station, and Dr. Jack was called in, but death took place before his arrival. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," no blame being attached to the driver.

div.head: FATAL FIRE IN MANCHESTER.--FOUR LIVER, LOST.-EXTRAOEDINARY CONDUCT OF FIREMEN.
div.p: FATAL FIRE IN MANCHESTER.--FOUR LIVER, LOST.-EXTRAOEDINARY CONDUCT OF FIREMEN.

Four lives were loot through a fire which broke out at a small stationer's shop in St. Andrew's-street, Ma:46es- ter, on Saturday. The shop was kept by a womlne named Martha Gains, a newsagent, and there were Hain., on the premises her son, David Gains, a young man, 26'. years of age; a servant, named Mary Owens, aged 17; and two lads, one named Thomas Owens, a brother of the last-named, aged 14, and Charles Clegg. also 14 years of age. The fire broke out after they had gone to bed. Mrs. Gains and Mary Owens occupied a room above the shop, David Gains an aoljoining room, and the two lads an upper 'room. Mrs Gains was the first of the inmates who became aware of the fire, and she at once left her bed and warned her son. The son rushed to the landing. and thinking his mother was following hint, and without giving others warning, rapidly made his way downstairs. Just as he reached the bottom the shutters and windows of the shop were broken in from the outside, and he was all but overcome by the great incoming rush of smoke and flames. Here was the fatal blunder that, in all probability. cost four lives. The wind rushed in and fanned the fire, and the only means or reatreat for those upstairs was at \ once cut off. Almost suffocated, David Gains managed to get out. His mother had not followed him. She may have gone back to warn Mary Owens and the two boys, or. being an old woman 87 years of age, she had possibly got just a little way down when the tire drove her back to her bedroom. Here it was, however, that she was eventually found. A crowd colleeted outside, and it in- cluded a number of firemen from outside towns, who were returniror from a fire brispide demonstration at • Ashton-under-Lyne. Information was also sent to the branch fire station at Fairfield-street Station, and within three minutes Fireman Wright was on the spot with the escape. Soon after more men came from Pollard. street, and at 11 36 there was a detachment from the Chief Station. A very serious charge is laid against the firemen who had been at the demonstration at 1 Ashton. Fireman Wright states that he arrived at 11 27, ind found the shop and the two rooms over it in flames. He placed the escape against the buildings, and went, to the window over the shop, where he had been told that Mrs. Gains was. He searched the room for some time, but could not find the woman. He then went to examine the other rooms used as bedrooms, but there was so Much smoke and the heat was so intense that he was driven back. On reaching the window at which he lad entered the building he found that the escape had been removed to another window. With great difficulty and in the face of blinding smoke he crawled along the cornice of the shop window to where the escape was. He saw that there was no possibility of res.- feline the people until the: fire had been somewhat subdued, and he at once attempted to get a jet at work from the mains. He alleges that e.nsiderable delay was caused by the outside firemen. One of them, in attempting to turn on the water, lind turned the tap the wrong way, and not only t, bat they broke the brass stand-tioint to which the jPI s were affixed. Meanwhile Asaistant-Superintendena • Savage and a force of men from the Central Fire Brigade Office arrived, and a jet was got to work. The firw having been subdued somewhat, Wright and engineet Hunt again entered the building, and in a room over the. -kap they found the charred remains of Mrs. Gains and gotry Owens, whose bodies were brought out and re- moved to a mortuary. In another room Wright and a fireman named Brooks found the two boys, and these. were at once brought out of the building and taken into an adjoining shop, where a medical man endeavoured unsuccessfully to restore animation. The tire was then completely subdued. An examination of the place showed that scone of the internal partitions were of wood, and that the whole of the contents of the place were of a very inflammable nature. The loss of fife is officially declared to be duo to the shop being broken onen and air being admitted without means being at hand to cheek the flames. The cause of the fire is put down to an escape of gas, which the young man, David Gains, says he looked for with a light. The inquest on the bodies of Mary Owen, Thos. Owen, Charles Clegg, and Martha Gain occupied the whole of Wednesday, and was resumed on Thursday. Evidence was given as to the nature of the fire and the conduct of the police and fireman. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. The jury acquitted the firemen and policemen, but severely censured the volunteer fire- man Copeland.

The plaintiff is twenty-four years of age, and the defendant a few years older. The defen- dant failed to appear.

SATURDAY, JUNE 16. 1888.

THE Government have had to acknowledge themselves beaten on the question of compensation to brewers and publicans. The feeling in the Rouse of Commons, and throughout the country, is so strong against the proposal to endow the beer- barrel as a national institution that there was little or no hope of their succeeding. So they have gurrendered with, or without, discretion. On Mon- day, when Mr. Smith, as leader of the House, was questioned upon the subject, he said nothing had Ilaenlt decided, and that, as the matter stood, the goinsing clauses of the Local Government Bill IPere " certainly " to be proceeded with; on Tues- 4aY Mr. Ritchie, the Minister in charge of the bill, announced that "the Government have resolved that they will not ask the House to proceed with the licensing clauses of the bill." It cannot be very flattering to "the trade" to find that Mr. Ritchie &fretted to treat the issue .as one -of minor impor- tance. "From the very first," he said, "the Gov- arnment did not consider that portion of the bill aa one which was in any sense vital to the rnea- &um." It, was a small matter, it seems, with this niongrel Ministry to attempt to endow the liquor traffic with hundreds of millions of money; though Witen Mr. GLADSTONE proposed to lend a portion 0413, of such a sum to Irish farmers, he was dealt 'With as if he was about to ruin the country. Again, when Mr. GLADSTONE was defeated, he resigned 4e a minister who had a character at stake; but When Lord SALISBURY is beaten, it is a matter of tio consequence—the clauses can be thrown over- board as so much lumber. They are not " vital" ; nothing is in fact to be regarded as "vital" which is deemed likely to affect the vitality of the Govern- Inca. They have no characters to lose, so they Cling to the only thing that is dear ,th them—their Places ! Well, it is something to put pressure on them through their fears; they go down without a blow before what they term "strenuous opposi- tion." They are beaten ignominiously, and have not earned the respect of either friend or foe. All that they can call their own is "self-contempt, bit- terer to drink than blood." If they believed

- that brewers and publicans had a legal and equit- able claim to compensation, they ought to have atood by that principle at whatever cost. Brewers °Ad publicans have a right to complain that they have been badly used in this matter by the Government; for they have been pushed to the front, forced to defend themselves on every side, kid then left, like Cardical WOLSEY, naked to their enemies. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN must feel that 11a) too, has been sold, for did he not go out of his 1'a.37 to champion compensation, even when he was told that the law was against him? How could ha think that the Government would abandon the ,!otopensation clauses as in no sense vital to the when he himself had described Mr. GLADSTONE 84 "past praying for" because he dared to dis- aPprove of them? Perhaps he will now think it is the Ministry that is "past praying for." It is certainly time for him to ask himself whether he is °II his head or his heels? There is an ugly story ' ring tai the effect that the member for West rainghara was at one time chairman of a 124rraingham Improvement Committee which im- PtQVed out of existence a number of tradesmen's 46/708. The shopkeepers waited upon Mr. CHAM- 11111iLati, and urged that they ought to be compen- . Bat,ted, seeing that by having their shops taken from 4116 in they had lost the business connection which : e3r had built up. But they got nothing; the :Ith°r of the doctrine of ransom had neither 7vwnrd nor a penny for them. All his sympathy 48 bottled up; and there was no getting out the bec'rk until a claim for compensation was put in by threlvera and publicans. Then the cork ftew out; c sYrapathy came with a rush; but oh, the pity It is wasted—absolutely wasted—for the t‘!revernment, in view of the "strenuous opposi- -10;" have practically declared that compensation t° Publicans is a matter of no consequence. The ellis°(18 h th_ as a moral—for Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, for rioet Publicans, and for the public; and that is t'° trust either a man or a Minister who dogs B.tielr to a principle because be has no principle stick to.

TtTESDAT liVit will be remembered by the Gov- ernment) rAOt only for the disastrous surrender onl the licensing qnestion; but for a defeat inflicted, later on, by means of one of their own supporters —Mr. L. 'Y. JENNINGS, the Tory member for Stockport. They might almost say with Hamlet —" one woe doth tread upon another's heels, so they follow." Mr. JENNINGS is one of those Conservatives, who, like Lord R. CHURCHILL, are in earnest in demanding a reform of the abuses of our system of military reorganisation; and to give effect to his views he moved "That the re- organisation in the Accountant-General's and Secretary's Departments of the 'Admiralty have injurious to the public interests by resulting in increased charges for thbse departments, and by needlessly adding to extravagant pensions and bonuses ; and that in any further re-organisations officials who are still able and willing to render service for the public money shall be 'provided with employment in other departments, instead of being forced to become useless burdens upon the country." The mischief of his resolution was that he proved his case, and not all the special pleading of Lord G. HAMILTON, or the friendly aid of Mr. CHILDERS, who defended his own action, could get rid of the strong impression which his speech produced. It was sought to dispose of Mr. .JENNixas by a side wind—by promise of inquiry, &c., but the member for Stockport stuck to his guns. He declined to take the hint that was given him by the party leaders to withdraw his mo- tion; a division was therefore taken, and the Gov- ernment were defeated. There was a majority against them of 19, there being 113 for Mr. JEN- NING'S motion, and 94 against it. This is not one of those cases, of course, to cause a Ministerial crisis; for Governments do not usually ally their fate with an abstract resolution; but when a Ministry suffers defeat twice in one evening there is no denying that it is discredited in the iiouse of Commons. It is a matter of history that it has been for some time so much in discredit with the country that it fears dissolution as the king of terrors. And yet, condemned as it is, in Parlia- ment and out of it, it is not unlikely, thanks to the hatred, or unreasoning dread, of Mr. GLAD- STONE on the part of Liberal Unionists, that it may drag on a miserable existence for several years. To such base uses have the Liberal Unionists come at last; and we say this more in sorrow than in anger.

THE Government Technical Instruction Bill is now in the hands of the public; but it cannot be said of it that it improves upon acquaintance with the full text of its provisions. It was under the consideration, last evening, of the Warrington Association for the Promotion of Technical Instruc- tion, arid the opinion was general that it will re- quire lartely amending to make it a good bill. It is an altogether timid, halting measure, and places so' many restrictions upon those who will have to carry it out that it is scarcely likbly to lead to success. The limit of expenditure is fixed, to begin with, at one penny in the pound—just as in the case of Free Libraries. Now, it may be that this will be quite as much as many communities will care to spend ;' but why should those who are willing to spend more be de- barred from doing what they deem best in the matter? School Boards will find themselves more or less crippled under the bill. They, may be called upon to aid other than board schools in the supply of such manual or technical instruction as they are giving to the children in board schools, "subject to such terms as may be agreed on or determined in pursuance of this act." If this clause means, as we take it to mean, that a certain portion of the money of the ratepayers shall be , handed over to the managers of voluntary schools to be spent in technical instruction, and apart from the control of the ratepayers, we venture to predict that it will meet with sturdy resistance. It leeks like a crafty move for getting in the thin end of the wedge for the endowment of denominational schools; and if it be adopted, it will put back the hands of the clock so far as educational reform is concerned. It is doubtless in harmony with the report which is about to be issued by the Royal Commission on Education; and that report, there is every reason to anticipate, will be of a reactionary kind. Pro- rision is also made for Free Library Committees bringing the act into operation, under certain specified conditions; and it may thus happen, where there is a School, Board at work, that two distinct bodies may be occupied in providing the supply of manual or technical instruction. Dual control is sure to work badly, and we cannot imagine how the Government came to think of such a thing, unless the design is to degrade the School Board system. Another difficulty which presents itself arises from the fact that technical instruction is practically limited, in the elementary schools, to children who have passed the sixth standard; and this means, as to the smaller towns, that there would never be a large and solid body to work upon. The standard will require re- ducing to the fifth—if the measure is to be of any value. It would be interesting to know what teachers in our national schools think of the bill; whether, in their opinion, it is likely to secure the end for which it is designed; and whether it is workable from the point of view of the elementary school. We shall be glad to open our columns to immediate discussion of the subject; for the measure is intended to be passed this session, and there is no time to lose.

A CREDITOR'S ANNOYANCE.—Before His 11011 OUT, Judge Thompson, at the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, Mr. J. P. Mearns, solicitor, appeared on behalf of John Prescott, of Ashton's farm. Burton- wood, and applied for the committal of John Henry Forshaw, of 9, Barrow-st., St. Helens. Mr. Mearns stated that the action was originally brought in the High Court, and a judgment summons had been taken out in that court. That was the fourth occasion on which he (Mr. Mearns) had had to ap- pear against that very stupid defendant. He had served one period of 21 days, and two periods of 40 days, and had expressed his willingness to serve further terms. The plaintiff was willing to accept any reasonable offer. An order had been made against the defendant to pay 30s a month, and he was now ten guineas in arrears. All he had was in his wife's name. The debt was for milk supplied, and a horse and cart, and the defendant now al- leged that he had no money.—Defendant informed his Honour that he had no money at all, but if he could borrow it he would pay the whole debt a. He was sold up under a bill of sale.—Mr. Meanie asked if he could make any offer.-Defendant replied that he could not.—His Honour committed him for 40 days, observing that he thought defendant's con- duct was a dishonest proceeding, and he could not be an honest man.
" TOUCR AND GO." The licensing clauses are like the Government— they are "abandoned."

It would seem that Mr. Chamberlain is in the way of abandonment. He has turned round on his own offspring—the Caucus. It was a very good child so long as it said " ditto " to Its father; but the moment it ventured to differ from him, why, then it became a disgrace to the family.

It was in this wise that the member for West Birmingham came to deliver himself. Mr. Shaw- Lefevre, on Tuesday, sought to amend the Local Government Bill by providing that one-third of the county council should retire annually instead of the whole council retiring every three years. Mr. Ritchie was in a corner, but "Joseph" came to his rescue by saying that "when people were con- stantly being called on to give a vote theybecame indifferent, and the whole matter fellinto the hands of caucuses and inachine politicians." This from the inventor of the machine! "Who could have thought it ? "

We publish to-day an interesting letter from Mr. Whitham which shows that he has as quick an eye for lineman as he had for English Toryism. He adds, in a private note, that Mrs. Whitham gave birth, on May 17th, to "a splendid specimen of babyhood," and that "both are doing well." It will be noticed that Mr. Whithoax has changed his address, which is now 13, Valparaiso-at., San Francisco.

A movement is oa foot which has got to the Parliamentary bill stage for the better regulation of private clubs. Publicans have a right to com- plain that some institutions are nothing better than drinking clubs. The registration which is proposed would be the death-blow of this class. There can be no objection to the new bill if it is not framed so as to interfere with the legitimate freedom of legitimate clubs.

Jackson has been laid by the heels at last ; and the marvel is that he has had such a long run. Booth, the mason who ultimately closed with him for breaking into : his house, seems to be taking some credit to himself for having all along sus- pected that his drinking chum was the Man- chester murderer. He does not appear to see that, if he suspected the mysterious stranger, it is no credit to him that he failed to communicate his suspicions to the police.

As to the Bradford police, there is a story going that even when they had Jackson in ga9l they did not know of their prize until the pri- soner told three youths, who were also in gaol, that he was the man who was wanted for the Manchester murder. Whether this be true or not, it is clear that when Jackson was apprehended it did not occur to the constable who lodged him in gaol that he might be the Manchester murderer. However, it is something to know that the ruffian is again under lock and key.

Everything goes to show that we made a mess of it when we annexed" Burmah. There is not much in the way of news, but the news is gener- ally bad. The latest item is to the effect that a sergeant andtwelve policemen, presumably natives, are in custody on a charge of robbing and burning six houses, carrying off girls, and killing a villager. This reveals, like a lightning fla'sh, a shocking state of things; and we fear there is ground for saying—" Thus bad begins, but worsp remains be- hind."

Two beggars brought before the magistrates within the past few days are types of the fra- ternity. One was begging as a "blind" man at Warrington. He was drunk, but he was not blind; the shade which he wore covered at least one lovely black eye. The other case was at Earlestown ; and in this instance .26s had been picked up with a begging letter. This imposter also got drunk. When will the public come to see that they are themselves at fault by aiding such rascals?

Crewe was happy on Saturday in receiving the gift of the Queen's Park from the London and North-Western Railway Co. And then think of its being opened by his Royal Highness the Great Duke of Cambridge The event sets • One think- ing how it would have gone with Warrington if the London and North-Western had laid their works at Warrington instead of at Crewe. The story goes that Lord Winmarleigh was approached on the subject but he did not see his way then. Ah, if he had but the chance now

John Henry Forshaw, of St. Helens, is the 'quintessence of stupidity. He owes a debt of £lO 108 Od in respect of transactions in milk and a horse and cart sold him, and prefers to go to gaol rather than pay. He has already " done " one period of 21 days and two of 40, and is now off for another 40 days. What makes his case look all the worse is the fact that when he is out of prison ' he carries on business in his wife's name. He is a tough subject, but he will perhaps find that Judge, Thompson can keep up the game with him. , The'Seeling in Warrington is just about as strong against compensating Mr. Paterson as against compensating publicans and if the Gas Committee are wise in time they will, like the Government, beat a retreat. It is all moonshine to talk, as some special pleaders are doing, about not being ungrateful to an old servant. When an old servant has been having two a year it is difficult to see where the gratitude should come in —unless it be on the part of the old servant. That retaining fee of £lOO a year must be dropped; it Won't do. • And what about the leakage of gas to which Alderman Burgess referred at the Councilmeeting ? We hear it stated that the leakage is in worn-out street mains ,• that it amounts to sixteen per cent.; and that it represents a loss to the ratepayers of four thousands of pounds per year The statement seems incredible, but what if it should prove to be true? And what if the leakage has not been reported to the committee when it might have been? And what if it has been going on for years?

There is or was a Ratepayers' Association. How is it that nothing is heard of it when ratepayers' questiops are to the front? Is it dead, or it is sleeping, or is it only playing the fool? It is no use the cuemittee doing a bit of hole-and-corner work. Let a meeting of the whole members be called; and, if there is any life in the organisation, let it make itself felt.

Robert Travis, after undergoing two years' im- prisonment on a sentence for life for a murder he never committed receives the Queen's pardon and a suit of clothes! Is this to be all ? Is he to be told that there is no provision for compensating him? Granted that the jury did their best, society now knows that it did, him a grievous wrong, and society should do its best to make some amends. If there is no law to enable us to do the right thing in such a case, that is a good reason why a bill should be run through both Houses in a week or ten days.

Mr. W. J. Lane is one of the Irish members who has been in gaol; but ,he is not quite so bad as Mr. Balfour's brush would paint him. On Tueaday night, at Cork, two children fell into the river at Pope's Quay. A strong current was run- ning at the time, and the children must have been drowned but for Mr. Lane, who took off his coat and sprang into the water, and with some diffi- culty succeeded in rescuing both children. He will get the medal of the Humane Scciety. Mr. Balfour will have to undergo a great change before he will be recognised as a humane man.

Henry George is out of favour with the United Labour Party of America. It is stated that he is to be expelled from the society because of his hav- ing violated the county constitution of the party, which declares that no member shall at any time fuse or dicker with any other political party. "Dicker—what the deuce is it to dicker ? " the English reader will probably ask. The word is American as to common use, and means, as the context would imply, bartering or bargaining. In Headley' s "Letters from Italy" we have the phrase "dickering with thievish Italian landlords " ; I and this as far back as 1849.
