div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

MOST PEOPLE ARE IGNORANT Of the value of eyesight. In many iustancee, when they first find their eyesight failing, they purchase all kinds of in- ferior manufactured spectacles, which in the end cause their eyes to burn and ache. To remedy this defect, A. Franks, of 95 and 97, Deansgate, and 44, Market-st., Manchester, 143, Lord-st., Southport, and GO, Whitefriargate, Hull, has invented his " Per- fection " Spectacles, which he adapts at either of the above addresses at 78 61 per pair. lie will guarantee that they are not to be equalled in the coun- try for clearness, coolness, and rest they impart to the eyes. Pamphlet " How to preserve the sight" free on application.---sidvt BRUNSWICK WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN.— From our advertisement columns it will be seen that the annual sermons in aid ef this school will be preached in St. Paul's Chapel, to-morrow (Sunday) be the Rev. W. L. Watkinson, of Scarborough. Mr. Watkinson, who has had conferred upon him the coveted distinction of Foam- icy Lecturer, Lecturer, is one of the most popular preachers in the Wesleyan ministry. Those who attend the services will no doubt have an intellectual treat, besides helping a worthy object. PRIMITIVE METHODIST ANNIVERSARY, WIDNES.—The annual sermons in connection with the Primitive Metho- dist Chapel, Hutchinson-St., Widnes, were preached on Sunday by the Rev. Fred Jeffs, of Preston. In the after- noon the DRY. R.Burdon, superintendent of the Wesleyan Circuit, delivered an address to the parents and scholars. There was a good congregation at each service, and the collections amounted to £2O. On Monday evening a sacred concert was given by the choir, assisted by a few . friends. There was a fair attendance. Mr: H. Timmis occupied the chair. ACCIDENTS AT WIDNES..—A young man named JameS Mahony was admitted into the Widnes Accident Hospi- tal, on Monday morning, suffering from a fracture of the skull and a broken wrist. He was employed at the Widnes Foundry, and while superintending an overhead travelling crane, he fell to the ground, and alighting on his head he sustained the serious injuries mentioned. He was unconscious on Monday and Tuesday, and now lies in a very precarious condition. Dr. Hutchinson is the medical attendant.—A young girl named Roach, whose parents live at 13, Peel-st., was following a crowd of people along Victoria-road, on Monday night, when she was knocked down, and broke her right arm near the wrist. LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT NORTHWICH.—Before the Government had announced their, intention of with- drawing the compensation clauses of the Local Govern- ment Bill, Mr. W. Handley, general secretary to the Northwich Division Liberal Association had commenced the organisation of an effective protest against the objec- tionable proposals. The demonstration has still to take place at Winnington Park, the residence of Mr. Brunner, and as will be seen from an advertisement, our member I and other gentlemen will be present and speak. The protest will now take a wider range than was intended, and other matters in the bill that require ventilation and amendment will fortis the subject of the speeches of the gentlemen. It is highly probable too, that a petition against the imprisonment of Mr. O'Brien and Mr. I Dillon will be prepared, and be ready to receive the sig- natures of the thousands who will assemble in the park. The temperance societies of the division will take a pro- minent part in the meeting. Every arrangement has been made for the convenience and comfort of the Run- corn contingent, who, if favoured with fine weather,will enjoy a beautiful sail up the Weaver Valley. In view of possible rain the boat will be covered, and the meeting will be held in a spacious tent. Refreshments will be provided on the ground at reasonable charges. We trust that Runcorn will be numerously represented. MARRIAGE OF MISS CAUSLAND, OF RUNCORN.—The marriage of Mr. Tom Millington, son of Mr. Thomas Millington, and Miss Mary Ann (May) Causland, eldest daughter of the Rev. J. Causland, minister of the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Greenway-road, Runcorn, was solemnised on Thursday afternoon at that place of worship. The bride was tastefully attired in a dress of white needlework, with wreath of orange blossoms and veil, and carried a bouquet of beautiful flowers, the gift of Miss L. Millington, of Manchester. The bridesmaids were Miss Florrie Causland, Miss Louisa Millington, Miss Nellie Causland, and Miss Bertha Millington, and they wore dresses of cream and blue. The groomsmen were the brother of the bride, Mr. James Dominick Booth Causland, aud Mr. Walter Millington. The service was performed by the Rev. J. Causland, the bride's father, who was assisted by the Rev. Mr. Dickinson. After the ceremony the happy pair were driven from the chapel to the residence of the bride's father in Waterloo-road, where the wedding breakfast was partaken of, there being about 30 invitel guests present. Mr. and Mrs. Millington subsequently left Runcprn for the Isle of Man, where they will spend the honeyinoon. The bride's cake was given by Mrs. Corns, whilst the wedding carriages ,were Supplied by Mr. Peter Brereton, Penketh-lane, Runcorn. The pre- sents were both numerous and costly, and comprised many articles both useful and ornamental. SOCIETY FOR THE PROPAGATION OF THE GOSPEL.—In connection with this society the annual sermons were preached at Runcorn, on Sunday. At the Parish Church the Rev. J. F. Phelps, vicar of Bosley, preached incom- ing and afternoon; at St. Michael's' the Rev. J. H. Wileockson, of Weston Point preached in the morning, and the Rev. G. 11. Seeley in the afternoon, and the Rev. G. F. Phelps in the evening. At Weston the Rev. G. A. Tindall preached in the morning and afternoon, and the Rev. G. H. Seeley in the evening. The Rev. Joseph Holden preached at Weston Point morn- ing and afternoon, and the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, vicar- of Runcorn. Collections were • made at each ser- vice. On Monday evening the annual public meeting was held in the National Schools Runcorn. The Rev. A. Maitland Wood, M.A., occupied the chair. The Rev. ,T. F. Phelps, who was for 31 years a resident in New- foundland, delivered a speech upon the work 'carried on by the society in that country. When he first went there there were only 20 clergy; now there were 50, and yet there was room for 50 more so far as the work went. If it were not for the aid given by the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel half of the work in the Newfoundland diocese would collapse at once. The Chairman announced that the total amount contributed to the society from Runcorn last year was £23 14s id. (Applause.) The Rev. J. Holden was appointed local secretary in place of the Rev. J. D. Ozanne. The usual votes of thanks concluded the proceedings. THUNDERSTORM AT RIINCORN.—About one o'clock OH Wednesday at noon, the neighbourhood of Runcorn was visited with a severe thunderstorm. Although not of long duration, the storm was of a very violent nature, and created much alarm amongst a portion of the in- habitants. The downpour Of rain was so heavy as to create quite a miniature deluge, and as usual when there is more than an ordinary downfall, the water rushed down Penketh-lane in considerable volume, and making its way across Bridge-st., flooded the Royal Hotel and the Mersey Vaults, and also the stable yard of Mr. S. Yam- wood. Hailstones of extraordinary size also descended. The lightning was very vivid, and the peals of thunder were loud and prolonged. Fortunately, throughout the town very little damage was done, but the Church of St. Michael's and All Angels, iii Greenway-road, was struck by the lightning, and injured to some ex- tent. sThe stone crosses, about three feet in height, which adorned the roof at the east and west end of the church were "clean cut off "at the base, and falling into the yard were smashed to atoms. The electric fluid also pierced the roof of each transept in two places, and singularly enough, the holes correspond both as regards size and position with each other. The leads of the roof were also torn up for a considerable distance. Happily the interior of the edifice was unharmed and about £4O will set matters to rights. A number of brick- layers, joiners, Sze., who were engaged in constructing some property in the neighbourhood of the church were evidently in the path of what is popularly known as the "thunderbolt," and each received a shock of electricity that created the greatest dismay amongst them. They rushed from the building in which they were sheltering from the storm with one accord, and in their haste they became jambeci. in the lobby. One of their fellow work- men who came upon the scene shortly afterwards de- scribes them as having the faces of ghosts. One of the men felt the effects of the shock next day, and was un- able to resume his work. A short distance away a youth was struck by the electric fluid and carried from one side of the room to the other.

RUNCORN STARR-BOWILETT BUILDING SOCIETY.—In Con- nection with the first Runcorn Society the thirtieth ap- propriation took place at the offices in Bridge-st. on Mbn- day evening. Mr. Povah occupied the chair. The result of the ballot was that Mr. Thomas Clair, of Runcorn, is entitled to the use of £2OO, free of interest, for 124 years. TRE WIDNES Wire BEATER. —John Duggan, of 14, High-st., was again brought before the Widnes magis- trates on a charge of inflicting grievous bodily harm to his wife Julia. Dr. Hutchinson certified that the woman was not in afit condition to take part in investigating the case. She, however, appeared in court, but did not on this occasion interrupt the proceedings.—The prisoner was remanded Or a week. STORM AT WIDNES.—A storm of short duration, but great intensity, broke over Widnes on Wednesday at noon. The lightning was of startling brilliancy, and the thunder claps were so loud that the idea was con- veyed that the buildings were being shaken with the shock. Rain descended in torrents, and at intervals DkilStOneS as largo as ordinary marbles fell with con- siderable force. No serious damage is reported. Dons AT LARGE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Ses- sions,,on Thursday, the following persons were charged with allowing their dogs to be at large :—George Davies, coal dealer, Kaludah Terrace; Henry Parkes, Frederick- et.; William Shufflebottom, Gladstone-st. ; Thomas Kelsall, Widnes-road; John Carney, Moon-st. ; Wm. Donogan, Railway-st. ; Patrick Duffy, Oxford-st. ; Ed- ward Percy, Victoria-St.; and Thomas Anderton, Mid- wood-st. A fine of Is, and costa 7s 6d, was imposed upon them. RoBBERS AT HALE.--William Shields, a well-known thief, and John Walsh, a youth, were brought before the Widnes magistrates, on Monday, charged with stealing a dish and 71bs. of beef, the property of Ciss Green, of Hale-road; and also with stealing 131 yards of calico, a piece of flannel, and an axe. belonging to Mr. Richard Lewis, of Ditton Lodge. P.C. Lewis met the prisoners at Hale, and observing that they appeared to be anxiously concealing something under their coats. he stopped them, and made an examination. He found the articles mentioned: The prisoners were remanded for a week, s that inquiries might be made concerning their history. OBSTRUCTING WIDNES-ROAD.—Thomas Hawkins, green- grocer, was summoned before the Widnee magistrates, on Thursday, to answer a charge of obstructing the foot- path in Widnes-road, on the 2nd June. P.C. Townley stated that there were three hampers and a box of oranges on the footpath, and several persons had to leave the footpath in consequence. He had cautioned the defendant a score of times about the practice. Mrs Hawkins, who appeared, said the constable did not need to have summoned her husband for what it was—trade was not that good in Widnes. A fine of Is and costs 8s 6d was imposed .—Samuel James Francis, greengrocer, of Widnes-road, was fir ed in a similar sum for a like offence committed on the same day. WIDNES CASES AT THE SESSIONS.—At the Liverpool County Quarter Sessions, during this week, the following sentences were passed :—Patrick Moran, 45, striker, inde- cently assaulting Alice Ditchfield, at Widnes, six months; Thomas Tansey, 19, labourer, maliciously damaging pro- perty at Widnes, six months; William Kinsella, 19, labourer, was sentenced to three months' imprisonment for having at Widnes, unlawfully wounded John Moffatt; Leo Ahrenfeldt, 23, cloth dealer, stealing from the Central Hotel, at Widnes, a silver Geneva watch and chain, the property of Harriet Vicars, and a silver watch and chain and revolver, the property of Albert Edward Wilson, four months; Patrick Costello, 36, labourer, maliciourly wounding John Connolly, at Widnes, three months. ROBBERY FROM A WIDNES HOTEL.—Mr. Thomas Ger- rard, of the Alexandra Hotel, has just been the victim of a dishonest servant. About a month ago a youth named William Dickson, who came from the neighbour- hood of Liverpool, was employed by Mr. Gerrard as bar- man. Late on Saturday night a parcel of money, amounting to over £2O, which was taken at the theatre, was placed on the dressing table in Mr. Gerrard's bed- room. The money was there on Sunday morning, but is Dickson, who went out in the afternoon, did not re- turn at the accustomed time, suspicions were aroused, and an examination revealed that the money had dis- appeared. A watch belonging to Mrs. Gerrard, and some other valuables which had been lying close to the money were, however, left behind. HOUSE ROBBERY IT Moss BANE. At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, John Conroy, a young man, was charged with having, on the 2nd April, stolen a coat, a vest, and a pair of socks, the property of Patrick Byrne, labourer, of 25, Walmsley-st. On the date in question Byrne was lodging at the house No. 2, Mary-st., Moss Bank, Widnes, and the prisoner also lived at the same house. The articles mentioned in the charge were hang- ing on the kitchen door at night, when Byrne went to his work and the next morning they could not be found. The prisoner was also missing, but he had left his clogs behind. On the same day the prisoner pledged the vest, with Ellis Bradshaw, of 12, Scotland-place, Liverpool, for a shilling.—P.C. Bruce apprehended the prisoner on the 6th inst. as he was leaving Preston gaol. He admit- ted his guilt, and was committed to take his trial at the next Liverpool Assizes. PROCEEDINGS AFFECTING Dons AT RUNCORN.—At Run: corn Petty Sessions,ton Monday, Thomas Clough, but- cher, Church-st.. was summoned for having his dog in- securely muzzled. The strap that was fixed on the dogs head was produced. Mr. Brundrit said that was not a muzzle. It was only a strap that slipped about in any way. The defendant said it was as Mr. Grice made it. Mr. Brundrit said he had nothing to do with that. A wire muzzle, or a leather muzzle on the same principle should be used. The defendant, who said he had now got a wire muzzle arm fined is, and costs lOs 6d. For allowing their dogs to be at large unmuzzled the follow- ing were each fined Is, and costs 8s 6d :—Charles Wilson. Greenway-road : Edward Holt, Gilbert-st. ; Edward Jeffs, Bridge-st. ; Joseph Grundy, Masonic Hotel; and Thos. Cooke, Greenway-road. For keeping a dog with- out e. license Joseph Hancock, of Lock-st., was fined 5s and costs. BOWLING MATO FiAsCO AT WIDNEs.—An amusing termination to a bowling match took place at the Ball Inn, Ditton, Widnes, yesterday afternoon. W. Rhodes, of Runcorn, and J. Hunt, of Ditton, had agreed to play a game of 51 up for £5 a side, and both men turned up at the time agreed upon. Hunt was disabled with a mbroken arm, and Rhodes complained that he was suffer- ing from an ulcerated throat, and therefore was unable to play. After giving Rhodes thre-e quarters of an hour in which to re-consider his decision not to play, Hunt went on the green and quickly scored the necessary 51 by himself. Subsequently Rhodes emerged from the hotel with his bowls in his hands and had a practice in the rain for about half an hour. He then expressed his willingness to play a game of 21 up if two "old hands," who were present, would fine the necessary stake. The affair was the cause of much merriment amongst the assembled bowlers. DRUNK AND DiSoRDERLY.—The following persons were each fined 5s and costs for being drunk and disorderly: —Conrad Polies, Beamont-st. ; John McGee, no resi- dence; Thos. Byrne, 38, Margaret-st.: Rebecca Rimmer, Water-st.; Joseph Rowlands, Carlife-st. • John McAlee, lEleanor-st. : and James Entwistle, Violet-st. Martin IBrannon, an army reserve man,who resides in Tanhouse- cottages, pleaded guilty to having, on the Bth May, threatened to assault Samuel Hurst, landlord of the lCommercial Inn, Page-lane. Because the prosecutor re- fused to serve him with a glass of ale on the ground that he was drunk, the prisonerthreatened to knock his brains out. He was ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for three months. William Hewitt, of 94, Midwood-st.. was fined lOs and costs for being arunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart. For creating a breach of the peace, on the 2nd June. Miles Burns, of Sutton's-lane, was bound over to be of good behaviour for three months. DAMAGING A RopE AT RisrScOßN.—William Farrell, builder and contractor, New Egerton-street, was sum- moned before the. Runcorn magistrates ea Monday to answer a sharge of having, on the 19th May, wilfully damaged a rope belonging to William Myles, foreman cutter to Messrs. Unsworth Brothers, who also lives in Egerton-st. Mr. Maddock, solicitor, appeared for the complainant. The children of Mr. Myles, it appeared, had fixed a clothes line between each side of the yard door, and were using it as a swing. It was alleged that the defendant, who was the owner of the property, cut down the rope without complaining to the complainant. The damage was laid at Is.—The defendant stated that the manner ill which the rope was used damaged the property, and inconvenienced the passers by. He asked the children to tell their ma to take it down, and one of the children returned and said her ma would not do so. Mr. Myles came out, and said the property 'was not his, (the defendant's), as it had a monkey upon it, and he replied that it had one in it as well.—Mr. Brundrit said this was a case which might have been kept out of court, and was only adding expense upon some one or other. If the defendant had spoken to the man or his wife instead of the children it would have been better.— The defendant was ordered to pay costs, Is 6d. A CRONTON DISPUTE.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, James Conway, a farm labourer in the em- ploy of Mrs. Hedgcock, Upton, summoned Wm. Sparkes, a file cutter at Crouton, for assaulting him on the Bth June. A cross-summons had been issued charging Con- way with a similar offence. John Radley, a young man, was charged with using threatening language to Con- way. Mr. F. J. Poole appeared on behalf of Conway, and,,Mr. J. W. Knowles was for the defendants. It ap- peared that the pigeons of the neighbourhood settled on Mrs. Hedgcock's land, and devoured the seed and dam- aged the crops; and Conway, in obedience to the orders of his mistress, shot at the birds. A pigeon belonging to Sparkes was killed, and as Conway was driving through Crouton to the colliery the defendants overtook him, and Sparkea demanded payment for his bird. He was told to apply to Mrs. Hedgcock, when he threa- tened that if Conway did not pay him he would take the worth of the bird out of him. The defendants attempted to get into the cart, and Conway drove back to the Unicorn Inn to seek protection. Here he was attacked by Sparkes, and struck in the face and body, and a scuffle ensued on the ground. On the other side, it was contended that Conway de dared himself man enough for both Sparkes and Radley, and was the first to use vio- lence. It was alleged that he struck Sparkes' head with a spade, causing a swelling as large as an egg.—The evidence was most comlictiag, and the Bench bound both Sparkes and Conway over to keep the peace for three months. The case against Radley was dismissed.

div.head: DEATH
div.p: DEATH
OF THE EMPEROR FREDERICK.

POTSDAM, FIIIDAY.—The Emperor passed quietly away at 11 o'clock this morning. A Central 'News telegram states that the Emperor's night was at times turbulent, and the weakness increased every hour. He was able to recognise the Empress as she took her place by the bedside, but relapsed into a state of stupor during the morning, and passed away painlessly about 11 o'clock. POTSDAM, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—The following further particulars concerning the Emperor's last hours have transpired :—" At midnight his Majesty palised half an hour in an armchair, and took some nourishment. At three o'clock the weakness increased alarmingly, and those members of the Imperial family who had left the Castle were summoned by telegraph to return. At ten this morning all access to the Castle was stopped.

div.head: EXCITEMENT IN BERLIN.
div.p: EXCITEMENT IN BERLIN.

Berlin telegrams published in the "St. James's Gazette" state that Berlin is in a state of intense excite- ment. Business is almost at a standstill. All the mem- bers of the family and the high ministers of State assembled in the death chamber. A ministerial Council has been sitting this morning, under the Presidency of Prince Bismarck. The minister of Justice went to Fried- richskron this morning._

div.head: OFFICIAL ANNOUNCEMENT.
div.p: THE OFFICIAL ANNOUNCEMENT.

The following official announcement of the Monarch's I death has been issued at Berlin :—" The Royal sufferer I has ended his earthly career. By God's decree, his 'Majesty the Emperor and King Frederick, our most gracious master, passed into eternal rest shortly after eleven o'clock this morning, 'after long and grievous sufferings, borne with admirable fortitude and submis- sion to God's will. The Royal House and our people, twice bereaved within so short a time, deeply mourn the all too early decease of their much-beloved ruler." RECEPTION OF THE NEWS IN LONDON.

The news of the death of the Emperor was received in Landon at three mittutes past 12, and was pablished in the streets a few minutes later. The intelligence created a profound impression, and the evening papers were eagerly bought up. Hundreds of calls were made and cards left at the German Embassy, and messages of condolence were telegraphed to Germany in great num- bers.

The falai news was at pnce sent on to the Queen and Prince of Wales, the latter of whom was at Sunningdale Park. A telegram was received at Marlborough House at noon, from Sunning&le, stating that their Royal Highnesses would be in London at lunch time.and order- ing the carriages. The Central News says :—The death of the German Emperor has created a profound impression in political circles as well as in commercial centres. The Govern- ment received a message from Sir Edward Malet at 10 o'clock, stating that the Emperor had passed a turbulent night, and at a quarter to 12 a second telegram was re- ceived in Downing-st. from the British Ambassador an- nouncing that death had put an end to the noble patient's sufferings. On many buildings the flags were at once lowered to half-mast, while numerous telegrams, con- veying words of sympathy and condolence, were des- patched to Potsdam and Berne. THE FEELING IN PARLIAMENT.

The lobby of the House of Commons was filled yester- day afternoon with groups of members discussing the news with serious demeanour' and on all sides there were expressions of sorrow at the melancholy fate of the Emperor, and of sympathy with his bereaved Consort. It is stated that on Monday A formal vote of condolence with the Empress and Imperial family will be moved, in both Houses of Parliaments. In the House of Commons yesterday afternoon Mr. W. 11. Smith and Sir William Harcourt referred with deep regret to the sad event.

div.head: FEELING I Trim: COUNTRY.
div.p: THE FEELING I Trim: COUNTRY.

When the, news of the death of the Emperor arrived on 'Change at Liverpool, there was con- siderable sensation for some time, and a cessation of business. Everywhere there was only one expression of feeling—one of profound admiration and regret for the departed Emperor and of sympathy for his illustrious Consort. A large number of gentlemen, more especially the foreign residents of the city, called at the German Consulate and left their condolences. Flags were hoisted half .mat on most of the public buildings. The majority of the vessels in dock hoisted their ensigns half-mast

high. The news of the Emperor's death was received with unfeigned sorrow in Manchester, which has a large Ger- man community. In Glasgow also much regret was ex- pressed. Flags in both towns were raised half-mast. When the announcement reached Warrington it came upon the people with something of the nature of a shock, despite the fact tha,t it was not nnexpected. Before the news came the critical condition of the Emperor was the subject of much comment, and when the final announce- ment was made it became the almost universal topic of conversation.

div.head: QUEEN AND THE _EMPEROR.
div.p: THE QUEEN AND THE _EMPEROR.

The earliest telegram to reach this country conveying the sad news was one to Her Majesty shortly before noon. This was immediately forwarded to Balmoral, from whence a loving motherly message was instantly transmitted to the Empress at Potsdam. The news was forwarded at the same time, over, his direct wire, to

the Prince of Wales at Sunningdale, Ascot, and His Royal Highness returned to town with the Princess and his daughters without delay, arriving at Marlborough House at a quarter-past two o'clock. It is understood that His Royal Highness will leave for Berlin this (Saturday) night, and it is expected that the Duke of Cambridge will accompany him. It is believed that the funeral service will be held at Westminster Abbey, and the Chapel Royal, if possible, simultaneously with the funeral service in Berlin. THE FUNERAL.

BERLIN, FRID tY AFTERNOON. In accordance with the expressed wish of the late Emperor Frederick he will be buried in the Garrison Church at Potsdam, where rest the remains of Frederick the Great and of the Great elector.

The new Emperor, William the Second, has already issued a proclamation announcing his accession. PARIS, FRIDAY EVENING. President Carnot has sent a telegram of sympathy to the New Emperor, THE EMPEROR'S CONDITION ON THURSDAY. The following telegrams give detailsof the Emperor's condition on Thursday : A Central News telegram dated Berlin, Thursday, says !—The news from Potsdam this morning is unhap- pily of the very gravest character. His Majesty's condi- tion is extremely critical, and fears for the worst are entertained. An Exchancfc Company's telegram, despatched from Berlin at 1-287 says :—.The Emperor Frederick has had a sudden relapse, and the doctors give little hope of his surviving throughout the day. POTSDAM, THURSDAY NOON.—The Crown Prince and Princess arrived this morning at F'dedrichskron. Prince Henry has arrived from Erdmansdorf. The Hereditary- Princess of Saxe Meiningen is also expected at Fried- richskron, where Doctor Friedberg, Minister of Justice, has just arrived. POTSDAM, THURSDAY AYTHRNOON.—.9iT Edward Malet, the British' Amba.isador, and Herr Friedberg, the Minis- ter of Justice, have just arrived at the Friedrichskroh palace; all the other ministers are expected during the afternoon. The condition of the Emperor shows no im- provement. The difficulty in breathing is very great, and the illustrious patient is now in a high fever. BERLIN, TTILTILSDAE, 12-30 P.M.—lt has now been stated beyond dispute that the Emperor has inflam- mation of the lungs. The end is believed to be fast approaching. THURSDAY, 1-52 r.m.—The Emperor of Germany is worse. Lock-jaw has set in. Prince Henry, who is the only member of the royal family absent, has been sum- moned bytelegraph. Photographers are present for the purpose of taking the death scene. 5-15 P.M.—The condition of the Emperor remains a 1... ...

most without change. His power of C.learing the throat by coughing is becoming less. The Crown Prince will remain at the Castle of Friedrichskron all night. The Imperial Chancellor and the __Minister of War...have re-

turned to Berlin, but Dr. Friedburg, the Minister of Justice, who has long been the confidential friend and adviser of the Emperor, remains here. Count Kutusoff, the personal military representative of the Czar at the Court of Berlin, came to Potsdam at two this afternoon to inquire forthe Emperor..
The Royal Theatre; are closed this evening. THE LATE EMPEROR.
Frederick William Niekelaus Karl

b. 1831), whO was Popularly ' known as the "Crown Prince," though since the creation of the Empire his title had been" Imperial Prince of Germany," was the eldest son of the late Emperor William. He was born at Pots- dam, and received the usual princely education for the army. At the outbreak of the war with Austria, in 1866, he was appointed to the command of the second army, with General von Blumenthal, as chief of his staff. By a series of clever manceuvres, and after some sharply con- tested engagements, the second army was led south- westwards from Silesia through the mountain passes into Bohemia. where it was just intime to support Prince Frederick Charles and the first army, who were waging a still doubtful contest against General Be,nedek at Sadowa. The appearance of the Crown Prince at once ensured the victory, and practically, put an end to the war. At the beginning of the Franco-Prussian War, the Crown Prince was in command of the third army, consisting of some eight army corps, or about 200,000 men. The first action was the assault at Weissenburg (August 4), and two days later this was followed by the memorable action of Worth, where the greater part of MacMalion's army was annihilated. The Crown Prince also highly distinguished himself by his passage of the Meuse on the day of Sedan. Three weeks later he was at Versailles, and remained with the troops beleaguering Paris till the conclusion of peace. In the middle of the following summer he visited England with the Crown Printess (Victoria Adelaide, Princess Royal of Great Britain), whom he married in 1858. The late Emperor, as Crown Prince, took no part in German Politicalaffairs. By the constitution of the Empire he was practically placed in the position of a political cypher. His personal sympathies were notoriously very Liberal, and in this direction he was no doubt to some extent impelled by his wife. The closing incidents of the Em- peror's career are full of gloom and sadness. About a year ago he was seized with a slight throat affection, which rapidly developed very dangerous, and, as was really at first suspected, fatal symptoms. His Imperial Highness, accompanied by his devoted wife, proceeded to San Remo, a favourite and very salubrious Italian watering place, where he was attended by Sir Morrell Mackenzie and many other distinguished physicians. His suffering was no doubt painfully aggravated by the fact that his venerable and illustrious father had been seized with illness, and gradually sank, dying of sheer old age, on the 9th March. The late Emperor ascended the throne at a time when the hand of death was laid upon him, and his latter days must have been greatly embittered by painful incidents of a strictly private and 'Personal nature. • THE NEW EMPEROR.

Frederic William Victor Albert, now Emperor of the German Empire and King of Prussia. was born January 27, 1859, and married in Febfuary, 1881, the 'Princess Augusta of Schleswig-Holstein. He has three children— Frederic William, born in 1882; Eitel Fritz, born in 1883 ; and Adalbert, born in 1884. Frederic William is above all things a Prussian officer, and has imbibed the ideas currant among the younger generations of Prus- sians. His marriage, which is believed to have been a love match, had a peculiarly happy aspect as the recon- ciliation between the Houses of SChleswig-Holstein and Hohenzollern after the quarrel of 1864. Since his arrival at man's estate Prince William, like the majority of his Prussian contemporaries, has looked upon his grand- father, the late Emperor, and his great servants, Bis- marck and Moltke, as his models. Accordingly he has devoted himself first and foremost to soldiering, and has the reputation of being a dashing and capable officer. His political lessons have been taken rather from Prince Bismarck than from his own father, and the young Prince was for a long time regarded as the special cham- pion and representative, of reaction.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. By "Annu.."

That Mr. Dobson's year of office as chairman of the Runcorn Commissioners expired at the last meeting. That during his term business has been conducted amicably and with general good will, and that as compared with some of his predecessors he has re dined upon a bed of roses. That his energetic and cheery cry of "Proof, gentle— men" will be missed. _ _
_ That people are wondering who his successor will b. _ _
That Mr. Samuel Taylor or Mr. W. Whittaker are about next "on turn." . .

. That both of these gentlemen are very popular in the town, and the elevation of one or the other would give satisfaction. That the appointment will be made on Wednesday next. That if true 'tis strange that the salt manufac- turers who are working at a great loss, according to their own showing, should object to a change of the Weaver Trust that would have the effect of re- ducing the tolls on salt. That the constitution of the Trust was condemned. in 1572, and that the feared change will come. That there is great jubilation in temperance circles about the withdrawal of the compensation clauses from the Local Government Bill. _ _

That the announcement following so closely upon the presentation of 12 yards of petition from Run- corn is very 'significant of the influence of that an- cient Cheshire town. That this, as Artemus Ward would say, is a " goak." That there are in Widnes many people who sup- port the view of your correspondent that it would be all the better if the officials of the public bodies would reside in the town and contribute to the rates from which they draw their salaries. That those who complain would perhaps be the- first to fly to brighter scenes if circumstances al- lowed.
That Widnes is not a heaven, nor the abode of angels. _

That it is again becoming notorious for the crime of violence that take place there. That the drink business is the cause of well-nigh 99 per cent. of the cases with which the magistrates have to deal. _ .
That the demands made upon the time of the few magistrates who have business in the town are very great, and more magistrates are imperatively needed. _ _

That Widnes Gas and Water Works are new ex- ceedingly well managed. That, with one exception, no town in Eng- land supplies gas at a cheaper price than Widnes. That it is a pity the surplus profit of the works cannot be appropriated to the reduction of the \rates of the town. _ _
That, however, they are not lost, but are devoted to clearing off the liabilities of the Board.

ROBBING A GRANDFATHER AT RUNCORN. Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. James Handley„ at Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday afternoon; Samuel Thompson, a young man, was brought up, on remand charged with having on the 4th June stolen £6O 4s from the dwelling-house of Mr. Semi. White, builder and property owner, Greenway-road. —Mr. W. H. Linaker said he appeared on behalf of the aggrieved party, whq, though not nominally,, was really the prosecutor. Mr. White was th; grandfather of the prisoner, and he desired that the prosecution should be withdrawn. Arrangements had been made, and a premium of .£lOO paid, to send the prisoner on a voyage of three or four years dura- tion to China, and he would there receive a certain amount of punishment and be deterred from the ebmmission of such offences as that with which he, was charged. The young man had been examined by Dr. McDougall and Dr. Robinson, and these gentlemen would state that he was a person of weak intellect. Under these circumstances Mr. Linaker urged that the Bench might accede to Mr. White's wishes.—Mr. Brundrit said the magistrates had no power to try the case, and therefore - could not take these points into consideration. They could hear what Dr. McDougall had to say in the matter. —Dr. McDougall stated that the prisoner was mentally deficient, morally deficient, and prudentially deficient. A person in his condition of mind was more liable to go astray and do wrong than one who was of sound mind. Linaker said Dr. Robinson was present to cor- roborate that statement. —The Bench decided to go on with the case.—The evidence showed that on the even- ing of the 4th inst Mr. Geo. Chrimes, who is agent to Mr. White, having collected the rents of the property, took the money to Mr. White's house. The snm amount- ing to £BO 4s Od was put in a cash box, which was locked and placed upon a side- board in the parlour. The prisoner was in the house at the time. About ten minutes later Elizabeth Hatton, the domestic servant, saw the prisoner walk through the kitchen to leave the house with the cash box under his coat. About the same time David Littlemore, a letter carrier, saw the prisoner running across a field towards the big pool, and then descend into a hollow. Inspector O'Donnell, having been informed of the robbery, went to the hollow in question and discovered the broken cash box bidden under an old tree stump in a pool of water. He traced the prisoner to Widnes, and next morning ap- prehended him at theMersev Hotel, Widnes. The priso- ner had the money in his possession, and when charged with stealing it he replied "I am guilty." The prisoner now said "I reserve my defence." He was committed to take his trial at the next quarter sessions. On the ap- plication of Mr. Linaker the prisoner was liberated on bail, himself in £5O and Mr. White in £lOO.

BOLTON V. WARRINGTON.—PIayed at Bolton, on Satur- day. On Bolton winning the toss, Fairclough put on Fleetwood at the refreshment pavilion end, and Crosfield opposite. Runs were made chiefly by Walker from Cros- field, and he gave way to Tinsley, while Fleetwood crossed over. The change worked, and Fleetwood got a hot return, which he held. Walker retired for Stanley, but his wicket was immediately displaced by a curiosity from Fleetwood. Not one batsman could fairly get at Fleetwood, who was now getting a lot of work on, and from both sides. Two catches were missed by Clarke in the long field, but the score was unaltered when the bats- men retired. Crosfield was put on vice Tinsley, and was snerAssful in taking three wickets, including Berry. Berry had played patiently for his 42, but he let out several times at both bowlers. Mylechreest kept wickets well, but afforded some amusement by the way he had to reach out at Fleetwood's big breaks. Warrington commenced badly, for Crosfield was out without scoring. Tinsley and Reynolds hit up 33, when Tinsley fell to a catch at cover-point. He had made a long drive for four and three threes. Clarke filled the vacant end, and for a time was content without hitting. Whitworth, however, soon came in for punishment, with two threes and a couple, and gave way to Tristram. The wicket was now, .getting difficult, for the sun was rapidly drying the sur- face. Chadwick was tried, and got two wickets in his first over. Clarke, however, got at him twice for three, and, aided by Woodhead, rised the score to 70. The lat- ter left by a high hit to mid-off, and Fleetwood took his place. Banks was tried for an over vice Tristram; but it was a real treat to the batsmen, as the following notches will testify :--1, 3, 3 from no ball, 4, 1 from no ball, land 1. With the exception of the last delivery each ball was to leg. Banks was taken off. Fleetwood, Mylechreest, and Kaye fell rapidly to Tristram, and after Fairclough had got one, Clarke was bowled by a shooter. His score of 48 was invaluable to his side, and certainly did much to win the match. He played the bowling confidently, and hit out with his visual freedom when oc- casion required. His score included a leg hit over the boundary for four, and eight threes. Tristram bowled with most success, and got four wickets for 20 rans. Score :

It is not often that intellectual and physical pre- eminence are so closely and unmistakeably :combined as in the case of Mr. W. M. F. Orr, the senior wrangler of Cambridge University this year. At the University races last week Mr. Orr carried off the first prizes in the mile, the two miles, the four miles, and the fifteen miles cycling events, winning all these races except the first- named- in an easy fashion. So much for his physical powers. His intellectual superiority was as emphati- cally testified when on Saturday he was'* gazetted "as senior wrangler, the highest honour of the year to be gained by an undergraduate. THE SHIP CANAL WORKS, AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.

NO. 22.— WESTON POINT AND WEAVER NAVIGATION. When the canal is completed it will, between the western end of "No Mall's Land" at Runcorn, and the triangular piece offind'ist'Frodsbana, formed by the confluenceof the Rivers Weavers and Mersey, and known as Frodsham Score or Marsh, be enclosed on its northern side by a substantial embankment built up in the estuary of the Mersey itself. If un- provided with loeks, this embankment woulç of necessity cut off all means of access to the Mersey from the existing docks at Runcorn and Weston Point, and also from the Weaver across the mouth of which it runs in order to reach the mainland at Frodsham Score, but to obviate this inconvenience it will be pierced by no fewer than three sets of jocks. The lock nearest Runcorn bridge will be directly opposite Fenton dock, the next to that will be nearly opposite the lighthouse at Weston Point, and the third set will closely adjoin this latter lock on the lower or west side. In addition to these locks there will be a tidal entrance from the Mersey to the Canal almost opposite the eastern end of Delamere dock at Weston Point. This last-named, or most western of the locks, which is spoken of in the Act as the Weston Mersey lock, is to be six hun- dred feet long and forty-five feet wide, with sills on the same level as the outer sill of Delamere dock. and with two pair of gates at teach end, each pair pointing in opposite directions, and also one pair of intermediate gates. PROTECTION OF THE WEAVER NAVIGATION. The construction of the canal and its subsidiary works cannot but interfere more or less with the present course of the Weaver navigation and we consequently find the rights of Trustees of the Wea- ver navigation are rather elaborately protected in the Act of Parliament. Before the Canal Company commence any work opposite to any part of the docks of the Trustees, they are to construct and make fit for use the portion of the canal lying be- tween a point duly specified and the entrance to the canal at Eastham. The water in this portion of the canal is to be maintained at not less than fourteen feet above the level of the Old Dock sill. The Canal Company are also to provide a‘lock near the Weston Marsh turnbridge, to communicate with the estuary of the Weaver on the one hand and with the Weston canal on the other, and having a length, breadth, and depth of the larger lock at Dutton. After this lock,—which, 'by the way, is described as" The Wes- ton Marsh lock' —has been completed, and until the Weston Mersey lock is open for the passage of traffic from the docks of the Trustees into the navi- gable channel of the Mersey, all the Weaver traffic is to be allowed to pass up and down the canal be- tween the Weston Marsh lock and Eastham free of any dues and tolls. After the completion of the Wes- ton Marsh lock, the Canal Company is at all times to maintain a channel of at least eighty feet in width and of a navigable depth of two feet below the Old Dock sill, between the lock and the canal, and also to buoy the channel to the satisfaction of the Trustees. From and after the opening of the canal for the Weaver traffic the canal company is to maintain in the canal a navigable depth of not less than three feet below the Old Dock sill between Weston Point and Eastham. During the construction of that stretch of canal lying between Eastham and the Old Quay at Run- corn, and until the Weston Mersey lock and its ap- proaches are completed the Canal Company must provide and maintain an access to the navigable channel of the Mersey from the docks and basins at Weston Point, so that there may be a good and suf- ficient passage into the Mersey at or above Weston Point, for all vessels trading between the Weaver Navigation and the ports of the upper Mersey. In case any obstruction to this passage is caused by, or in consequence of, the works of the company, the latter shall forthwith, after notice in writing from the Weaver Trustees, remove or remedy the obstruc- tion, and pay to the Trustees full compensation for, and indemnify them against all loss or damage oc- casioned by the default of the companyin forthwith complying with the notice. After the completion of the canal the company are at all times to main- tain a navigable depth of water, equal to the depth ' on the sills of the various docks and basins at Wes- ' ton, between these docks and basins and the deep water of the canal, and between the canal and the Weston Mersey lock ; and, also, to maintain an access between the Weston Mersey lock and the navigable channel of the Mersey, the bottom of such access being at a height of not more than three feet . six inches above Delamere Dock sill. The Trustees are, further, to be paid the increased cost of main- taining the existing depth of all the docks and basins belonging to them at Weston Point, and if, in consequence of any dredging or other work by the Canal Company any injury is caused to property of the Trustees the Company are to repair and make good the same. In like manner a provision is enac- ted that, at all times after the completion of the canal, the Company are to maintain a depth equal to the present depth of water adjoining any dock or river walls, or wharves of the Trustees abutting on the canal, and the Company will not be entitled to charge any wharfage rates in respect of any vessels or cargo for the use of the particular dock or river- wall or wharf.

ICE AND FLOODS' When in times of severe frost the Company are requested in writing by the Weaver Trustees to break and remove all ice in the Weaver, between f'rodsham weir and the entrance to Frodsham lock, which shall in any manner prejudice the Weaver Navigation, they will have to do so, and will also pay to the Trustees full compensation for, and in- demnify them against, all loss or damage occasioned by any default of the Company in so doing. In case the Company do not immediately break and remove the ice, the Trustees may do so at the reasonable expense of the Company, but the Company will not in such case be relieved from the payment of any damages to i which they are liable n this respect. If, during the construction of the canal or any of its incidental works between the Old Quay Docks and Frodsham Score, and before the Weston Marsh Lock and the channel therefrom to the Mersey at Eastham are opened for the Weaver traffic, the navigable access from the Mersey to the docks at Weston Point is, by reason of any act of the canal company, or of any of the persons in their employ, or under contract with them, obstructed or rendered less deep than heretofore the Company must., after notice in hand- writing from the Trustees, remove or remedy the obstruction, and pay to the Trustees and the traders on the Weaver Navigation fullcosapensation for the damage that had been occasioned. It is likewise provided 'that in the event of the docks, wharves, or river walls, or other works of the Trustees sus- taining any damage through the works of the Company, the latter must, at their awn expense, underpin, or by other necessary means, repair the injury, and alsocompensate the Trustees and the traders on the Weaver Nayigation fee the loss they had sustained. FRODSHAM SCORE. With regard to Frodsham Score we find it laid down "for the protection of the Marquis of Choi- mondeley " that if, in the execution of the Ship Canal works the Company do anything to lessen or prejudicially affect the present supply or flow of fresh or salt water to the Score and the adjacent meadow., they must at their own cost provide em- ploy and" for ever after maintain" in good working order, such syphons, pumps, or other works or cis- terns as shall be reasonably necessary for the pur- pose of ensuring to the swme extent as heretofore a sufficient supply of fresh and salt water to the mea- dows.

EASTHAIVI AND ELLESMERE PORT. Nine steam navvies are at work on the section extend- ing from Eastham to Ellesmere Port. Two of them are working in the second lift down and one has cut a gullet about 500 yards long to, a depth of 35 feet from the sur- face. The gullet is 50 feet wide and in very hard clay. Two large Lancashire boilers have been brought to sup- ply steam for the Cornish pumps that are to be put into the main sump, as it is expected that much water will be met in the third lift, which will be in rock. Much progress has been made with .the estuary embankments, and the stone-dressing yard is assuming a busy aspect. Piles of stone are being got ready for protecting the em- bankments. There are now on this section nine steam cranes, one crane excavator, nine steam navvies, four- teen locomotives, and 1,200 men. It is connected with section No. 2by telephone The temporary mission- room atEastham is giving place to a larger and perma- nent structure, to seat about 300 persons. Some thirty or forty more huts have been recently built, and another 15-horse stable is being erected. A man named Prosser has had his leg broken while working on this section by being knocked down with awaggon._
ACCIDENT AT ACTON GRANGE. As a navvy named Whiting was following his employ- ment on the Ship Canal works at Acton Grange on Mon-

day, he met with a serious accident, which resulted in the breaking of his right leg. As he was working a quantity of earth fell off a waggon. The injured man was removed to the hut that is used as a temporary hos- pital, where he was put under the care of Dr. Adams, the medical officer for that section. lie is progressing favourably. _ FIRE AT ACTON GRANGE. . _ _

A fire of a destructive character occurred on the works at Acton Grange on Monday, an engine shed, recently erected there being burnt down. The outbreak occurred between two and three o'clock in the morning. A num- ber of men were engaged in cleaning the engines, when some paraffin which was being used became Ignited, and the wooden shed was soon in flames. An attempt was made by some of the night men to extinguish them, but they spread with such rapidity that the task was aban- doned, and the shed was soon totally destroyed. The loss, and the damage that was occasioned to two of the engines which could not be removed, is estimated at several hundred pounds, but it will be fully covered by insurance.

div.head: _STEALING POULTRY.
div.p: _STEALING POULTRY.

At Chester County Petty Sessions, on Saturday, a labourer employed as a horse driver on the Ince section of the Manchester Ship Canal, and giving his name as Alfred Burton, was charged with the theft of a fowl from the stable of Mr. er . Percival. A police officer found the prisoner sleeping in a hut built with sods, with the hen, which was dead, concealed under his shirt.—Prisoner, who pleaded guilty, saying he was drunk when he com- mitted the theft, was fined 20s and costs, or seven days.

div.head: DAMAGE ON THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: DAMAGE ON THE SHIP CANAL.

William Collins, an elderly man, a fustian cutter at Lymm, was summoned before the Lymm Petty Sessions, on Friday. at the instance of Mr. Walker, the Ship Canal contractor, for having caused damage to the extent of 6d to an iron railing on the Ship Canal at Mickley' Hill. P.C. Buchanan gave evidence to the effect that defend- ant had climbed over the iron railings on to the canal grounds, and in doing so bent the railings. The case was dismissed after the defendant had been cau- tioned.

div.head: ANOTHER VISIT TO WARBURTON. BY A " GRADELY
div.p: ANOTHER VISIT TO WARBURTON. BY A " GRADELY

Your correspondent " Looker Ort" a month or two ago described a visit that he paid to the Ship Canal works at Warburton, and advised his readers that the most expeditious way to reach the scene of operations there was to book from Bank Quay or Arpley Stations to the little village of Heatley, which brings the traveller within a brisk quarter of tin hour's walk of the bridge at Warburton. This is no doubt the most expeditious way. It is, in fact, too expeditious for my liking, and so the other day when I also paid a visit to the same place I deter- mined to do it on " shanks's pony." The walk is a pretty long one, but in bright summer weather it is a pleasant journey. There is often some little in- cident or another to be met with on the road, too, and a person with a little spare time cn his hands who doesn't exactly know how to use it, might do far worse than saunter as far as Warburton by road. He can call in by the way at some of the old-fashioned public-houses to be found in the villages passed. and have a rest and refreshment as well. On my journey I called at a comfortable-looking wayside inn for that purpose, and found the fare excellent. The hest of the establishment had his mantle- piece adorned with mottoes that were not very ornamental, but were rather plain-spoken. One ran:—
"Use no language in this room That you would scorn to use at home."

Excellent ad;ice ; and a motto that mine host's cus- tomers would do well to bear in mind. The desir- ability of customers paying in, ready cash for their ale and what not was delicately urged in the fol- lowing manner "To pay my bills U know I must; That makes me careful who I trust." Then again there were those old-fashioned cards in which some object or another is, wherever possible, substituted in the place of a word. For instance, take the notice—" Our cigars at 2d cannot be sur- passed." On a fancy card is the word "our," then there are representations of a cigar, a hat, a can, a knot, and a bee, whilst the " 2d, ' and "surpassed" are printed in ordinary lettering. Another, in the same house, sings the qualities of the brew thusly— "l have sought both far and near, 2 find a glass of good strong beer, And at last I found it here." There are many more of the kind to be found in village " pubs " all over the country, ard they form a by no means uninteresting study. But to proceed. The incidents on the road were, after all, only few and far between, and there was a scarcity of pedestrians. Just when approaching the toll-bridge at Warburton, however, I met a sickly looking chap with a most melancholy and sorrowful countenance. He was on the road in search of work, and was making his way to Patricroft, but at the toll-bridge at Warburton he had met with a check. The requisite half-penny was not forthcoming, and he had been turned back. Of course, "A gradely lad" could soon put a matter like that right, while the wav-farer denounced the iniquity of the toll system in unmeasured terms.

Once over the bridge, and a great change is seen. The other moment you were delighting in the rural look of things, and the quiet and simplicity of the country. You have paid a half-penny, crossed over the bridge, and now enter a veritable pandemonium of screeching loco- motives, engines grinding away at mother earth with appalling effeat, steam cranes swinging round with their burdens, the clang of the blacksmith's anvil, and many other varied and stirring sounds. The work here has assumed large proportions, and several steam nav- vies are kept constantly at work making the cutting wider and deeper. The Barton section I learn from a civil workman, will be joined somewhere In the neigh- bourhood of Irlam, and actual operations are in progress to a point nearly close to the Boat House at Hollins Green, an accommodation line of rails running almost 'up to the- very door. The house has, I hear it mentioned, been purchased by the contractor for the canal. 'leis storerooms, offices, sheds, and living places that have been erected on the ground in profusion, to a great ex- tent heighten the interest of the scene. The "buzz" from the steam saw mill is always heard, a clattering rioise proceeds from the blacksmith's shed, and the visitor-is a person of some nerve if he does not get a bit confused at air this noise, and at the number of trains constantly running about on the lines of railway that are laid in all directions.

The buildings known as " huts " for the navvies are very comfortable places indeed, and are kept clean and tidy in appearance. At one end of a row of these huts is a place set apart as a hospital and surgery, which fact is announced to all concerned by a door plate. A large building used for office work is sr stone's—throw away. In it there-are several rooms, and the fittings are substantial. The- passer-by can, as he goes along, see spruce clerks busy at their desks in these rooms. On the wharf close to the river there are a couple of steam cranes,. and a bridgespanning the Warburton-road has been erected. It has, indeed, been in use some time, and there is aline of rani.; laid on it. This bridge connects the work on the meadows at each side of Warburton-rd., and there is a large amount of traffic over it. Several embankments are being constructed with the excavated soil, and the proverbial "oldest inhabitant" of the dis- trict will soon fail to recognise the place, ao great is the changethat is being wrought. The labours. of the steam navvies are assisted by gangs of men, other gangs are engaged onthe spoil' banks. while yet others are em- ployed taking up the surface earth and following other occupations. The variety is au& as to confuse the in- experienced in sucbmatters, but as a matter of fact the most complete order is maintained, and under the guid- ing power of a master hand, the great undertaking here, as on the other sections, is progressing at an astonishing speed.. . .

A good few visitors make their way to this part of the canal works, and groups of persons are daily to be seen watching the fangs-of the massive steam navvies tearing up the soil and depositingit in the train orwaggons wait- ing to receive it. The earth so far excavated has been of aryielding character and less difficulty- in regard to water in the cuttings Las been met with than has been the-case on some of the other sections. The people who live in the villages round about the works say that as yet no very great impetus to trade has been felt, though theinflux of labour into the district is having some effect.. Local publicaws and people who let lodgings have up to the present received by far the greater por- tion of the benefit. The person who cs stationed at the bridge at Warburton to receive tolls seems prepared to make hay while the sun shines, for whilst his good lady; or some member of the family, takes the half-pennies of the passengers, he devotes himself to business at a little- shop that has been erected on one side of the bridge. The money received in tolls must now be very much more than formerly, as there has been a tremendous increase in traffic.

It may be mentioned that at noon on Tuesday about fifty men struck work in consequence of a request loran advance in the rate of pay being refused. I had a chat with one of the, strike hands, and he said that the rate of pay- he and the others who had left work had been re- ceiving was tlicl an hour. This they wished to be in- creased to ssl an hour, which they considered themselves to be entitled to when the trying nature of their work is taken into account. They also allege that 5d an hour is given on other sections.

A charge of uttering forged bills of exchange to a con- siderable amount was on Wednesday preferred at the Salford Borough Court against a bankrupt named Malcolm. The prisoner was committed for trials and an application for his admission to bail was refused. BEI-rum HOUSES —The Burnley police recently pounced upon a number of public-houses which were supposed to be used for betting purposes, with the result that about 200 summonses were issued by the magistrates. Ten publicans, on Wedneseay, appeared before the magistra- trates to answer the charge laid against them, and in each case a fine of LIO, and in some of them a. minor penalty in addition, was imposed.

THE SONS OF ST. GEORGE. BY H. WHITHAM. A very striking feature of social life in San Fran- cisco is the clannish feeling that seems to prevail. There are Cosmopolitan Schools. The press pushes Cosmopolitaniem to the front, but of the real inter- mixing of the races you see little or nothing. The new arrival hoed.ls out that certain districts of the city are given over, entirely to the representa- tives of the varitrus nations, and for mere comfort's sake he seeks the fellowship of his own kin in this "City by the Sea." Englishmen are in this matter somewhat favouied, or have at least an advantage, inasmuch as their language is the legal "Open Sesame" to all business, and gains them ingress , and egress to all pleasure parties. But with all this the Engliehman seeks closer companionship with the erstwhile resident of the" right little, tight little island." A very noticeable feature in the city is that pub- . lic houses, or saloons, and restaurants, are named and conducted on Tines familiar to the customers' national tastes. This all helps to keep alive race prejudice, and keeps the citizens from forming the compact body necessary for municipal pur- poses. I have referted to race prejudice. It is not a subject I like/ to toueli upon, because I think, nay, I am sure, that so long as it exists workmen will continue to be the mere tools of capital, which, whether it likes or no, must take advantage of labour's disorganized state. But race prejudice in America does something more than this. Germans, Italians, Spaniards. Swedes, Norwegians. and I ven- ture to say every race under the sun, even including the Celestial pigtail, get on prettywell together, but not so the English and the Irish. Englishmen at home have no idea how bitter the feeling is here between these two races. - Talk of a United Kingdom, why anyone would think that the two races had been brought up as strict followers of the unwritten law of vendetta, to see the hatred existing here. Hence it follows, as the outcome of this hatred, that the two races range themselves under their respective banners, and I find myself a Son of St. George, a society which meets together "as Englishmen. their sons or grandsons, for the purpose of infusing among them a spirit of love and patriotism for the country in which they or their ancestors were bon'. and 'a regard for the republic in which they live."

_ I must leave the Irishman here. He, poor devil, has no right to either love or patriotism for the country in which he was born. He may have a "re- gard" for it; more than that would be presumption. For the Englishman is reserved all the "love and patriotism" for his native land; America must be content to receive his " regard " I know some of your readers will be vastly amused when I tell them that this society, as judged of by its twe representa- tives in the press, the St. George's Journal," and the "British American," is a downright, outright, Tory society, differing very little from the Orange society. But what are its objects? In the Lodge, of course, neither politics nor yet religion are fit subjects for discussion. A good job this, for me at least. The Lodge meets each Tuesday evening, at eight, and closes somewhere between ten and mid- night. The 'members seem to have each graduated in the historical Circumlocution Office, and deserve tickets for the able manner in which they make Lodge business hold out. Further than this in Lodge secrets I eannot go. Perhaps I may say that I have knelt on the right knee, had the sword laid on my shoulder, and the Garter placed below my knee, and been bidden to rise a knight of St. George. I was never initiated a member of the Land League, nor yet have I at any time been a member of any Fenian society; . Yet, I fancy these societies are much like the one I am referring to, in that a great deal is done for which no rule could be quoted. One has to go ontside the Lodge and outside the rules to find what is done. To give benefits in time of sick- ness, and to provide a Lodge-room for the trans- action of financial Matters, seem to me to be mere accidents; to form a strong political party for in- fluencing State affairs would appear to be the real object. Now what are the State affai•li to which atten- Von is first directed? Of course naturalisation tikes first seat. Emigration for nine months end- ing September 30, 1887, from the United Kingdom to the United States, shows—English, 86,336; Scotch, 20,013; Irish, 62,407; total British; 169,756. With such numbers coming to the 'States, of course it is incumbent upon each man that he takes up his duties of citizenship at once, and prepares for the fight that is surely coming. Two things trouble the British American's mind, and help to make him Tory in politics. The first is the fear lest Ireland ' should be successful in her efforts to gain Home Rule. The next, and worst of all, is a great horror lest, gaining this, the whole of the British Empire should become subject to the Church of Rome. I own to having strong feelings on this question, but have thought the Irish people capable of taking care of themselves. Should they be successful in throw- ing off English rule and absentee landlordism, and rush into the arms of either a Ramish or a Protes- tant Church, well, tbe people would have them- selves to blame, and theirs would be the consequent suffering. It has often been a wonder to me how it came about that Englishmen migrating to' America should in nearly every case become Tory in politics. Since becoming a Son of St. George, and a reader of the Order's literature, the wonder has ceased. A loose- ness of thought, combined with an inadequate imowledge of British history, accounts for it. 41en who at home never thought of meddling with ploli- tics, who found life not worth living, and did not give themselves the trouble to know the reason why, come out here, and, finding an association of fellow countrymen prepared to welcome them with open arms, they join the lodge, and feel almost at home as they listen to the strains : Each true son of dear Old England Meets a hearty welcome here, Enter, stranger, freely enter, None but friends around thee move; Offerinr, thee with English frankness- Englisifhearts and English love." After becoming a member of the Order, and satis- fying himself that two of the first requisites in life are gained, that is, social companionship and a small provision for a rainy day, he looks around for the records a the business and reports of the Order. Taking up either the "St. George's Journal" or the "British American," they are found full to overflow- ing with articles and correspondence on two ques- tions, and two alone. viz., Irish., Home Rule, and Roman Catholicism. We read that "Two organisa- tions are attracting the attention of thoughtful and patriotic men." One is the "Roman Catholic con- spiracy with the Irish vote, the other is the British American Association." The latter, in consequence of the "•degeneracy and unpatriotic" character of our pubNc men in that they pander to "any combi- nation," and are willing "to gain the Irish vote" to sacrifice their country and their freedom, have combined for freedom's sake. A stirring, appeal is made to Englishmen to become naturalised, so that by a solid vote they may resist the Irish vote, which is" wielded by a priesthood that aims at the sub*, gation of the country, and bringing it tinder the control of a foreign despot." When men have it constantly dinned in their ears that the Irish Roman Catholics are "sworn one and all to get con- trol of the civil power, to suppress liberty, extirpate heretics, and place the country at the feet of the Roman pontiff," they are apt in time to believe all the rubbish. The. importance of the British vote is never lost sight of. The English are told to "unite them- selves in harmonious organisations to maintain and manifest their manliness and high standing in society." It is with something like dismay that they are told to observe the "-solid phalanx of the Irish marching on their gradual and political . power." We have pointed out to us the "desperate conspiracies the Irish have always planned and resorted to against the English people and English Government." If this be all true, the Irish, and especially the Roman Church, must have inherited more than their share f original sin, and are to be pitied and guarded against. I would suggest that as Balfour is so successful in putting down Parnell, getting the landlords. all their rents, filling the prisons by coercion acts, and restoring peace and plenty to Ireland, that you should -send him over here. He might restore the British American to something like a sane state of mind. Such is a brief outline of the stuff placed before the sons Of St. George, dangled as a kind of bogey, inducing him to think that "American freemen are pushed out of all City and State control," and that we should come to the front and "determine to the best of a solid vote to do all we can to remedy a preeoncerted system by which every avenue to office and control is being besieged by aliens to the exclusion of the native elements. What A glorious privilege it is to be an Eaglishntan ! 13, Valparaiso-st. San Francisco, May 22nd 1888.
