div.head: FROM LONDON LEITER.SI
div.p: FROM LONDON LEITER.SI

Lord and Lady Tennyson, who have been residing in the Isle of Wight for several months, are about to leave Farringford for Aldworth, their place on the Hampshire Downs, neir Haslemere. They in- tend to pass next winter on the Riviera, probably at Cannes.

Here are a few interesting items concerning Car- dinal Manning. The Cardinal rises at six in the winter and five in the summer. After having de- voted half an hour to meditation he says mass in his private chapel, and then passes thirty minutes in thanksgiving. At seven o'clock in the summer and eight o'clock in the winter he partakes of a light breakfast, and afterwards passes a few hours over his private correspondence and the newspapers. the rest of the morning is devoted to matt-rs be- longing to his archdiocese and to literary work. Lord James Douglas was released from prison on Wednesday. He has been locked up for a fortnight, but he made an affidavit which was handed up to Mr. Justice Chitty this morning that be never saw file pasteboard wrapper 4ceived by Miss Scott, and, moreover, he swore that the famous Christmas card which the lady's counsel sitgested was improper, but which Lady Florence Dixie, his sister, says was nothing of the kind, was selected casually out of a heap of other cards in a shop at Mentone. There was practically no opposition to the application, and therefore Lord James Douglas was able to eat his dinner to-night as a five man.

T It Is =Meal to find a governor writing to the Secretary of State and pointing out that his revenue and the prosperity of his people have been affected by the failure of :the bathing season. Such, how- ever, is the duty of Governor Sir Terence O'Brien. Sir Terence is Governor of Heligoland. Heligoland is dependent on its bathing season for itsprosperity. During the height of the last summer bathing sea- son, when (says Sir Terence) "our expenses were greatest," there came a break in the weather, which reduced the revenue from £9215 to £BB2O. Still Sir Terence is able to make both ends meet. Sea-bath- ing may fail, but the resources of an O'Brien are never exhausted. He finished the year with £270 to the good.. He is also able to add that there is no public debt. Happy Sir Terence! Happy Heligo- land!

Colonel King-Harman, notwithstanding thestrong 1 opposition to his appointment as Under-Secretary to kShe Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland, was personally ' popular, even amongst those who most strongly demonstrated against the bill securing to him a salary, for he was cheery and pleasant in private relations. He was, I think' the best-looking man in the House of Commons. Ayear or two ago, if any- one had been asked to point out the two Dl.P.'s who looked the finest specimens of physique in the House, he would have pointed to Colonel King- Harman and Colonel Tottenham, and now they are both dead, whilst many who looked as though a strong wind would blow them away are still living.

Canon Rawlinson must almost regret that he ac- cepted the living of All Hallows, Lombard-st. He is getting it on all sides. Some say he is too old, others that he is a very poor preacher, and now it is asserted that he favours Ritualism. This last charge is not fair. Professor Rawlinson signed the remonstrance against the Purchas Judgment, and is anything but a narrow-minded ecclesiastic. But he cannot even be called a High Churchman, It is hoped none the less by many of his personal friends that he will see his way to resign not only his post at Oxford. but his canonry at Canterbufy if he re- tains the valuable City living. The feeling against pluralism is growing stronger, and it is clear that those who set it at defiance do not by any means promote the best interests of the Church.. Between Sir G. Trevelyan and Mr. Chamberlain there have been passages of marked disagreement, and it is characteristic of the courage of the former that he is about to visit Birmingham and to ad- dress the Liberal Two Thousand—a name• of much import which was formerly associated with the guidance of Mr. Chamberlain. This interesting meeting will come off in the Curzon Hall next week, the day appointed for hearing and probably deter- mining Mr. Dillon's appeal. It is more than prob. able that when Sir George Trevelyan is speaking Mr. Dillon will have been consigned to a long and, in hfs case, dangerous imprisonment. The sentence, if it so falls, will be regarded with real grief and pain by the great body of Mr. Dillon's Liberal col- Femme in the House of Commons, to whom he has become much endeared by the combination of sim- plicity and earnestness, of delicacy and refinement, which are apparent in his interesting character.

There has' been some pretty " wigging" in Con- servative circles in view of the defeat of the Go- vernment on Tuesday night. There were, among others, several Ministers who were absent from their seats, and who have had a very bad quarter of an hour in consequence. Ascot week tells heavily against the Conservative Government, and next sit- tingjs looked forward to with some anxiety on the Treasury bench. A peremptory whip has been issued, requiring the attendance of all members who have not paired. Pairs from the Liberal side are in great request. Mr. Labouchere says he has raised his terms. He will pair now only on con- sideration of a box seat in the drive to Ascot, a luncheon, and £lO to nothing put on the favourite in his name.

The leaders of the Opposition have determined to resist 'the attempt of the Government to • elimi- nate from the Local Government Bill clause 9, which empowers County Councils to close public- houses on Sundays, Good Fridays, and Christmas Days. A further statement—that an effort will be made to retain clause 10, which provides for the transfer of the licensing powers from the magis- trates to the County Councils—is at least prema- . tare. No decision upon this point has been come , to, and the tendencies at the moment aro in the- direction of leaving the subject alone. On Wed- day afternoon a meeting of the temperance party was held in the House of Commons, at which the whole subject was debated, There was perfect unanimity as to the action that should be taken in respect of the ninth clause, but such diversity of opinion was expressed touching the transference of licensing powers to the, County Councils, that no- resolution on the sidaject was submitted. Tears, idle. tears, len them fall for the unmarried sister-in-law. Another year is likely to pass and no redress will be found for her grievances. Still she sits iamenting her unmarriageable state. On Wed- nesday the House-of Commons just touched upon the bill. A majority for it was assured. An amend- ment to make the-brother-in-law also marriagealaie did not call for serious debate, tae brether-in-law being wiser than the sister-in-law, and being in no anxiety to geb married to his brother's widow. The promoters of the measure thought that by the avoidance of speechmaking, they would get to the division. They actually wanted to move the closure before there had been a debate, but the Speaker would not have it. Then rose the slow, solemn, tall, cypress-like Mr. Talbot From his accents one might have imagined that he was discussing a funeral rather than a marriage, and indeed a funeral it proved to be. His oration put an end to the bill for the year 1888, for at 5-30 thp debate stood adjourned.

Mrs. Langtry has purchased in California a mag- nificent farm of 4,500 acres, of which 1,000 are plan- ted in wheat. There are vineyards, fruit orchards, a beautiful lake, and cattle ranges on the property, which will be called Sandringham, in honour of the Prince of Wales. Mrs. Langtry's usual good fortune has secured the opening of a railroad through the ranche, which will give her a private station near her residence and easy access to San Franciseo.and its markets. She has finished her dramatic season, and is taking a rest upon this splendid estate. In order to hold her title. securely She will become naturalised as an American citizen. A silver mine has been discovered on land owned by her, and may give her another mine of wealth. During her

months of recreation she will engage in literary avocations, having promised to write her Recollec- tions,to be published simultaneously in England and America, and a novel of London life for a weekly paper.
GENERAL NEWS.

John Mills was committed for trial at Manchester. on Tuesday, charged with throwing vitriol on a woman whom it is a4leged he had bigamously married. Ile bad served ten years for similarly disfiguring his first wife.

Considerable excitement NMI occasionedat Bath-row, Northampton, on Monday, by a fire in a house in which two children, aged three years and nine weeks respectively, were locked. On a neighbour entering the bedroom window, one child was dead, and the other seriously injured. At one a.m. on Saturday the cotton in a goods rain from Liverpool to Oldham was observed to be on fire. On arriving at Bury the train was stopped, and Ihe waggon uncoupled and run to the engine tank, where the flames were extinguished. The damage is estimated at £3O, and is not insured. About 9 30 a.m., on Monday, a man dropped dead in one of the principal streets in Bolton, causing a painful sensation. It was subsequently aecertained that the deceased was a foreman at an ironfoundry in the town, and named John Horrocks. He was 48 years old. The cause of death is supposed to be heart disease., Mona Gott) Drscoveirtns ne NORTII WArats.—An im- portant discovery of gold has been made at the foot of Moel Amman Mountains, Flintshire, by a gentleman who has had experience in Australian gold mines. The sssly having, proved satisfactory. a large gang of men set to work on the land, a take-note having been secured from the Crown Lands Commissioners at a nominal rent.

The Manchester coroner held an inquest, on Monday, on the body of J. Bradburn, who committed suicide, under shocking circumstances, on Saturday afternoon. He went to the top storey of his house, and having es.l!ed out to the psople in the street to get out of the way, he leaped from the window. failing into the area—a distance of 40 feet Death was instantaneous. The deceased had been drinking heavily. A verdict of "Suicide while tem- porarily insane" was returned.

At the Rhoisdda Valley Police Court, on Monday, two grocers were charged with a breech of the Margarine ' Act. They had sold margarine from a cask kept under the counter, and not ticketed as the Act requireg, but the magistrate decided that legally no offence 'had been ;committed, as the law, stated it was only when mar- ;garine was exposed for sale that the ticket indicating its composition should be placed upon it. The sum- monses were, therefore. dismissed. The stipendiary urged' the speedy amendment of the wording of the Act. At an inquest held at Manchester; on the bodies of four persons who. met their deaths in the fire whic,h.oc, curred on S'aturday night in St Andrew's-street, sever/0 members of the Manchester Fire Brigade deposed that their-operations were rendered terribly difficult by the interference of a panic-stricken crowd, which surged around them, prior to the arrival of a strong police force. Moreover, they were stupidly hampered by some strange firemen, who had been participating in a cele- bration in the district, and some of whom were intoxi- cated. The inquest was adjourned. SIP-Temp ACCIDENT AT A COLLTF,RY.-011 Saturday a 'number of persons, chiefly children were pickine coal on a colliery refuse heap adjoining the Midland Railway, at I-tension and Barlow sidings, WhittingtAn. The heap, which consiked principally of' ashes and slag, is con- berning; ands cavity had formed in the centre. Two children—Jaber Castle, aged 13, and Augustus fiumplueys, nine—suddenly disappeared in the burning mess.. They were irtunediattsly extricated, and found to hare been fearfully burned. They afterwards died at C'lesterfield Frospltali BAD GEOGRAPHY ON THE BENCIL—Mr. Greenwood ap- plied on Saturday to. Mr. justice Kay, in the Chancery Division, forthe payment out of . court, of three-fourths of a sum of monev,.and suggested that the remaining fourth in court should' be. invested in Rotherham Cor- poration Stock.—Mn Justice Kay: What town P—Mr. Greenwood: Rotherham.—Mr. Justice Kay: Where is Rotherham P—Mr. Greenwood: In Yorkshire.—Mr. Jus- tice Kay: r have no power to authorise investment in- Corporation stock„but if I had I should prefer to order ' ,he investment in the stook of a town I had heard of before. ;

PAIZAITIN LADY OIITIZATTED AT BOLTON AND NOTTING- irAM.—ID a quarrel between some women at Bolton, on siaturclay /night, one, named Davies, seized a lighted paraffin lanip and hurled it at another, named Mac- dnnagh, whose clothing was ignited, causing fearful injuries, which will in all probability prove fatal.— li woman named Bewley, who was severely bUrned few weeks ago, has died at Nottingham General Hospital. In a quarrel with his wife, Alfred Bowley hit the woman severe blow. She reeled against the table, upsetting a paraffin lamp. The oil ran on to her clothes, and she WAS, soon enveloped in frames. Alfred Bowley's arms were much scorched in attempting to extinguish the lames. Bowley was arrested, but is on bail.

FATAL) Rksuvr or Ftrs,--On Saturday, the Derby C'oroner opened an inquest on the body of Sidney Kirk, aged 16; who died from injuries received on the Ist inst. by being trampled upon by a cow in an entry in St. Mary's-gate, Derby. The cow ran into an entry, and several bays, incleitling, the deceased, went after it. A mongst them was a youth named Joseph Adams, em- ployed at a bicycle mAnufactory, and he admitted in evi- iollCo that he ran out of the entry when the cow turned mid closed the door after him, leaving deceased and several other boys in the entry with the cow. The re- suit was that the deceased was trampled on and butted by he row, till he received injuries which caused his death. Adams said he closed the door for fun, and admitted that deceased could have got out of the way hao he not done so. The inquest was adjourned.
INBpwriow or PORTSMOUTH HARBOUR.—A special 'rain containing Lord Charles Beresford and a large number of members, of Parliament, among whom _ . _

the Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain, limn de Worms; Sir. Robert Fowler; Sir Walter Barttelot, and Lord Brassey; left Victoria Station, London, at nine on Saturday, for Portsmouth Harbour. Mr. .:4arle, the general manager of the company, was at Victoria Station, to superintend the departure of the train. The party, after witnessing some exreriments,"returned to town in the afternoon.. At a luncheon in the dockyard Lord Hartington, ih. proposing the health of Lord Tharles Beresford. said their visit must have convinced ~veryone, however ignorant and inexperienced. how .ntilTh. room there was fer differences of opinion on naval questions. SPRIOUS RAILWAY' COELISION AT NRWCASTLB. —A serious railway collision occurred at 4 15.?..rnt0. sotnatSiuonn,- isty just outside. the. west end of V., ,r Newcastle-on-Tyne. A abort goods tr, ,osed of an ~ngineand five wagvons. wai staining. he platform at which the- passenger tickets are usually collected, when .a. passenger train from Conset t. then due, came up. The- dtiver was unable to. see the stationary goods train by reason of a curve in, the line, and the train came round the curve with a. considerable force and smashed ' into the rear of the-goods train. The van of the latter WaS lifted from.the mita, and, breaking through a .stone uarapet,,fell into the sidings about 20ft. beneath. Por- i unately the guard had fust previously left his van. The , name/ewers in the Consett train were all thrown violently 1 from their seats, and many sustained severe cuts-and contusions. About 30 were removed to the Infirmary; where their wounds were dressed. They were all, how- ever, able shortly afterwards to proceed to their-homes. EXTRAORDINARY SUICIDE IN A RAILWAY GALLIUM:IR.— rin the arrival of the. 5-15 a.m. train from King's Cross at Peterboro', on Saturday, the body of a gentleman about 40 years of age was found in a first-class carriage. He lid been shot through the heart. A revolver was lying, by his side. On him was found two cards, with name, Robert M. K. Tickell, Dublin Evening Mail. On the back ,of one was written, "Wire George Tickell, Esq., Mail; Diiblin. Your son shot himself whilst travelling from, London to l'eterbore' this morning. He is dead." On the back of another card were the words, "On the roach from London- to Peterboro'. An ill-spent life is fitly ter.. rninated by a cowardly act —Robert Tickell, 9th June 1888."—An inquest was held on Monday. Mr.. G. Ticket,. IF., Dublin, identified the body as that of his-son, who, he said, underwent an operation in London on Thursday for a disease of the throat similar to the Emperor of Germany's. He had been told that the. growth was malignant, and he became depressed. A verdict of "Suicide- while of unsound mind" was returned. 'The funeral took place at the cemetery on Tuesday afternoon, wreaths being placed on the coffin by the journalists and Freemasons of the city. SMALLPDX' IN Hor.r..—A Hull telegram states that smallpox there shows no signs of abatement. The medi- cal otßeer admits that there are 38 cases in the hospital, but adds that they are all' of a 441 type. TERRIBLE ASSAULT.—A man named Jones,, on Thurs- day, shot at a woman, named Harris, at Aston, near Bir- mingham, with whomej¢e had been intimate during her husband's absence: He also shot at the woman's hus- band, and at a girl aged two, a daughter of Mrs. Harris, and struck an infant of three months with a revolver. All three are seriously, it not fatally, injured. Jones has been taken into custody.

ALLEGED:SERIOUS WIFE ASSAULT AT ' WARRINGTON. Denis Mannion, of Winwick-road, was brought up on remand at an Occasional Court on Monday, on a charge of having done grievous bodily harm to his wife on the Bth inst. The evidence of .the Coinplainant was to the effect that on the day named she went to her house after seeing, a neighbour. There was no fire in the grate, and her husband asked her where she had been. She stated that sbe would not tell him, and, on asking for hie tea, ebe told him to wait for it. Prisoner was breaking coal with a hatchet, when complainant told him to out of the way and struck him with a key. lie then knocked her down with his fist, and she a blow from something when on the floor. E\ri- dance was also given by Dr. J. Tar-villa Smith? house-surgeon at the Infirmary, who said that be found a ragged wound on the scalp of the complain, ant, towards the back of the head. There were" several cuts, each about half an inch in length? radiating from the centre of the wound. The in- juries were such as might have been caused by blow from a hatchet. Pcisoner was committed te take his trial at the Quarter Sessions at Liverpool. Prisoner was brought up at the COunty Sessions on Tuesday, and was acquitted.

At Widnes Perty Sessions, on Thursday, before , Mr, E. K. Muspratt and Mr. H. Wade Deacon, IRichard Garton, postmaster, Appleton, was sum- , moned to show cause why he should not contribute towards the maintenance of the illegitimate child 'of Ellen Morris. Mr. W. T. Husband appeared for, the complainant, and Mr. J. W. Knowles appeared, ' for the defendant. The defendant admitted 01 paternity of the child, and the question for Ow_ Bench to decide was the amount of the contribur:i tion to be paid. From the statement of Mr,. Hue-- band, and the evidence of the complainant, it appeared k.., that the wife of the defendant, who had borne him, sirs children, had obtained a divorce from him. Recently,. Mra. Morris had been keeping 'house for the defendant, , .and the daughter had been acting as postmistress.. Dur-1 ing. this time an intimacy sprang up between the defend", al ant and the daughter, with. the result that the latter: gave birth to a female child on the 12th May. It vr stated that the defendant, besides being a postmasteri. for fulfilling which office he. was paid about £25 a year,* the defendant was a master. bricksetter, and earnecb about 36s or £2 per week. He was the owner of the' post-office building and several' other cottages, and was ' the possessor of five £lOO shares in the Midiandl' Railway. A few days ago he said he had £l,OOO, and attempted to induce the complainant to go , away with him. He had offerecrto pay 5s per week to- wards the child if she would not go into court. For the: defence it was alleged that the property was mortgaged' for £BO9, and the whole of the rents were needed to pay the interest. The railway shares were deposited with his solicitor to pay to costs of the divorce proceeding's. He had not earned more than £.l per week as a brick- . setter for a long time.—Mr. Knowles said the divorce proceedings would cost about £2oo.—Mr. Husband : Nothing of. the sort.—The Bench made an order upon' to pay 5s per week until the child attained the age of 13 years, together with the costs and ,the advocates fee.
TILE WARRINGTON VOLUNTEERS.

, This (Saturday) afternoon the Warrington Volun teers—the 18t Battalion (Prince-of Wales Volun- teers) South Lancashire Regiment—proceed to Southport to there go under canvas for a week. The full, strength of the battaliowis between 500 and 600, and it is expected that out of that number. about 400 men will go into camp. They are to parade at three o'clock this afternoon at the Drill Shed in fulX dress, with leggings and haversacks, and will proceed to Southport by, the 3-30 p.m. train from the Central Station. On arriving at the rail- way station at Warrington the battalion will be formed into four's deep by the officer commanding the compan- ies, and the non-commissioned officers wilibbe posted, sg far as practicable, with their sections. Rifles are to be held between the knees during the journey by rail. When the train is ready to start " attention " will be sounded, and instructions have been given that silence must be strictly maintained. On arrival at Southport the "halt "'will be sounded, and the men, who will pre- viously have arranged their accoutrements, will get out of the train and "fall in" in the same manner as when starting. After arriving at their destination the me" will have a march of three miles to the place of encaml meat. The battalion will return to head-quartet on the 23rd instant, and on 'the afternoon the day previous, next Friday, the inspection will 1 place. Colonel Twentyman will bathe inspecting officer To-morrow (Sunday) morning divine service will be,con• ' ducted by the Rev. R. W. H. Siddall, and the band of the corps will play during the afternoon. A fatigue party left Warrington soon after noon on Thursday for the purpose, of pitching tents and making the necessari preparatiomfor the reception of the men. The battalion will be under the command of Colonel Greenall, and the other officers who will accompany the corps will be Lieut.-Colonel Bolton, Capt. J. Bridge, Capt. J. C. Ridg- way, Captain H. J. Widdows, Captain H. F. Gooch, Car tam J. D. Buckton, Captain V. W. Baynes, Lieutenant" T. Smith, Lieutenant J. A. Eclelsten, Lieutenant F. Appleton. Quartermaster T. Hutchinson, Acting Char, lain Rev. It. W. H. Siddall, and Captain and Adjutaro F. A. Adam. The permanent staff sergeants are—Sergt,; Major P. Fennelly, Sergeant-Instructor M. McCoy, an" Sergeant-Instructor C. Birch. There was a Commanding Officers' parade on Saturday, whenthetattation marchea from the Drill Hall to the'Recreation ground in the Park. Here they went through drill. On Monday evening the men wereeddressed by Colonel Greenall in reference W their going into camp. After speaking of other matte the Colonel expressed the hope that the men would haTe a nice time at Southport, and said that he would do 'hi! best to }Jaffe them made as comfortabls as possible. Tb- haversaoks and kit baga were served ont to the men 011 Wednesday at headquarters.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. ,SATURDAY.—Before Aldermen Burgess and Holmes. HEARTLESS Ferfmn.—Patrick Quinn, a labourer, brought up in custody on a charge of having, on the of may, left the town deserting his son, aged 10, Vtl leaving him chargeable to the common fund of the ,orrington Union. Mr. Shearer (relieving officer) 'ated that the boy was brought up a week ago in the tleet wretched condition. He had been living anywhere ;.!_e could in the streets, and Ivas sent to the workhouse tT the magistrates. The pYisoner had since removed to "idnes, leaving his son behind. Prisoner did not care 'What became of any of his children. The Guardians 'Would be satisfied if Quinn would pay expenses, as he Was taking the boy with him.—The Bench decided to '43olrn the ease for a fortnight in order to give prisoner ePportunity to pay.—The Chief Constable said that Prisoner was a very "tricky"' man, and would probably attempt to escape without paying.—The Chairman ac- cordingly cautioned the prisoner before he was dis- charged. STRANGE RESULT OF A " CATARACT."—JOhII Dagnall, ,a labouring man, who appeared with] his eyes concealed by a large green shade, was charged with having been oru nk, and having begged, in Sankey-st., on the previous , 'Laz Y. P.C. Monoghan said that he saw the prisoner go Ito several shops, and received complaints about him. "hen his request for assistance was refused, he became veryabusive. Prisoner pretended to be blind.—The ;fief Constable: Lift up your shade.—Prisoner objected, Ying that he had had a " cataract "taken from his eye '-• `mle time ago.—The shade, however, having been re- • by a constable, the" cataract" in question was • overed to be a bad black eye.—The Chief Constable: • I understand the cataract. —Prisoner was heard to lay that the discolouration was owing to his having col- with a street corner. The Bench ordered him to .„.6° to gaol for fourteen days, with hard labour. `'ionnay.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), and Aldermen Harrison and Davies. lIRUNEENNESS.—The following cases were disposed of: Z''ate Barker, in Irlam-st., on Saturday night, dis- 'seed ; Frederick Clarke, in Knutsford-road, on Sun- Y night, sent to gaol for 14 days with hard labour; illiam Thompson, in Horsemarket-st., on Saturday 'light, committed to prison for? days ; Mary Mulholland, 4,lMersey-st , on the Ist June, fined ss, including costs; rllethas Smart, in St. James'-st., Latchford, on the Ist 11_, fined 5s including costs; Henry Diamond, in u-oev-st., on aturday night, and also for assaulting "fel% Oxley at the same time and place, was sent to gaol or one month with hard labour. OBSTINATE LEGS.—Thomas Hibbert was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Sankey-st. on AJAlrday night.—The Chief Constable said that defen- ;VA \vas a respectable man, but wad not accustomed to Tarrington strong beer.--Alderman Harrison: And his ~,eigo proved obstinate ?—The Chief Constable: Yes.— 4ble defendant was dismissed with a caution. irt pi:eVOIING THElVFS.—breorge Gresty (13), and William bag (13), were charged with stealing from the stall the Market of John McMahon, three oranges, value i„ • en Saturday afternoon.—Mr. Hunt (chief constable), " stating the case, said that it was Gresty's third ap- Peb arance and he believed that he earned his own living Ypilfering and "took something 'home besides ;" the parents, of both boys were to blame. On Saturday night 4.1,!e mother of Fleming was drunk, while her son was in ""elock-up.—The magistrates ordered the lads to go to pri 'up. for one month, and then to a reformatory for five Years.

Qui`Ractsoma LABoortans.—Peter Higgins and John Wierton were charged with committing a breach of the Peace ev by fighting on the 3rd inst. They were each bound recer to keep the peace for -six months, in their own „Zgnisances of £5,.. arxd one surety of £5, or, in default, "Y.en days' imprisonment. Fititela POGlLlBT.—Margaret O'Brien pleaded guilty

to fighting in Scotland-road, on the 4th Joule. The magistrates ordered her to be bound over to keep the peace for six months, in her own recognisances of £5, and one surety of £5, or, in default of payment, 14 days' imprisonment. OBSTRUCTION.—Joseph Scott, grocer, Bridge-st., was ordered td pay a nominal fine of Is forhaving obstructed the footpath in Bridge-st. with some casks on the 6th June. LODGING-HOUSE KEEPERS IN TROUBLE. Elizabeth Thomason, 6, Morris-yard, off Silver-street, was charged with keeping lodgers without having her house regis- tered, on the 31st May. Defendant was fined 5s and costs.—George Rider. 26, Victoria-st., was charged with a similar offence on the same date. Mr. Church (inspec- tor), stated that there were ix the house, which was adapted for six persons, 5 of a family and? lodgers. De- fendant was fined 108 and costs.—John Briers, 16, Wil- liam-st.. was charged with a similar offence on the Same date. In this house, which was adapted for six, then were 4of the family and 5 lodgers. Defendant wasfined 10s and costa. Sellout. Arrsutblweit CLszs.—The following persons were fined for not sending their children regularly to school, Mr. George Riley prosecuting on behalf of the School Attendance Committee :—Edward Murray, forge- man, Winwick-st., sth time, ss; Thomas Rider, forge- man, Pierpoint-st., 2nd time, ss; Thomas Connolly, labourer, Gaskell-st., 2s 6d; William Higham, forgeman, Stamford-st., 2s 6d; Henry Bennett, tanner, Lythgoes- lane, ss; John Harrop, glass maker, Battersby-lane, ss; Peter Hankinson, tinker, Cropper's-brow, ss; Joseph Whitlow, butcher, Fennell-St., Se; Thomas Bate, Old- road, ss; William Syers, hawker, 55. WEDNESDAY.— Before Mr. John Fairclough, Alderman Chandley, and Mr. R. Garnett. CHILD DESERTION. John Quinn was charged with having deserted his child, who on the 24th ult. became chargeable to the common fund of the Union. It was stated that prisoner would do nothing towards support- ing his wife and family. He was sent to prison for a month.—Annie Higgins was charged with having de- serted her two children. As they had not been in the workhouse long, and as the case was not pressed, the magistrates dismissed the prisoner. Mr. B. Shearer prosecuted in lioth cases. Titentspe.Y.—Before Major Litton. DRUNKENNESS.--WilliaM Flattery, ironworker. 19, Beswick-st., was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in King-st. on Wednesday afternoon. It was his first appearance, and, as he received a good char- acter, he was discharged. FRlDAY.—Before Aldermen Harrison and Holmes. ALLEGED WIFE ASSAULT.—Robert Mullholland, Mersey- et., was brought up on a charge of having committed a breach of the peace by assaulting Mary Mullholland, his wife, on the afternoon previous. He was ordered to be bound over to be of good behaviour in two sureties of £lO each, and in his own recognisances of £lO. WILFUL DAMAGE.—A man named James Rowson was summoned for having damaged growing oats in a field belonging to Peter Winstanley, farmer, Orford. It was alleged that the defendant and others, who were cours- ing, went into the oatfield after a hare, and damaged the oats. The case was withdrawn on defendant promising not to repeat the offence, and to pay the costs of the case. ALLEGED OBSTRUCTION.—Thomas Broderick and Thos. Watson were summoned for having obstructed the foot- path in Church-place, on the 10th inst. As it appeared that the men moved away as soon as requested, the case was dismissed.

LYMM PETTY SESSIONS. FILIDLY.—Before Messrs. T. P. Norris (in the chair), W. Long, C. Lister, and H. Stanton. A REVENUE PROSECUTION.—Major E. P. Browne, of Portland House, Church Green, Lyrnm, was summoned for using armorial bearings without paying license, and also for using a carriage weighing more than 4 cwt., without paying the full duty for the same. Mr. Spencer, supervisor, Warrington, prosecuted on behalf of the in- land revenue authorities, and Mr. Addenbrooke, of Lymm, defended. Defendant pleaded guilty, and it was stated in his behalf that he had recently changed his carriage, and the coachbuilder told him the new one was no heavier than the old one, on which duty had been paid, but it turned out to be over six cwt. With regard to the armorial bearings, Major Browne had been under the impression that, being an officer in her Majesty's army, he was exempt from paying the tax. A fine of lOs and costs was imposed in regard to the carriage, and 20s and costs in respect of the armorial bearings. ASSAULT ON A BAILIFF.—Joseph Hurst, a powerful- looking man, living in Sandy-lane, Lymm, was charged with having assaulted William Burrows, a county court bailiff, whilst in the discharge of his duties, on the 22nd May. Mr. Longton, of Warrington, prosecuted. It appeared that on the day in question Burrows went to defendant's house to execute a warrant of the Warring- ton County Court in respect of a sum of 55 4d. At his house Hurst assaulted him without any provocation, and refused to pay the amount. The bailiff consequently took him into custody, and on their way to the station linrst again seriously assaulted him, and also a man named Gibbons, whom he called to his assistance, and afterwards escaped. Hurst's wife afterwards paid the 5s 4d, and consequently her husband was not taken to gaol.—Defendant pleaded guilty, and expressed sorrow for haying committed the assault, and stated that he was now in regular work on the Ship Canal—A fine of lOs and costs, 21s 641 in all, was imposed. Doo CAses.—The following persons were summoned for having allowed dogs to be at large unmuzzled con- trary to orders, viz.:—John Houghton, farmer, Thelwall; J. R. Tomlinson, Lymm; John Brierley, Lymm; Mary Ellen Rouse, Lymm; A. Bedell, Lymm; and Charles Pope. The Chairman said the bench were much opposed to the order under which those cases were brought, but they were obliged to impose a penalty, and therefore they would simply fine each defendant ss. including costs. BREACH or amE PEACE.—Thomas Brook, who claimed that he was the " quietest man in Lymm," was charged with committing a breach of the peace at Lymm on the 4th June.—The case was dismissed. Slot OF DITCH WATER.—An elderly man named Wm. Holt was charged with having, on the 15th May, unlaw- fully taken water belonging to the Lymm Water Co. It was stated that the well which supplies the house defen- dant lives in with water had been out of repair, and he consequently took some from the company's pipes.— Defendant said he had drunk ditch water for a week, • and was sick of it.—ln reply to Mr. Lister Mr. H. Cam- ' eron, who was present on behalf of the Water Company, said the Local Board did not compel the landlord of the house in question to supply company's water because ' the well water was supposed to be sufficiently good.—lt was further stated that the well had been repaired, and ; defendant was dismissed with a caution. ALLEGED LARCENY.—AIfred Leather and Jane Leather , were charged with having stolen several articles of clothing, the property of John Clare. It Appea.red that i the female defendant s a sister of Clare, and thirt there had been some dispute as to whom the articles in ques- tion had been left by their mother, who died recently.— The defendants were cautioned and discharged.

RTJNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MownAv.—Before Mr. John Brundrit, Mr. James Handley, and Mr. G. L. Davies. DRUNK.—Thomas Knight, Thomas Rogers, and Geo. Towey were each fined 6s and costs for drunkenness. ASTRAY.—For allowing his pony to stray in Mough- land-lane, on the 26th May, Peter Woods was fined 2s 6d and costs. A DISORDERLY CHAnecrEn.—Sarah Alice Clarke, an unfortunate, was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour for disorderly conduct. OBSTRUCTING THE FOOTPATH.—WiIIiam John Daven- port, John Cunliffe, and Joseph Floxworth, youths, pleaded guilty to having, on the evening of the Ist June, obstructed Regent-st. by loitering on the footpath.—P.C. 78 said there had been many complaints of this practice. —Davenport and Cunliffe were each fined 6d, and costs 2s 6d. Hoxworth, who had been previously fined for a like offence, was mulcted in the sum of 2s fia, and costs 8s 6d.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Mr. A. Thomas and Sir. G. L. Davies. BconAa.s.—John Boardman a tramp, was sentenced to seven days' hard labour fer begging in High-st. on the previous day.—Minnie Hyde. aged 22, who was stated to ,be a native of India, was also charged with begging. A stian named James Hyde stated that the prisoner was his brother's wife, and they were lodging in Mersey-st., only having been in the town two days.—The prisoner said that by nieans of a letter (produced) she had kept the witness, his wife and children, and herself. She promised to leave the town if she was discharged, and on this understanding she was liberated. The letter was retained. ALLEGED DISORDERLY CONDI:MT.—Louisa Spencer and Rachael Rawlinson were charged with disorderly beha- viour in Church-st. on Friday night.—lnspector O'Don- nell said he heard the prisoners using obscene language and causing a disturbance. The prisoners were dis- charged with a caution.—Thomas MeThomson, a sailor, was summoned for being drunk and disorderly, and at- tempting to rescue the two women mentioned above. It appeared that when the Inspector was dealing with the women the prisoner attacked him', and had to be sum- moned.—A fine of lOs and costs, 7s 411, was imposed. Diturac.—William Henry Wright was fined 10s and costs, or 14 days' hard labour, for being drunk and disorderly in Church-st.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. E. K. Muspratt, and Mr. H.
Wade Deacon.

TEMPORARY AUTHORITY to sell intoxicating liquors on the sports field, Farnworth, from 5 o'clock to half-past nine on Friday evening, and from noon to eight o'clock on Saturday was granted to John James Ramsey of the Sandfield Hotel, Walton on the Hill Liverpool. , '

COILING OF AGE CELEBRATIONS.—Mr. R. Herriman, of the Mersey Hotel, applied for permission to keep a por- tion of his house open on Monday, the 25th inst., beyond the stipulated time oti the occasion of a supper and ball being held there to celebrate the coming of age of Mr. J. ShtOebottom, of Gladstone-st. Mr. Herriman asked to keep open until six o'clock next morning.—The Bench granted permission for that portion of the house to be kept open until 3 a.m. on condition that no intoxicating liquor was sold after eleven o'clock.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued front page 6) WESTON. . The principal work carried on in this section is one of preparation. Piles continue to accumulate, and a num- ber of men are engaged in sheathing the pointed ends with iron ready for piercing the bed of the Mersey. The joiners and blacksmiths are kept in constant employ- ment. The Mersey Conservancy Board have withdrawn their interdict, and this week Mr. Weston's men have been busily engaged constructing the stage on the Fred- sham Marsh in the estuary of the Weaver, and in a few days the American, German, and French navvies will be landed, and the work of excavation on the Marsh com- menced in real earnest. The men in the employ of Mr. T. Kirkham have begun the erection of quite a colony of workmen's dwellings on the Marsh.

div.head: RUNCORN BRIDGE AND THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: RUNCORN BRIDGE AND THE SHIP CANAL.
(From "The Manchester Examiner and Times.")

Peering into the future, the artist presents Run- corn as it is to be. Dealing in "futures" is, ot course, a risky business, but we have a tolerable certainty t 'let the speculation in this case is pretty safe. The visionary element here is rather chas- tened than glowing. Our Ship Canal enthusiasts will think there is even a modesty in the picture; that more vessels should be steaming their way up the canal; that more tugs should be hauling up the sailing ships towards our docks at this end; that the cranes at work are absurdly insufficient. To such we may reply that these are the dreams of a more distant time than the artist has ventured to look forward to, lie presents the prose of two or three years hence, not the poetry of a further day. The time may come when the sunniest dream will be realised; when at Runcorn quays, as at Man- chester, vast warehouses will lift their heads, stored with the foodstuffs of the west or with the luscious fruit of the tropics; when the chips will come sailing home, here to our very doors, with the raw cotton of the Southern States, or the fibre of Surat, or precious crates with the fruit of a more generous soil. These things we are content to wait for. Meantime, let not ambition mock our more reasonable expectations. Our forecast is eminently safe; mechanically, we may say it is exact. The Ship Canal plans will give us this precise picture. The explanation necessary is not considerable. The standpoint is with Runcorn Bridge to the left, and the tall sombre chimneys of Widnes rising opposite. The bridge remains untouched. The foresight of the harbour authorities and traders of a quarter of a century ago gave it us at a lofty elevation, which permits the passage of big ships. The big ships have been absent all this time, and it is the Ship Canal which at last is to give reality to the vague hopes which were in the air twenty-five years ago. The course of the canal will be plainly seen in the picture. A hundred and fifty feet away from the Cheshire or Runcorn bank of the river is a river wall or embankment, coming from a point some distance above the town, and exactly halving the left-hand span of the bridge. Between this embankment and the shore is the line of the canal. If we could see a little further to the right we should find the present Runcorn and Latchford Canal, with an elaborate trystera of locks dropping into the Mersey, and ex- tensive quays. At first a rival to the Bridgewater, but subsequently a feeder to that waterway; now it belongs to the Ship Canal Company, and its channel is to form part of the wider trench which is to con- nect us with the sea. If we could trace further the line of river wall, beyond the Runcorn Bridge, we should pass by the Bridgewater Docks jut below, the Weaver Navigation Docks at Weston Point, and then, taking a bold sweep across the mouth of the Weaver, should re-enter the land at the upper end of the Cheshire marshes, known as Frodsham Score. For the remaining ten miles the canal runs in a straight line, partly skirting the Mersey, and partly, in the way already described, forming part of the estuary. The picture may be taken as a very ade- quate representation of the section of the canal to be built out of the estuary at Runcorn. On the near side of the river wall is the placid, unfretted chan- nel of our new waterway, stolen, as it were, at this point from the noble but useless seaway; on the •other side the Mersey will still continue to rise and fall as the tide ebbs and flows; a glorious sheet at high tide, but a waste of sand and mud, devided by tiny streams, when the current passes down to the sea. Or, to put the case differently, on one side of the wall we have a great channel which is simply • useless, and on the other a conlparatively narrow way which will bring rich freights from the sea 30 miles inland.

LORD BRASSES/ AND THE EDDISBURE LIBERALS. —Lord Brassey has accepted the presidency of the Eddisbury Liberal Association, and has sent a dona- tion of £2O towards the funds. At a meeting .held a few days ago it was stated that the association was in debt to the ext.mt of £BO, and an amount was subscribed in the room which, with the donation of Lord Brassey and a sirailar one from Mr. James Tomkinson, was sufficient to wipe off the debt.

_ THE HOME InoN TRADE.—The English iron mar- ket is getting steadier, its tone having somewhat improved during the past week. There is a fair business generally, and prices are firmer. The bet- tbr tendency in the Glasgow warrant market, which began to show itself last week, has continued dur- ing the present week, and this movement has in- fluenced Scotch makers' quotations' which are about 6d a ton higher. Cleveland iron has also gone up, to the extent of another 3d a ton, and is now quoted at 31s 6d. Although trade in pig-iron is quiet in Lancashire, prices are firmer. Bessemer iron is stronger, and is a ton higher in the north- west, being now quoted 43s for mixed parcels. Manufactured iron remains steady on the whole, even in the north of England, where the disturbed state in the shipbuilding trade still continues.— Iron. COOKERY LECTBRES.—We take the following from South Banbury Parish Magazine :—" Miss Beswick, as announced in our last number, gave three letters on plain cooking. We are sorry that the very class for whom these lectures were pro- Tided, the working mothers, were conspicuous by their absence. We hope this may have arisen from the time of year; we trust it does not show that the wives of the working-men of Banbury do not care to know how to make the best ot small means, nor to improve the cooking in their homes. Much -valuable information was attained by those who did attend, and we hope that in many homes the fruits of the work of the Banbury Central School of Cookery may show themselves in increased com- forts." Miss Beswick is the daughter of Mr. W. Beswick, Arley, Cheshire. She was trained as a teacher at Arley School, but, after being at college, she became attached to the staff of the Liverpool School of Cookery, and is now one of their recog- nised teachers and lecturers. She has been at Ban- bury about six months; and, previous to that, gave a series of lectures at Hyde on cookery. ELF:critic BELLS.—Garland. Bell Hanger, Bridge-st., War- vington.—Advt. div.p: RUNCORN.

Operations here are still confined to the work of exca- vation, and this is being carried on with the energy that has characterised the proceedings from the commence- ment. In five weeks there will be a "big ditch" as far as the Old Quay Canal, and then the task of still further deepening the cutting will be undertaken. So far as present appearances go there is no intention of grap- pling in the immediate future with the great engmeer- ing difficulties which face the contractor in the estuary. There is nothing of a novel character to report, and it is satisfactory that there is an entire absence of accidents at present. Mr. Walker has inspected the section during the present week. LYMM AND TIIELSVALL.

At Statham the -S-te-anTn—av;;;:—WhiCir—li.as been on the ground for some weeks past has now got to work, and is rapidly displacing the soil. The bridge over Statham- lane is now complete, and another is being erected "o pass over head. The laying out of the new brickrield is being carried forward vigorously, arches for brick drying being in course of erection. At Thelwall the "American" steam navvies are kept hard at work, that in front of Morris Brook Farmhouse, in particular, doing great exe- cution upon the yielding subsoil. This navvy, although the latest of the trio at work, has already excavated for itself a deep cutting in which it is almost hidden from the view of people standing on Thelwall-lane, only a few yards away. The "Jubilee" navvy does not seem to have been equal to the work required of it, and during the week it has been taken to pieces, and for the most part taken from the ground...,

div.head: ECCLES AND BARTON.
div.p: ECCLES AND BARTON.

I Nearly a thousand hands are now employed on the section between Weaste and Stickin's Island, under the engineering control of Mr. Bourke. The negotiations for the purchase of land in the Flixton and Irlam section below Stickin's Island have, as a whole, been brought to a conclusion, for the contractor has at last got posses- sion, and begun to "break it up," but as yet not many men can be engaged. Mr. W. 0. Meade King is the Ship Canal Company's cnzineer in charge of the Irlam section, which extends on the Manchester side up to Sticken's Island. At the latter place the activity in- creases, and vast quantities of earth have been moved, but only a tithe of what has yet to be effected by the hundreds of spadesmen and by the French steam navvy. It has not yet been determined whether the Frenchnavvy is capable of executing as much labour as the inventor claims for it, but the visitor is certainly full of admira- tion for it. The rock is being moved in large quantities in the Irwell Valley close to Eccles, by blasting. Work night and day is continued on Sticken's Island. THE FATAL ACCIDENT AT BARTON.

Yesterday week, Mr. F. Price, coroner, held an Inquiry at Barton, concerning the death of Harry Mitchell, aged 21, residing at 218, Park-st Patricroft, who was killed at the Ship Canal Works, Barton, on the Wednesday at- ternoon previous. On the afternoon in question about forty men left the yard in a train of four waggons and an engine near the Rock House Inn, at flirt' minutes to one, for Sticken's Island. Before starting witness warned the men not to sit on the end of the waggors, as there had been a man killed at Eastham doing the same thing. In reply he heard somebody swearing. The men should have sat at the bottom of the waggons. When at the , end of their journey he found tiler were short a men. , A return ,journey was then made,, by about a score of men, deceased and witness antongst the rannber They had got about 500 yards when thewagons coming down the incline overtook the engine, which had shut off steam. Deceased, who had nothing to hold on by, was jerked backwards. Witness shouted to the driver to stop, and he went to the deceased, who was lying face downwards across one of the rails, witlehis head inside the four-foot. He was alive an,d witness raised him but he gasped two or three. times and died—At the close ef the inquest attention was caned to the necessity for a public- mortuary.— Mr. Nott, who appeared Roy the canal contractor, said so far as the contractor was concerned, he ought to state thkt it was their intention to provide mortuaries for the reception of those fatally injured in the words during the construction of the canal at Bartbn, Cadis- head, and other important centres on the. line of the canal. Wonld the Coroner consider they were justified in detaining the body P—The Coroner said net after the police signified their intention to remove it.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

SALFORD AND STRETPoRD BOUNDARY: On Thursday evening, at a meeting of the ratepayers of Stretford, held in the Town Hall, Chester-road; Mr.' S. Rasa (one of the overseers of the township) presiding, it was resolve,/ "That the overseers of the township of Stretford he and are hereby empowered to take such steps as my be necessary for opposing in Parliament that part of the Manchester Ship Canal (No. 1888,. which proposes to alter the township's boundary, ana thereby tatrarasfer to Salford a valuable portion of the- rating area of Stretford, and that the expenrve of such opposition (including the preliminary expenses already incurred). be paid out of the poor rate." The Chairmary characterised the action of the. Salford Corporation in proposing the alteration in the boundary whiela would cede ratalle property to the annual value of £BOO front, the Stretford township, in return for agrimitural land which would yield only about ZB, as land grabbing, and such as ought to be strenuously opposed.

div.head: WIDNES ATHLETIC CLUB SPORTS.
div.p: WIDNES ATHLETIC CLUB SPORTS.

The 21st annual festival of the Widnes Athletic Club was commenced last evening in the Sports Field, Farnworth. The arrangements were con- ceived and carried out in the usual thorough and efficient manner, but unfortunately the success of the sports was considerably-militated against by the unpropitious weather. A very dull sky and a cold wind were disagreeable element e in the evening's 'amusement; happily the threatened rain did not descend.. There were about one thousand spectators present. Last night's events were of merely local interest, as the competitions. were confined to athletes residing within the district of Widnes. To-day numerous valuable Prizes are offered forcompetition by amateur athletes of 'whatever nationality, and the ath- letes who have recently arrived in this country from America have entered for several of the events. Mr. Walter Platt discharged the onerous duties of handi- capper. official timekeeper, and reieree, while Mr. T. Wilkinson, of Sheffield, officiated as starter. The judges were Messrs. F. H. Gossage, and C. E. Barlow (Widnes A .C.), and Messrs. Abraham and Ramsdale (N.C.C.A.). The office of secretary was ably filled by Mx. J. W. Davies. Results:— 120 YARDS FLAT RACE.—,lst prize, case of silver-mounted carvers, value £5 ss; 2ttd, art gold bronze inkstand; 3rd. tankard. Run in five heats, the winners being G. Hartland, Widnes F.C. (5) ; W. Jones, Runcorn P.O. (I) ; W. Dean, Huvton Quarry P.C. (8) ; J. Worml, Warrington (4) ; and A. 6. Pearce, Warrington. Final : 1, Pearce; 2, W. Dean; 3, G. Hartland. Two MILES BICYCLE RACE ILaNnmaP.—There were nine entries, and lour competed. Ist prize, 11. Allen, Warrington (scratch) ; 2nd. R. G. Garnett, Warrington (scratch) ; 3rd, J. B. Webster, Warrington (49 yards) ; R. Ttirton , Widnes (250 yards). The race virtually lay between the two first placed. Allen, playing a waiting game, went up to Webster In the last lap, and, going the stronger, won by about SIX yards.

TUG OF WAR.—The final in this event will be decided to- day by two teams of six men in the employ of the Widnes Alkali Company, who respectively defeated teams from the works of Messrs. N. Mathieson and Co., Messrs. John Hut- chinson and Co., and Messrs. Thomas Snape and Co. The first prize is six sets of knives and forks, and the second six copper kettles. ONE MILE FLAT RACE BANDICAP.—Iet !prize (silver watch value £5 10s), J. Kelly, Widnes Harriers (35 yards) : 2nd (marble clock), E. Gordon, Widnes P.C. (55 yards) 3rd (flask), W. Woods, Runcorn (75 yards.) The largest field of the evening turned out for this event, there being 14 contes- tants. When about two laps were to be run. Gordon rushed to the front, and took a long lead, followed by Kelly and Moores. Coming in the straight Gordon appeared done up, and was passed by Kelly, who won by about five yards. Afterwards Gordon was called before the judges to explain his running, but the result of the interview has not trans- pired. QUARTER-MILE FLAT RACE HANDICAP.—Iet (silver cup, presented by Mr. F. H. Gossage, Esq. J.P.), W. Kershaw, Widnes C.C. (30 yards); 2nd, (silver-plated biscuit box), F. Franklin, Widnes Harriers (23 yards) ; 3rd (sugar basket and sifter), F. Wright, Widnes F.C. (23 yards). This was thebest- contested race of the evening, and Kershaw scored a very popular victory by about four yards.

div.head: MARRIAGE AT ALTRINCHAM OF A RUNCORN LADY.
div.p: MARRIAGE AT ALTRINCHAM OF A RUNCORN LADY.

The marriage of Miss Agnes Walker Speaktnan, daughter of the late Mr. David Speakman, of Run- corn, and sister of the celebrated football player, Mr. H. C. Speakman, who has earned Celebrity in New Zealand and Australia by his splendid play with the team which recently went over there from Xngland, took place at Is roadheath on Saturday. The bride was married frora the house of Mr. Green, of the Bridgewater trustees, where she had lived for 14 years, the wedding breakfast being provided by Mr. and Mrs. Green, who did all they could to show their high appreciation of and friendship for the bride. Additional interest was taken in the event , owing to the bridegroom, Mr. W. Carr, of Liverpool, being the nephew of Mr. Eccles, warehouseman at the Ship Canal warehouse, Rroadheath. The mar- riage took place at St. George's Church, before a large congregation, and was celebrated by the Rev. J. W. Challoner, the bride being given away by her younger brother, Mr. David Speakman, Miss Eccles acting as bridesmaid, and Mr. Martin as best man. During the breakfast which followed, Mr, A. E. Green, in a few appropriate words presented a purse of gold to the bride, which had been contri- buted by Mr. and Mrs. Green and family as a token of their high appreciation and friendship, and Mr. Green proposed the health of the bride and bride- groom, which was drunk with enthusiasm, Mr. Carr replying in a very neat speech, expressing his pleasure at the kindly feeling displayed.

div.head: FRODSH AM.
div.p: FRODSH AM.

ANNIVIIRSARY •SERVICES.—On Sunday afternoon and evening sermons were preached lb the Wesleyan Chapel, Helsby. by the Rev. Thomas Baines, of St. Helens. The collections received at these services and the service held on Wednesday evening, when the Rev. Charles Garrett preached, amounted to the sum of £lB 15s 100. Citeacn MISSIONARY SOCIETY.—On Sunday, two ser- mons were preached in the Parish Church, Frodsham, in aid of the above society, by the Rev. J. E. Padfield, mis- sionary from India; and on Monday evening the annual meeting was held in the Town Hall, when the Rev. 11. B. Blogg, vicar, presided. The Rev. M. Harclinge, vicar of Barrow, ,and the Rev. J. E. Padfield, attended as a deputation. The Chairman, in opening the meeting, referred briefly to the report which he had received from the secretary of the Frodsham district as to the amounts which had been received during the year ended 31st December last, and on comparing this report with the one for the previous year, he was glad to find a small increase in the receipts. The. Rev. M. Hardinge said it gave him great pleasure to engage in any missionary work. He considered the best way of keeping up an in- terestin missionary work was by reading the missionary reports and periodicals. Rev. .1. E. Padfield stated that he quite agreed with the chairman that k was a great honourto be allowed to be workers in the propagation of the Gospel amongst far off nations. He referred to the various branches of labour in which he had been engaged whilst in India. and urged upon his bearers the necessity of making a special petition every Sabbath day that God would so.pour out his spirit on all the meuebers of the church, whether at home or abroad. Mr. R. Foulkes, Frodshana+ here asked permission to say a. few words with regard to the Rocnish doings et several of the vice- presidents of the Church Missionary Society,. &c., but owing to the lateness of thehour, the chairman could not see his wary clear to grant Mr. Foulkes the requisite per- mission. Dr. Weaver thereupon moved a hearty vote of thanks to the chairman and deputation for their excel- lent addresses. which was carried unanimously,, and the meeting mane to a close directly afterwards.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly' 722-eeting7:4;;;;lield--aTt:-Che Town Hall on Tuesday. Mr. F. H.. Gossage presided, and there were present Messrs. Carey, Wright, Brown, Cook, Heyes, Taylor, Gaskell, W. W. Gossage. Houghton, Handley, Ji T. Allen (clerk), T: Higginson (sur- veyor), and di Dickson (inspector). THZ LOCAL.GOYERNMBITD BILL. •

Mr. Handley reported that in accordance with a reso- lution of the Board Dr. O'Keeffe and himself attended a deputation, from Lancasfdre to Mr. Ritchie, President of the Local Government Beard,in Loudon,on the previous Tuesday, with regard to the Local Government Bill. The deputation consisted of magistrates, and the repre- sentatives of 42 local boards, 31 unions.and 1/boroughs, r and Mr. Ritchie appeared to be muchimpressed by the large representation of the various industries of Lanca- shire. Six llghtred Kay-Shuttleworth3 M.P. spoke on behalf of the deputation, and it was stated that the rate- able valuoof Lancashire was 18 millions. The rateable value of the 11 boroughs that were to be' made into county boroughs was over 9 millions, and the mainten- ance of county roads cost £Bl,OOO a year. These 11 boroughs had only 38 miles of main road, which cost £l2,ooota year, and, the other parts of the county had 564 miles of main road, which cost £89,000 a year. Sir Ughtred Kay-Shuttleworth armed that the cost should be equalised between, the boroughs and the,copnty. If the wheel and van tax, and the other taxes that were to be transferred, were to be divided between the county and the boroughs according to the rateable value, it mcould be most unjust to the county. The best plan would be to distribute the taxes according to the mileage of the roads. He believed that Sir ff. K. Shuttleworth had given notice of an amend- ment to the bill with a view to carrying out this idea. In Parliament, on Friday, Mr. Ritchie referred to the deputation he had received from Lancashire, and said he had decided to appoint a. small commission to go into the mater, so that it showed that the interview had a very good effect. He (Mr. Handley) proposed that the clerk be instructed to write to the member for the Widnes Division (Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss), and -ask him to support Sir U. K. Shuttleworth's amendment, and to watch the bill very narrowly, because it was manifest to all of them that if those eleven boroughs got half of the Government taxes that were to be transferred it would be very unjust.—Mr. Gaskell seconded the motion,which was carried unanimously.

A Jotter was read from the Local Government Board with reference to the apprehended risk of pollution to which the water at the Widnes Local Board's Netherlev pumving station is liable, owing to the proximity of the

outfall sewer from the sewage farm of the Huyton-with- Roby Local Board. The locality had been visited by one of their inspectors, and they were now advised as a re- sult of his investigations that there is no reason at pre- sent to believe that the water in the well would be pol- luted by sewage matter from the outfall pipe in question. —Mr. Wright remarked that he was present at the inspection. The Huyton people said they would do their best to avoid causing any nuisance.

dAS AND WATBR COMMITTEE.—TnE YEAR'S PROFITS.— _ ENGINEER'S SALARY INCREASED.

The minutes of the Gas and Water Committee con- tained the report of the engineer, who stated that the mean rainfall for the month was .415 inches. The water in stock was 9,396,033 gallons. The illuminating power , of the gas during the month had averaged 17'59 candles. Mr. A. Norman Tate certified that he had tested the gas on the 11th ult. and found it to be equal to 18.05 can- dles, and free from sulphuretted hydrogen. A statement W 55 submitted for year. ending 25th March, 1888, show- ing a profit of £968 9s 81 on water account, and £1,719 I.os 10d oregas account. It was recommended that the price of water for meter be reduced 10 percent. from the Ist July, and that the price of a domestic supply be based upon 5 per cent, of the rateable value. It was also recommended that the price of gas from the Ist July next be as follows :—To consumers within the limits of 1867 Act—Below 3,000,000 cubic feet per an- num, 2s 3d per 1,000 cubic feet; 5,000,000 cubic feet and over per annum, 2s id per 1,000 cubic feet; to con- sumers beyond the limits of 1867 Act, a reduction of 3d per 1,000 cubic feet; all subject to a discount of 3d per. 1,000 cubic feet. For public lamps the charges would be Brays £4, and ordinary £1 12s per annum. It was further recommended that the salary of Mr. Carr, gas and water engineer, be increased fmm £3OO to £4OO per annum.—Mr. Haskell, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the reduction in the price of water for domestic use was equal to lot per cent.. Alluding to the profit made, Mr. Haskell said the figures hardly showed the correct posi- tion. In connection with both gas and water there had been a great deal of extraordinary expenditure in im- provements, which had resulted in increased efficiency. and increased production. Taking into consideration the probable increase in consumption during the current year, the committee anticipated that upon waiter they wourd'have an availablerprnflt of £2,500, and upon gas Of about £2,000. Therefore' they proposed the reduction in price. They must bearin mind that a great deal of the success was due to the engineer, Mr. Carr, who came to the works in 1882, at a very difficult period of their history.. There was a fear of a scarcity of water, and by his recommendation alterations had been made to the engines at Stocks Well and Netherley, which had re- suited in doubling the water-supply. If they had gone on charging their 1882 price forges at the present time, the consumers would have paid £0954 more than they did under the present price, and the water consumers would have paid £4,343 per annum more than they did under the price now suggested. These two sums amount to £11,297, which the gas, and war consumers had kept in their pockets: Mr. Haskell referred in detail to improve- ments intrcduced by Mr. Carr.—Mr. Brown secondeft the proposition, and pointed out that a cottager could now have gas put into his house and have a gas burning fin four hours per day at a cost, including rent of meter, of 3d per week. He did not think oil, taking into account the breakages- of glass and the r;sk of fire, could com- pare with it. He pointed out that-Mr. Carr's salary was much below the average of such- towns as Warrington, Burnley, Macclesfield, Wigan, Burr-, &c., and spoke in terms of prarse of M!. Carr's ability and energy.—Mr. Wright said that during the six years he had been with the Board Mir. Carr had had his salary increased on two occasions, each time of £5O, and now it was proposed to increase his salary by a further amount of £lOO. He- would not say anything against Mr_ Carr as a man, or about his ability, but he objected to salaries being in- creased at this rate.—Mr. Cook supported the recor.a- mendation, and said when they bad a good servant they ought te pay him well.—The minutes were adopted,— Mr. Wright did not vote.

div.head: HIGHWAY MATTRYLS.
div.p: HIGHWAY MATTRYLS.

The Highway Committee recommended that the cros- sings in Lugsdale-road, at junctions of Major Cross-st., Wareing-st., and Sutton's-lane be • paved with six inch cube setts. That tenders be obtained for asphalting the footwalk in Lugsdale-road from Major Cross-st. to Sut- ton's-lane, and from the Presbytery, to Lugsdale That the surveyor prepare estimates, &c., for a portable tank for flushing sewers.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Taylor. 1 commtvrvx. The Medical Officer of Health reported to this commit- tee that during May there were 39 births and 43 deaths, being at the respective rates of 33-6 and 16-6 per 1,000. Fourteen deaths occurred amongst children under nne year, and fwar amongst children between one and five years. There had been one death from phtlaisis follbw- mg typhoid fever; the person was a discharged patient from the Infectious Diseases Hospital.—The Nuisance' Inspector reported that there had been one case of scar- let fever: the patient was now convalescent and notur- ther case had occurred in the same house, whichihad been disinfected. The receipts at the market for- the month amounted to £57 2s 3d,. being an increase or£l7 us 2d, as compared with May, 1887.—Mr. Carey, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the nuisance inspector•had visited Rainhill Sewage Farm, axtcb there was no complaint to make-at the present time. With regard to- the removal of nightsoil in Widnes arrange- ments had been made by which the work of the-contrac- tor should be inspected each morning. The committee hoped that this would result in greater efficiency.
FINANCE:

The• Finance Committee. recommended that £l,OOO gas accost and £5OO water account be used to repay loans. Accounts amounting to, £8,528 6s 10d were passed for paynxent.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Mx. Handley.
THE 5.1.07t/AL INSPECTION.

The annual inspection was fixed to I:ake place on the 28th inst. The Board went into committee to consider the amount paid for extras for Warrinetonrroad sewer, and the terms for easement through Widnes Marsh for the Moos Bank sewer,

div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD

The monthly meeting of the above-named Board was held at the Cemetery Lodge on Wednesday. afternoon. There were present Messrs. W. 11. Rogerson (chairman), ,J. Liandley, S. Taylor, IL Morris, W. Littler, IL Coleburn, and W.F. Salkeld (secretary,),--Mr. Handley stated that the Finance Com- mittee had met that day. The fees received during the past two months amounted to 4.50 H 12a Eld, which, with £8 14s 9d rent of Held, made the total receipts £59 Ts 3d. The wages paid during the same period amounted to £2.1 10s, leaving a balance of £37 17s 3d, which had been placed in the bank. Accounts amounting to £l9 13s ed were passed and recommended for payment. He pro- posed the adoptiori of the minutes,which wereconerined,

—The Chairman stated that Mr. John Simpson had spoken to him a week or two ago, and had asked him whether he thought the Board would take into considera- tion the desirability of reducing the fees for interments chargeable to persons who resided outside the town, which were double those charged to residents inßuncorn. Mr. Coleburn was of opinion that no alteration could be made without the consent of the Secretary of State.—Mr. Handley said there were difficulties in the way of lower- ing the fees. Weston was a township which did not con- tribute in any way to the cemetery, and the expenses were at present heavy, and in years te come would pro- bably be heavier, as there would be the question of the drainage of the new land, which would be a serious ex- pense. It had, however, struck him that single fees might be charged for the minister and sexton.—Mr. Lit- tler did not think the Board was justified in chargieg double fees for the minister and sexton.—Mr. Taylor said the cemetery had been a burden on the ratepayers of the town ever since it had been made, and outsiders had the facility for burying there. In justice to the rate- payers of the town he did not think outsiders should be placed on the same footing as the ratepayers of Runcorn. So far as the minister and grave-digger were concerned they did no more work for outsiders than for townspeople. —Mr. Coleburn said that when it was contemplated to ;Italie the cemetery: the townships of Halton and Weston were both consulted, but tney refused to join Runcorn, er they would have come in for single fees. If they re- lieved the township of Weston they would saddle the ratepayers of Runcorn to an additional extent.— On the proposition of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Handley, it was decided to refer the matter to the Finance Committee.—lt was shown that the interments for the past two months had been 52, as compared with 37 in corresponding period last year, showing an increase of 15, and the amount received for fees £4B 2s 6cl, as against £39 14s 6d, an increase of £8 Cs 6d.—lt was decided to call a meeting to appoint three persons to fill the vacan- cies on the Board caused by the retirement of Messrs. Wm. Whittaker, W. Mellor, and E. brawn, who go out of office by rotation, all of whom are eligible for re-elec- tion.—The Secretary was instructed to write to Mr. John Wilson calling his attention to the damage done to shrubs and flowers in the cemetery by the smoke from his brickkiln.—This was the whole of the business.
LATEST NEWS.
At Wolverhampton on Friday a prJvision dealer named Bayliss was fined £5 and costs for selling American lard adulterated to the extent of 34 per cent with Cotton- seed oil.

A warder named Daly has been dismissed from Sligo poi by order of the General Prisons Board for having al- lowed prohibited articles in possession of Mr. David Sheehy, M.P. who was sentenced to six weeks' im- prisonment in Sligo gaol. Tire AYR ELECTION.—The Hon. Evelyn Ashley, Liberal Unionist, and Captain Sinclair, Crladstonian Liberal, were nominated at Ayr, on Saturday, as candidates for the vacancy in the representation of Ayr Burghs. , The polling took place yesterday. There are 5,449 electors on the register. The result will bedeclared about three p.m. to-day (Saturday.) A FISHING Boer firm Down.—About midnight on , Thursday a steamer ran down a fishing-boat off Pater- noster Rocks, near Jersey. and notwithstanding the cries of the crew proceeded on her way. The boat contained three men—Jblin Barrett, Douglas Barrett, and Cle- ment Duquesne—who were all drowned. Several fishermen nearby saw the collision, but could not find the victims. KILLED BY LDISEITNING.— Information reached Edin- burgh on Friday that during a thundenitorm which pre- vailed for several hours at Elawick an extraordinary fatality occurred. Whilst a ploughman at tiewhe Mains Farm was ploughing with two horses he and his team were struck by lightning. The ploughman himself and both animals were killed instanteously. The man was 29 3,earsof age, and married. ANOTHER LIBEL ON MR GLADSTONE. Mr. Job Bone having published a letter in Glasgow alleging he had seen a private letter from Mr. Gladstone on the licensing question opposed to his public utterances. Mr. Gladstone replies Mr. Bone can have seen no such letter as he describes, for no such letter exists. His charge is grossly untrue. My declarations and acts are in harmony with one another. lam not aware of having written a sin- gle letter, on subject of the licensing under sealof pri- vacy." ,

THE " TIMES " LIBEL ACTION. - The ArronNer- GENERAL, replying to a question, declined to give any information on the subject of The approaching trial of an action for libel against the "Times " from which either direct or indirect statements could be drawn.
THE NATIONM. DEBT Supplemeatary Bill was read a third time.

• THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.---The House then went into committee on the Local Giovemment Bill, clause 3 being under consideration. It contained provisions for transferring to county councils the administrative business of quarter sessions.—Sir W. Lewsox moved an amendment providing that the preparation and revision of basis or standard, for county rate should be the basis of standard of all rates levialtie in the country.—Mr. Rrrexia explained that it was at first intended to make the valuation of all rates uniform, but at the s last moment it had been sounl impossible to deal with the matter satisfactorily in the present *bill. He hoped .to be able to deal with the subject aseparate. bill on another occasion.—Mter discussion, the amend- meat was withdrawn, and the words, "the preparation and revision of a basis or standard for the county rater;' were introduced in the statement of the duties of the Councits.—Mr. HENEAGE prop osed that the appointment, control, and dismissal of chiet constables, and the management of the police, should be vested in County Counells.—Sir W. BARTELLOT considered that the.eon- trol of the police should be left in the hands of the rsagis- trates, and Sir W. Fons Tan wished to place the police under the control of representatfves of the ratepaTers.— Mr. GLADSTONE thought that they might trust the popu- llar elected body with the administration of law and order. Ile had no mistrust of anybody in thtt matter. He was far from thinking that magistrates misused their ' powers over the police, but he thought the plan proposed ' more acceptable, more conservative, more in, accordance with the ancient usages of the country, and more expe- dient. He readily supported the arriendasent. They were about' to create new.bodies for county government,, and they could only invest them with dignity by giving, them powers of public importance—After further discussion the amendment was rejected by 2e4 to 218 votes. THE Noirrn SEA F[SHERIES BILL, was read a third time.

THE CASE OF Mn. TAYLOIL—Sir R.. lanninman moved that a select committee be appointed to inquire into the, case of Mr. William Taylor, late Commissioner at Putaa,, who had been dismissed from that post 31 years ago for conduct which, in the opinion a the House, saved a great province from the horrors of the Indian mutiny. No real inquiry had ever taken place, and an investiga- tion was necessary.—Sir Lt. HAVELOCK AtEEN seconded the amendment, and bore personal testimony to Yr. Taylor's wisdom during the mutiny. • DRESCOT UNION.—CONTRACTS FOR PROVISIONS, &c.—Persons desirous of contracting with the Guardians of this Union, for the next six months, for supplying *it the Workhouse the several articles hereinafter named, viz., flour, oatmeal, salt, butter, cheese, eggs, groceries, wine and spirits, coal, burgy, linen and woollen drapery, ironmongery, earthen- ware, leather, brushes, coffins, and other articles, are requested to deliver sealed tenders, upon forms to be obtained at my office, at the Board-room of the said Union, in Whiston, on or before Thursday, the 21st June, before 10 a.m. Such tenders will be opened at the meeting of the Guardians on the last- named day, The Guardians will also take tenders for new milk and fresh butter for twelve months. Samples of wiper- ishable articles required may be seen at the Workhouse. Security will be required for the performarice of the contracts. The Guardians do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any tender.—By order of the Board? S. H. HARTLEY, Union Clerk. Union Offices, Whistdo, Prescot, 7th June, 1828.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. John Brock and Mr. H. Wade Deacon. I DEUNKENNESS.—A fine of Ss and costs was imposed upon each of the following persons :—Ann Shea, Sutton- lane; Sarah Jervis, Water-st. ; Joseph Shaw, no resi- dence; John Konaghan, Catherine-st. ; Joseph Harrison, Helena-st. ; John Fitzharris, 53, Victoria-st. ; Thomas Walsh, no residence, and Michael Byrne, of Golborne. Michael Mannion' of Warrington-road, was fined 7s 6d and costs—John Keogh, of 36, Milton-road, was charged with being drunk upon the premises of James Chapman, Grosvenor Hotel, on Saturday night, and he was fined 5s and costs. V.i.ouvas.—John Murphy, a tramp, was charged with being drunk and begging, in Victoria-road. P.C. Dean stated that the prisoner went into a number of shops and when he did not receive anything he used most abusive language to the inmates—He was sent to gaol for a month.—James Molynea.ux, of no residence, was sen- tenced to seven days' hard labour, for sleeping in a pig- stye. ' PETTY LAIICENY.—Mary Ann Sullivan, an old offender, was brought up on remand charged with having on f!itit- urday, the 2nd June, stolen a• crab from the shop of James McCririe Victona-road, and also a yiew of beef from the shop of Esther Singleton, butcher, Victoria-rd. She was committed to the Se.ssions for trial.—Ann Bes- wick, of Sankey-st., was charged with stealing coal, value Id, from the works of Messrs. Hutchinson & Co. The woman pleaded guilty, and she was fined 10s, or in default, 7 days' hard labour.—John Hushes and John Harrison, boys, 12 years of age, who reside with their parents in Widnes, were charged with stealing from some waggons in the yard of Messrs. Hutchinson & Co., a quantity of rope worth is 3d. The boys were caught in the act by P.C. Richardson, and were each fined ss. TuEsmtv.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage. DittrxxxxxEss.—Thomas Sumner, 17, Halton View; Mary Hale, 4, High-st. ; and Ann Walker, of Pear-st., were each fined 5s and costs for drunkenness.
